content:
Change feed (CDC) # GET /_changes serves a collection’s change log tail from the shard engines’ WALs, so external systems can replicate Pizza data elsewhere — off-site disaster recovery, secondary indexing, audit pipelines — with a standard poll loop:
GET /demo:orders/_changes?since=abc:3,def:1&limit=1000 { "results": [ {"shard":"abc…","rolling_id":0,"epoch_id":4,"seq":0, "id":"0,7","key":"u1","op":"create","doc":{"qty":3}}, {"shard":"abc…","rolling_id":0,"epoch_id":4,"seq":1, "id":"0,8","op":"delete"} ], "cursors": {"abc…": 4, "def…": 1}, "purged_below": {"abc…": 3}, "active": {"abc…": 5}, "pending": true } Request # GET /_changes GET /<targets>/_changes Path parameters # targets (Optional, string) Comma-separated collection names (wildcard supported); the target-less form feeds every collection. Query parameters # since (Optional, string) Per-shard epoch cursors from a previous response, shard_hex:epoch,shard_hex:epoch. Omit to start from the beginning of the retained tail. limit (Optional, integer) Maximum rows to return. Defaults to 1000. Consuming the feed # Poll with the cursors of the previous response as the next since (persist the cursors — they are the checkpoint). pending: true means more rows exist beyond limit; poll again immediately, otherwise poll at your cadence. Compare each cursor against purged_below: a cursor below that floor means the WAL retention window (wal.local.retention_epoch / retention_bytes) has already purged part of the tail for that shard. The tail is incomplete — run a full resync (search + re-bulk into the DR cluster) and resume from the current cursors. graph TD P("poll — since = the cursors you saved") --> R["rows + new cursors"] R -->|"pending: true — rows remain past limit"| P R --> C{"every cursor at or abovepurged_below?"} C -->|"yes — the tail is complete"| W["persist the cursors,poll again at your cadence"] C -->|"no — retention already purgedpart of the tail"| X["full resync: search + re-bulk,resume from the current cursors"] Every write path (index/replace/update/delete) appends a WAL entry on the primary and every replica, so the feed reads from whichever copy of the shard group is allocated to the node serving the request (primary preferred).
title: Change feed (CDC)

content:
Batch document operation # Provides a efficient way to perform multiple index, create, delete, and update operations in a single request.
Examples # POST /_bulk { "index" : { "_index" : "test", "_id" : "1" } } { "field1" : "value1" } { "delete" : { "_index" : "test", "_id" : "2" } } { "create" : { "_index" : "test", "_id" : "3" } } { "field1" : "value3" } { "update" : {"_id" : "1", "_index" : "test"} } { "doc" : {"field2" : "value2"} } The API returns the following result:
{ "took": 30, "errors": false, "items": [ { "index": { "_collection": "default:test", "_id": "0,0", "result": "created", ... } }, { "delete": { "_collection": "default:test", "_id": "0,1", "result": "not_found", ... } }, { "create": { "_collection": "default:test", "_id": "0,2", "result": "created", ... } }, { "update": { "_collection": "default:test", "_id": "0,0", "result": "updated", ... } } ] } Request # POST /_bulk POST /<target>/_bulk Path parameters # <target> (Optional, string) Name of the collection to target. Actions that don’t explicitly specify their target in the action line use it. Query parameters # realtime (Optional, boolean, default: true) Request-level write-mode switch that overrides schema property-level realtime settings for every document in this request: false applies the batch WAL-only (durable immediately, searchable after the offline epoch build). key_as_id (Optional, boolean, default: false) compatibility rendering: keyed documents answer with the user key AS _id (see the index API). sync_replication (Optional, boolean) Opt back into synchronous inline replication for this request (wait for the replica RPC and count it in the response). Request body # The actions are specified in the request body using a newline delimited JSON (NDJSON) structure:
action_and_meta_data\n optional_source\n action_and_meta_data\n optional_source\n .... action_and_meta_data\n optional_source\n The index and create actions expect a source on the next line, and have the same semantics as the standard API: create fails if a document with the same ID already exists in the target, index adds or replaces a document as necessary. On a routed collection every index/create source must carry the collection’s routing field as a scalar — an item that omits it (or sends null or a non-scalar) fails with a per-item 400, because the routing value is what places the document. A routing key on the action line is accepted and ignored; placement always follows the payload’s routing field.
update expects a JSON object on the next line with the same body as the partial update API: a partial doc object to merge and/or an ordered ops operator list. Other fields (such as script or upsert) are rejected.
delete does not expect a source on the next line and has the same semantics as the standard delete API.
Because this format uses literal \n’s as delimiters, make sure that the JSON actions and sources are not pretty printed.
If you provide a <target> in the request path, it is used for any actions that don’t explicitly specify an _index argument.
create # Indexes the specified document if it does not already exist. The following line must contain the source data to be indexed.
_namespace (Optional, string) Name of the namespace to perform the action on. _collection (Optional, string) Name of the collection to perform the action on. This parameter is required if a <target> is not specified in the request path. _index (Optional, string) A shortcut to specify the namespace and collection in [<namespace>:]<collection> syntax. This parameter conflicts with <_namespace> and <_collection>. _id (Optional, string) The document ID. If no ID is specified, a document ID is automatically generated. delete # Removes the specified document from the index.
_namespace (Optional, string) Name of the namespace to perform the action on. _collection (Optional, string) Name of the collection to perform the action on. This parameter is required if a <target> is not specified in the request path. _index (Optional, string) A shortcut to specify the namespace and collection in [<namespace>:]<collection> syntax. This parameter conflicts with <_namespace> and <_collection>. _id (Required, string) The document ID. index # Indexes the specified document. If the document exists, replaces the document and increments the version. The following line must contain the source data to be indexed.
_namespace (Optional, string) Name of the namespace to perform the action on. _collection (Optional, string) Name of the collection to perform the action on. This parameter is required if a <target> is not specified in the request path. _index (Optional, string) A shortcut to specify the namespace and collection in [<namespace>:]<collection> syntax. This parameter conflicts with <_namespace> and <_collection>. _id (Optional, string) The document ID. If no ID is specified, a document ID is automatically generated. update # Partially updates the specified document with the source on the next line.
_namespace (Optional, string) Name of the namespace to perform the action on. _collection (Optional, string) Name of the collection to perform the action on. This parameter is required if a <target> is not specified in the request path. _index (Optional, string) A shortcut to specify the namespace and collection in [<namespace>:]<collection> syntax. This parameter conflicts with <_namespace> and <_collection>. _id (Required, string) The document ID. retry_on_conflict (Optional, integer, default: 3) Optimistic-concurrency retries for the read-modify-write — same semantics as the _update API’s query parameter. doc # The partial document to merge. Optional for update operations (an ops-only source line is also valid).
ops # Ordered list of update operators, same as the partial update API. Optional for update operations.
<fields> # The document source to index. Required for create and index operations.
title: Batch document operation

content:
Composite aggregation # Paginated multi-source bucket aggregation: the composite key is a tuple built from several sources (a terms field, a histogram interval, a date_histogram, a geotile_grid), and pages are pulled with an after cursor. It does what a single terms cannot: group by several dimensions at once, and stream all combinations without oversizing size.
How it works # Each entry in sources is named: { "day": { … } } binds day to one dimension of the composite key. A bucket’s key maps each source name to its value; buckets come back in ascending key order — first source most significant, values compared as numbers when both are (numbers sort before strings), as strings otherwise.
There is no doc_count ordering and no truncation: every combination occurring in the matched documents is materialized, and size only slices the sorted list into pages — the full set is always reachable by cursor, where terms keeps its top-size buckets and drops the rest.
A page carries an after_key, the key of its last bucket. Pass it back as after and the next page holds only buckets sorting strictly greater. A short final page still carries an after_key; the walk ends when a page comes back empty.
Per document: a terms source over a multi-valued field yields one value per element, so one document can land in several buckets; a document missing a value for any source is dropped. histogram keys are floor(v / interval) * interval, date_histogram keys are epoch milliseconds (offset/time_zone shift boundaries), geotile_grid keys are map tiles; sub-aggregations run only for the returned page.
SQL GROUP BY … LIMIT plans lower through composite — LIMIT becomes size, one source per grouping key.
Examples # Page through merchant combinations, five buckets at a time — the SQL side is GROUP BY … LIMIT plus the envelope’s keyset cursor:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "matrix": { "composite": { "size": 100, "sources": [ { "merchant": { "terms": { "field": "merchant" } } }, { "day": { "date_histogram": { "field": "date", "calendar_interval": "day" } } } ], "after": { "merchant": "shop_b", "day": 1700000000000 } } } } } Use cases # Cross-tab reports. sales crossed type × status lands in 9 of 12 possible cells (mug was never pending, sticker only ever pending); nest sum(amount) for revenue per cell. Export the full bucket space. terms cuts to its top size; composite walks everything — loop after until the empty page, five rows at a time over the 9 cells above. Deep pagination. after walks high-cardinality keys page by page. Time × dimension matrices. date_histogram by day plus terms on type gives one bucket per day-and-type that occurred across the 120 sales (2024-01-01 through 2025-04-21). Parameters for composite # size (Optional, integer, default: 10) Maximum number of composite buckets to return per page. sources (Required, array) Named sources, one per dimension of the composite key, as { "<name>": { "<type>": { … } } }; <type> is one of: terms — distinct values of a field (an order is accepted; keys always come back ascending). histogram — numeric buckets of a fixed numeric interval. date_histogram — calendar_interval (minute…year) or fixed_interval (e.g. "30m"; the legacy interval still works), plus offset, time_zone, format. Keys are epoch milliseconds. geotile_grid — map tiles at precision (default 7, max 29). after (Optional, object) Pagination cursor — the previous page’s after_key. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Related # terms — top-N buckets by doc_count, no cursor multi_terms — tuple keys from several fields date_histogram — the time source, standalone geotile_grid — the map-tile source, standalone
title: Composite aggregation

content:
Children aggregation # A single-bucket aggregation that scopes its sub-aggregations to the child documents of a relation field (parent-child joins). In a corpus where parents and children share an index, it is the lens that looks at the child side while the outer query talks about parents.
How it works # Engine note: the current implementation runs sub-aggregations over the scoped document set keyed by the relation; it does not resolve per-parent child sets.
Concretely, the engine returns ONE bucket, keyed by the type name, whose doc_count is the size of the current candidate set, with the sub-aggregations executed over that same set. It does not walk the relation to isolate actual child documents, and per-parent grouping (one bucket per parent) is not available — full parent-child join semantics need join support at the storage layer. Treat it as a labelled scope for relation-oriented analysis, and pair it with the traverse query when the graph edges themselves matter.
Examples # Articles carry a related_to relation; look at the relation’s child side:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The response is a one-element buckets array carrying the relation name as its key, with the sub-aggregations flattened inside:
{ ... "aggregations": { "related": { "buckets": [ { "key": "related_to", "doc_count": 44, "top_tags": { "buckets": [ { "key": "optimizer", "doc_count": 2 }, { "key": "search", "doc_count": 2 }, ... ] } } ] } } } Use cases # Child-side rollups. Keep the outer query about the parent scope while a nested terms/sum reports child-shaped statistics under a clearly labelled bucket. Relation health checks. A value_count under the bucket plus a traverse walk of the edges shows whether declared relations are actually populated.
Graph neighbourhood stats. On an edge-shaped corpus like articles (related_to edges between 20 nodes), the bucket labels a scope whose sub-aggregations describe the documents carrying edges. Migration scaffolding. Queries written against the ES shape parse and run, so porting an existing parent-child dashboard degrades to a scoped aggregate instead of failing outright. Parameters for children # type (Required, string) Name of the child relation to aggregate. aggs (Optional, object) Sub-aggregations over the child documents. Related # nested — the nested-object counterpart, with full engine support Relational field parameters — declaring references / relation fields in the schema Traverse query — walking relation edges as a graph Join query — cross-collection semi-joins
title: Children aggregation

content:
Scripted metric aggregation # A metrics aggregation whose result is computed by your own scripts, in four phases, running on Pizza’s sandboxed script engine (see the script language reference).
How it works # One state map per segment, folded once at the end:
Phase Runs Scope init_script once per segment state, params map_script once per document state, doc, params combine_script once per segment state, params reduce_script once, at the end states, params state is a map you own — initialize it in init_script, accumulate into it in map_script. combine_script folds one segment’s state into a single value (a script that ends in a statement returns the state itself, the default when combine_script is omitted). reduce_script receives all combined values as the states array; if it is omitted, a single state passes through unchanged and several come back as an array — the parts, rather than a wrong merge. Builds without the scripting feature return null for the whole aggregation.
Document fields are reachable in the doc-values shape:
doc.price.value — the first value of price for the current document doc.price.values — all values (multi-value fields) doc['price'].value — the bracket spelling a field the document doesn’t have has no entry — doc.missing.value errors Example: total and average order value # Total revenue, order count and average order value in one pass (120 docs, total 6750, average 56.25 on the sample data):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Example: filtered sum with params # Only hat orders count; params carries the filter value (all four phases see params). On the sample data: 1800 over 30 orders.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Use cases # One pass, several metrics — total, count and average in a single sweep, or any bundle of dependent numbers a plain metric agg cannot produce together. Filtered accumulation — count or sum only the rows a params value selects (the hat revenue above), without a wrapping filter bucket. Custom metrics — medians-of-groups, per-key tallies (state.by_type[x] += 1), or any shape a map plus a reduce can hold, when no built-in agg fits. Multi-state reductions — collect a list per segment and merge the lists in reduce_script, the pattern for top-N-by-group inside a script. Parameters # Name Type Description init_script string Sets up the initial state. Optional. map_script string Executed per document. Optional (a doc-count-only agg needs none). combine_script string Folds a segment’s state to one value. Defaults to the state. reduce_script string Folds the states array to the result. See below. params object Extra variables visible in every phase as params.<name>. Notes and limits # Language: scripts are Rhai, not Painless. Everything in the language reference applies — in particular there is no ?: ternary and strings use double quotes (doc[‘x’] single-quoted refs are rewritten for you). state.list arrays work with push: state.items.push(doc.price.value) mutates the state, not a copy.
Distributed: under fan-out each shard returns its combined values; the coordinator runs reduce_script over them in shard-arrival order; a reduce_script that is not order-independent (non-commutative) is the script author’s problem. Cost: map_script runs once per matched document at roughly two microseconds per document. Keep it small; a sum agg with field is always faster than a scripted sum. Errors in any phase abort the aggregation and come back as {"error": "<phase>: <message>"} rather than a wrong number. The single-value metric aggs (sum, avg, …) also accept a per-doc script as their value source — see scripted value sources. Use scripted_metric when one script must see the whole bucket shape (filters, multi-state reductions), the plain metric script when one expression per doc is enough. Related # Pipeline scripts — the Rhai language reference: syntax, doc/params bindings, and the limits of the sandbox. Scripted value sources — the cheaper per-document script form on sum, avg, min, max, value_count and cardinality. bucket_script — a script over bucket metrics (after the aggregation), where scripted_metric scripts run per document (during it).
title: Scripted metric aggregation

content:
Rescore # rescore re-ranks the top window of hits with a second query — an expensive precision pass (phrase, vector similarity, a narrow filter match) applied only where it can change the final page, instead of to every matching document.
POST /my-collection/_search How it works # Rescore is engine-native. When a request carries a rescore block, the collector widens its gather to max(from + size, window) candidates, the first-pass query ranks them, and the store layer then applies the rescore to the collected set (apply_rescore_to_result in lib/engine/src/store/layered/generic_reader.rs, blending in lib/engine/src/search/scorer/mod.rs):
Each hit INSIDE the window is scored by the rescore query and blended: new = query_weight × first_pass + rescore_query_weight × rescore. A window hit the rescore query does not match contributes 0 from the second term. Hits OUTSIDE the window keep their first-pass score SCALED by query_weight — the weight applies to the whole result set, not just the window. The full list is re-sorted so the re-scored window interleaves with the untouched tail, then truncated to from + size. The blend is always the weighted sum above — the internal scorer chain also knows multiply/avg/max/min modes, but the request API exposes only total. One rescorer per request: the native dialect is a single object (the gateway rejects the array form with a 400).
Wire-form status: the ES-compatibility layer understands the Elasticsearch shape (window_size plus a nested query: {rescore_query, …} object), translates it to the native flat dialect, applies only the FIRST rescorer of an array, and enforces the validations — window below 10000, and collapse + rescore mutually exclusive. Through the Pizza gateway itself, send the native form below; the nested form is a parse error today, and the native path does not (yet) reject the collapse mix.
Examples # Lift the request-log needle out of a match-all haystack: every logs document scores 1.0 on the first pass; the rescore adds three times the search match score to the top 50 — 1.0 × 1.0 + 3.0 × 2.566 ≈ 8.70 for the strongest matches, so the 25 GET /search requests jump above the other 145.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Shrink the window to 2 and only the two leading hits get the treatment — every other hit keeps 1.0 × query_weight. That boundary is the whole point of the feature: pay for the expensive query on 2 or 50 documents, never on all 150 (or 150 million).
Phrase precision on top of loose matching — base query wide, phrase rescore exact:
{ "query": { "match": { "field": "text", "query": "wood fired pizza" } }, "rescore": { "window": 10, "query": { "phrase": { "field": "text", "query": "wood fired" } }, "query_weight": 0.7, "rescore_query_weight": 1.5 }, "size": 5 } Use cases # Vector precision pass. Text match for recall, vector similarity over the top 10 for order — Stage 4 of the hybrid pipeline. Phrase tightening. Loose match recall with a phrase rescore so exact word order wins the top slots without punishing the recall underneath. Boost a narrow signal. “Order by relevance, but let recent VIP activity win ties” — a filter-shaped rescore query over a small window is cheaper than scoring it for the whole corpus. Bandwidth-guarded reranking. Keep the window at or just above from + size; anything larger spends second-pass score on hits the caller will never see. Parameters for rescore # window (Optional, integer, default: 10) How many top hits to re-score. The collector gathers at least max(from + size, window) candidates. query (Required, object) The rescoring query — any query type, executed over the window; its score is blended into each in-window hit. query_weight (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Weight of the first-pass score, for in-window blends and the outside-window scaling alike. rescore_query_weight (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Weight of the rescore query’s score. Notes # retrieve (hybrid) requests cannot carry rescore — the gateway rejects the mix; use Stage 4 only with a plain query. score_functions and rescore compose freely on one plain query (functions shape the first-pass score, rescore then blends the second). An all-match_all pair makes the arithmetic easy to eyeball: base 1, rescore 1, so scores read as pure weights (5/15 in the conformance case above). Related # Hybrid search pipeline — rescore is Stage 4 of the retrieve → fuse → score_functions → rescore chain. Sort and pagination — the other result-shaping half; rescore re-sorts by blended score, sort fixes the order outright. Field collapsing — the third member of the result-shaping family; the ES-compat layer rejects the collapse + rescore mix. vector query — the usual resident of the query slot for similarity rescoring.
title: Rescore

content:
Pipeline scripts # Three pipeline aggregations evaluate a user-supplied script per bucket: bucket_script (compute a new metric per bucket),
bucket_selector (keep/drop predicate), and
moving_fn (window statistic). moving_avg is a moving_fn with a fixed averaging script. The same engine powers
scripted_metric (scripts per document instead of per bucket) and the scripted value sources on the single-value metric aggs (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality), the per-hit script_fields of a search request (fetch phase), and the
scripted queries — script_score, script filters, the _script sort.
Scripts run in a sandboxed Rhai engine — not Painless. Simple ES arithmetic (params.r / params.n, MovingFunctions.max(values)) compiles unchanged; Java interop, classes and method calls beyond the helpers below do not.
A guided example # Revenue per day, a per-bucket ratio, and a rolling 7-day maximum — one request, three scripted and non-scripted aggregations side by side:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. A selector with a compound script — statements, a let binding, and a boolean expression as the result. Per-order revenue must exceed 50 AND total revenue 1500: t-shirt (30/order) and mug (1350 total) drop, hat and sticker stay:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The selector itself leaves no trace in the response — it only filters the bucket list of the aggregation that owns it.
Variables # Variable Available in Meaning params.<name> bucket_script, bucket_selector Sibling metric named by buckets_path ({"r": "revenue"} → params.r). <name> bucket_script, bucket_selector Same value, bare spelling — r instead of params.r. values moving_fn Floating-point array of the current window, oldest first. Both spellings of a buckets_path variable work; params.<name> is what stock ES scripts use. Metrics arrive as floats.
The language # The last expression is the script’s result. Statements available:
let ratio = params.r / params.n; // binding (and // comments) if ratio > 10 { 1.0 } else { 0.0 } // conditional expression for v in values { s += v; } // iterate a window let i = 0; while i < 3 { i += 1; } // loop switch params.n { 1 => 10.0, _ => 20.0 } Watch integer division: 5 / 2 is 2, and any int-by-int expression truncates — values.len() / 2 over a 3-bucket window is 1, not 1.5. When either side is a float the result is a float: params.r / 2 and 5.0 / 2 are both fine (params.* variables and values[...] elements are floats). Adding .0 to a literal never hurts.
Operators: + - * / %, ** (power), comparisons == != < <= > >=, logical && || !. There is no ?: ternary — use an if/else expression instead.
Arrays support values.len(), indexing (values[0], values[values.len() - 1]), iteration, closures, and values.filter(|v| v > 15) / values.map(|v| v * 2). The whole expression still must reduce to a number for bucket_script — e.g. values.filter(|v| v > 100).len() is a valid metric, values.filter(|v| v > 100) alone is not (a non-numeric result becomes a null value, not an error).
A few more script shapes that work:
values.max() - values.min() // spread of the window let total = mf_sum(values); values[values.len() - 1] / total let s = 0.0; for v in values { s += v; } s / values.len() Math # x.sqrt(), x.abs() (also abs(x)), x.floor(), x.round(), and x ** n for powers. ceil, the pow(x, n) function form, and ?: are not available.
MovingFunctions helpers # Elasticsearch moving_fn scripts call helpers through the MovingFunctions namespace. Those calls work unchanged:
Helper Result MovingFunctions.max(values) / min(values) Window maximum / minimum. MovingFunctions.sum(values) Window sum (0 for an empty window). MovingFunctions.unweightedAvg(values) Arithmetic mean. MovingFunctions.linearWeightedAvg(values) Mean with linearly rising weights — the newest value weighs n, the oldest 1. MovingFunctions.stdDev(values, avg) Population standard deviation around the given mean. MovingFunctions.ewma(values, alpha) Exponentially weighted moving average: s = alpha·x + (1-alpha)·s. The same functions also work as array methods / plain calls: values.max(), values.min(), mf_sum(values), mf_ewma(values, 0.5). Other names under MovingFunctions fail to compile.
bucket_selector truthiness # The predicate result is interpreted as: a boolean, taken as-is; a number, true when non-zero (0.0 is false); anything else — a string, an array — defaults to true (keep the bucket). Prefer explicit comparisons; "enough" is truthy, params.r > 150 says what you mean.
Use cases # Derived per-bucket metrics — bucket_script ratios and scores: average order value (params.r / params.n), conversion rates, weighted quality scores. Metric-based bucket filtering — bucket_selector as the HAVING clause of aggregations: keep buckets above a threshold, drop buckets with too little data. Rolling window statistics — moving_fn over values: trailing max/min envelopes, windowed sums, stability bands from stdDev. Conditional logic in one request — let bindings and if/else expressions replace the post-processing pass that would otherwise run client-side over the raw buckets. Failure and limits # A script that fails to compile yields a null metric (moving_fn returns no buckets). A runtime failure — an empty window where a statistic is undefined, a non-numeric element — nulls that bucket’s value; bucket_selector keeps the bucket.
Each evaluation runs under sandbox limits: 100,000 operations, expression depth 64 (32 inside function calls), strings up to 4 KB, arrays up to 10,000 elements, maps up to 1,000 entries. Compiled scripts are cached by source text (bounded at 1,024 entries — a flood of unique scripts flushes the cache and recompiles rather than growing memory), so identical scripts compile once.
Related # The scripted pipeline aggregations: bucket_script,
bucket_selector,
moving_fn — and
moving_avg, its fixed-average specialization
Document-level scripting: scripted_metric,
script_fields,
script_score — documents the MovingFunctions helpers this engine re-implements
title: Pipeline scripts

content:
Nested aggregation # A single-bucket aggregation that scopes its sub-aggregations to a nested object path. Nested field values are addressable as dotted columns, so sub-aggregations read variants.color style fields directly — counting per array element where it matters, not per parent document.
reverse_nested (only valid inside a nested aggregation) jumps back out to the parent-document scope.
How it works # The engine returns a single bucket shaped { "doc_count": <parents>, …sub-aggs }. Sub-aggregations run over the parent documents, but the nested path’s values live in multivalue dotted columns, so a terms on variants.color buckets every array ELEMENT: over the 30 teaching products with 60 variant elements, black / white / blue each collect 20. One exception is top_hits, which is element-level here: each hit is one stored element carrying _nested: {field, offset} identity, sorted per the requested sort.
reverse_nested returns one bucket keyed reverse_nested over the same parent set — the ladder back out after diving into a path.
Examples # Products carry a variants array; aggregate one value per parent product inside the nested scope, then reverse back out:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. colors counts elements (20 / 20 / 20 across 60 variants); back_out reports the 30 parent products:
{ ... "aggregations": { "in_variants": { "doc_count": 30, "colors": { "buckets": [ { "key": "black", "doc_count": 20 }, { "key": "blue", "doc_count": 20 }, { "key": "white", "doc_count": 20 } ] }, "back_out": { "buckets": [ { "key": "reverse_nested", "doc_count": 30 } ] } } } } Use cases # Per-variant inventory. Count sizes or colors across every variant element while the outer query stays at product grain. Element-level top lists. top_hits under nested returns individual variants (with _nested offsets), not whole products. Line-item analytics. Orders with nested line_items: sum per item field inside the path, then reverse_nested for order-level context in the same request. Inner-hit preview. Pair with the nested query to see which elements matched and which statistics they feed.
Parameters for nested # path (Required, string) Path of the nested object (dotted). aggs (Optional, object) Sub-aggregations in nested scope. Parameters for reverse_nested # aggs (Optional, object) Sub-aggregations back in the parent scope. Related # children — the relation-field counterpart Nested query — element-wise matching within one array element top_hits — element-level hits under nested terms — the workhorse inside a nested scope
title: Nested aggregation

content:
Top metrics aggregation # A metrics aggregation that returns metric values from the leading matching documents — a cheaper alternative to top_hits when you only need field values, not whole documents.
Engine note: sort is accepted for compatibility; the current implementation returns the metrics of the first size matching documents.
How it works # top_metrics walks the bucket’s documents and emits one entry per document for the first size of them, in index order. Each entry maps every configured metric field to its value in that document. The response is the flat form {"top": [{"price": 15.0}, …]}.
Metric fields must be numeric — a field that is missing, or not a number (strings included), comes back as null in the entry.
The sort clause is parsed but does not steer the pick yet — the “top” documents are simply the first size matching documents.
The column-store fast path reads each metric straight from the segment columns; the executor path reads per-document column values.
Under distributed fan-out the coordinator keeps its own shard’s entries — there is no re-pick step in the merge.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Over the 120 sales this returns the first sale’s price (15.0); with "size": 3 you get the first three sales’ prices.
One exemplar value per merchant — the usual nesting:
POST /sales/_search { "size": 0, "aggs": { "merchants": { "terms": { "field": "merchant" }, "aggs": { "sample_price": { "top_metrics": { "metrics": [{ "field": "price" }, { "field": "qty" }] } } } } } } Each of the four merchant buckets (30 sales each) gets a sample_price.top entry mapping price and qty to the bucket’s first sale.
Use cases # One number per bucket — dashboards that show each group’s exemplar value (a price, a status) without paying for full document sources. Cheaper top_hits — when only a field or two from the leading documents matter, skip source assembly entirely. Per-category representative — terms(category) with top_metrics inside surfaces a sample value per category, ready for a table column. Parameters for top_metrics # metrics (Required, object array) field entries whose values are returned. sort (Optional, array) Sort clause selecting the “top” documents. size (Optional, integer, default: 1) How many top entries to return. Related # top_hits — full documents, nested element hits, and a sort that ranks. terms — the bucket aggregation it usually nests in.
title: Top metrics aggregation

content:
Scripted queries # Scripts in the search request: script_score to compute the score, a script predicate in a boolean filter, and a _script sort key. All run on Pizza’s sandboxed script engine (see the script language reference) — Rhai, not Painless, but the doc[‘x’].value, _score, params.<name> spellings run unmodified.
script_score — score by script # Wrap a query; the script’s value replaces the score. The script sees _score (the wrapped query’s BM25 score), doc (the hit’s _source in doc-values shape) and params:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Ranking follows the script — the three hits come back in amount order, with _score equal to amount. A script that needs the base relevance:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Nested script_score wrappers chain: the inner script computes the score the outer script’s _score sees. An evaluation error fails the request with a message naming script_score.
script — filter by predicate # The script query, a boolean predicate per document, in any clause position of a bool:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The script must evaluate to a boolean; anything else is a named error. Predicates apply to the collected window after the base query runs — post_filter-class semantics: the window is bounded by from + size (or collect_size when set), and aggregations are not narrowed. When you need aggs over the filtered set, add a range/term filter alongside the script (those execute inside the segment, narrowing everything). Deep per-segment script filtering is on the roadmap, demand-gated.
_script — sort key by script # A sort clause whose key is computed per hit of the returned page — the same page-sized rule as script_fields:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. At most one _script clause per request. Numbers compare numerically, strings lexicographically, and a script that returns nothing places per the missing policy. The computed key surfaces as the hit’s sort value. Page membership is decided by the preceding ranking — _script re-orders the page, it does not re-rank the whole candidate set.
The script_score function in score_functions # Inside score_functions (function scoring), the script_score function form nests the script under "script", and combines through score_mode / boost_mode like the other functions:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Parameters for script_score # query (Required, query) The wrapped query; its hits form the candidate window the script re-scores. script (Required, string or object) The scoring script — an inline string or { "source": …, "params": … }. _score, doc and params are in scope; the script’s value replaces the score. min_score (unsupported) Not implemented on the script_score query; thresholds on the computed score must be applied by the caller. The script filter query takes a single script parameter in the same two forms, nested once more ({ "script": { "script": … } } — the double-nested form).
Use cases # Business scoring. Rank by margin, inventory age or any stored number the text ranker cannot see — doc['amount'].value as the score, or _score * doc['qty'].value to blend relevance with volume (both playgrounds above). Non-declarable predicates. A script filter in a bool expresses conditions no DSL clause covers — parity checks, cross-field arithmetic, threshold ratios — evaluated per document of the collected window. Computed sort keys. The _script sort orders the returned page by a per-hit expression (price with VAT applied) without storing the derived value. Custom function scoring. Inside score_functions, a script is one more decay-or-boost function, combined through score_mode / boost_mode with the others. Related # Pipeline scripts — the script language reference: syntax, sandbox limits, and the helper functions available on every scripting surface, this one included. sort — field-based sorting; _script is its computed-key clause. script_fields — the fetch-phase sibling: computed values returned per hit, page-sized like _script. hybrid — the score_functions context where the script_score function form lives. Notes and limits # Cost: scripts evaluate per hit of the collected window — roughly 2–5 µs per hit per script, native. script_score widens collection to collect_size (default 10000) so the script ranks real candidates; the page is trimmed afterwards. The check for scripted queries on a non-script request costs ~17 ns (one tree walk), so the feature is free when unused. Sandboxed: the same containment as every other script surface — operation cap (a runaway while true {} fails the request in milliseconds, never hangs), no host or network IO, bounded sizes. _score and doc are per-eval copies: assigning to them inside a script changes nothing outside that one evaluation. min_score on the script_score query is not implemented.
title: Scripted queries

content:
Geotile grid aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation grouping geo_point values into zoom/x/y map tiles — the native grid of web maps. Where geohash_grid speaks in geohash strings, this one emits exactly the tile addresses a Leaflet/MapLibre layer already understands, so clustering needs no coordinate translation.
How it works # Each point is mapped to its Web-Mercator tile: x and y are computed from longitude/latitude scaled by 2^zoom, latitude clamped to the projection’s ±85.0511° limit. precision is the zoom level — 0–29, default 7 (a tile spans ~300 km at the equator; each zoom step halves it). The bucket key is the z/x/y string, e.g. Amsterdam at zoom 8 → 8/131/84.
Buckets are sorted by doc_count descending with a key-ascending tie-break, then truncated to size. Points outside the field are skipped, and sub-aggregations run per tile. The same tile grid is also available as a composite source when the grid is too dense for one page.
Examples # Zoom 5 tiles:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Keys like 5/26/13 address the tile at zoom 5, column 26, row 13. Over the 15 teaching places, zoom 5 puts 6 documents in 5/26/13, 2 each in 5/25/13 and 5/26/12, and 1 in each of five more tiles:
{ ... "aggregations": { "tiles": { "buckets": [ { "key": "5/26/13", "doc_count": 6 }, { "key": "5/25/13", "doc_count": 2 }, { "key": "5/26/12", "doc_count": 2 }, { "key": "5/23/11", "doc_count": 1 }, ... ] } } } A tile spans 360° / 2^zoom of longitude — about 1,250 km at the equator at zoom 5, 300 km at the default zoom 7, 1.2 km at zoom 12 — and shrinks toward the poles exactly as Mercator tiles do, so the bucket counts line up with what the rendered map shows.
Use cases # Tile-server clustering. The keys line up one-to-one with map tiles; drop counts into the layer and the map clusters itself. Zoom-aware dashboards. Match precision to the map’s current zoom so the grid resolution always tracks what the user sees. Regional rollups. Low zooms (0–4) give country-scale buckets for headline stats; sub-aggregations carry per-tile sums and averages. Viewport prefetch. Request one zoom above the current view to precompute the clusters revealed by the next zoom-in. Parameters for geotile_grid # field (Required, string) geo_point field you wish to aggregate. precision (Optional, integer, default: 7) Tile zoom 0–29; higher values are clamped to 29. size (Optional, integer, default: 10000) Maximum buckets returned. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per tile. Related # geohash_grid — the same grid in geohash cell coordinates geo_distance — rings around a point instead of a grid composite — paginated geotile_grid source for dense fields geo_bounds — bounding box of the points, handy for picking the zoom
title: Geotile grid aggregation

content:
Delete a document # Delete a specific document from the specified collection by specifying its unique identifier.
Examples # Delete the document 0,0 from collection my-collection:
DELETE /my-collection/_doc/0,0 The API returns the following result:
{ "_id": "0,0", "_version": 0, "result": "deleted", ... } Deleting a document again (or fetching it after deletion) answers 404 with "result": "not_found" — the delete itself still succeeds and reports "result": "deleted" only for a document that was live.
Key mappings survive deletion: creating a new document with the key of a deleted document succeeds (result: "created") and reuses that document’s original _id, instead of allocating a new one.
Request # DELETE /<target>/_doc/<doc_id> Path parameters # <target> (Required, string) Name of the collection to target. <doc_id> (Required, string) Unique identifier for the document, support both _key or _id. Query parameters # routing (Required for a key-addressed delete on a routed collection) — the routing VALUE that places the document (hash(<value>) — or its salted partition set, see salting). A bare key has no home partition there and answers 400.
title: Delete a document

content:
Top hits aggregation # Keeps track of the most relevant documents being aggregated — useful inside a bucket aggregation (e.g. terms) to return the best-matching documents per bucket. Where most metric aggs reduce a bucket to one number, top_hits keeps the documents themselves.
How it works # top_hits runs over a bucket’s document set and returns up to size documents in a hits envelope: hits.total — a plain count of the bucket’s documents — and hits.hits[], each entry carrying _id (the engine’s internal numeric document id) and _source.
Sort leniency. The sort body accepts every spelling — a bare string ("amount"), an array of strings or objects, or a single {"field": "order"} object — and normalizes them all to an object array; a bare field name means asc. Flat buckets. The column-store fast path and the executor path both walk the bucket’s candidate documents and fetch each stored source. In the current engine the hits come back in index order: the normalized sort is not yet applied to flat-bucket ranking. Nested buckets sort for real. Under a nested aggregation, top_hits is element-level: each hit is one stored element of the nested path, identified by _nested: {field, offset}, and the elements are sorted per the sort spec — numeric when both sides parse as numbers, lexicographic otherwise, missing values sorting last under asc.
_source. true / false / a list of fields all parse; the current implementation returns the full stored source either way. Fan-out. Shard hit lists are concatenated and truncated back to size at the coordinator. Request knobs such as from are not parsed and are ignored. Examples # Top 3 sales per merchant:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "top_merchants": { "terms": { "field": "merchant" }, "aggs": { "top_sales": { "top_hits": { "size": 3, "sort": [{ "field": "amount", "order": "desc" }] } } } } } } Inside each terms bucket hits.total is the bucket’s document count (30 per merchant on the teaching dataset), and the entries are the bucket’s leading documents in index order.
Use cases # Top-N rows per group — the classic shape: terms on merchant or category with a small top_hits inside, so one request returns the group counts and a few representative rows per group. A representative product per category — terms(category) over the 30 products with top_hits: {size: 1} yields one exemplar row per category for a listing page. Nested element extraction — under nested, surface stored child elements (a product’s variants, an order’s line items) ranked by an element field. Bucket debugging — when a bucket’s count surprises you, attach top_hits and read the documents that actually fell into it. Facet previews — “show me the documents behind this facet value” without issuing a second search per value. Parameters for top_hits # size (Optional, integer, default: 3) Number of top hits to return per bucket. sort (Optional) Sort order for the top hits. Accepts "field", ["a", "b"] and [{ "field": "asc" }] forms — all normalize to an object array. _source (Optional) true, false, or a list of fields to include. The full stored source is returned either way. Related # top_metrics — when one field value from the top document is enough and whole documents are too heavy. terms — the bucket aggregation top_hits usually lives in. nested — element-level top hits with real sorting.
title: Top hits aggregation

content:
Salting (salt-split routing) # Manage salt-split assignments for a collection whose schema declares a routing field ("routing": true). One hot routing value — the mega tenant, the biggest org — funnels every write into a single partition; salting splits that value across a SET of partitions so the hot key stops being a placement bottleneck.
The API never moves data by itself: assignments state intent, the write path consumes them live (the very next write of an assigned value lands inside its partition set), and migrating documents that are already placed is a separate rehash operation. The joins tutorial walks the complete sequence against a live node.
Assign or clear salt splits # PUT /<target>/_salting { "threshold": 4, "assignments": {"org-mega": 4} } Full-replace semantics, like routing allocation: the second PUT states the complete assignment set — an assignment disappears unless restated. Pass an empty assignments object to keep only the threshold (nothing salted).
Path parameters # <target> (Required, string) The collection — it must declare exactly one routing field; the salted values are values OF that field. Request body # threshold (Required, integer) The doc-count threshold at which the feed flags a routing value as a salting candidate. Candidate flagging needs a declared threshold; the assignments themselves are never auto-applied.
assignments (Required, object) Mapping of routing value → split count. Split counts are validated to 2..=64 and keys must be non-empty. Response # The assignment set rendered with each value’s computed partition set — the frozen engine contract hash(<value> #<i>) % partitions for i in 0..splits, sorted and deduped (the effective spread can be below splits, and the response reports what IS):
{ "acknowledged": true, "routing_field": "org_id", "threshold": 4, "status": "assigned (salt-split routing active on writes)", "assignments": [ {"value": "org-mega", "splits": 4, "partitions": [76, 83, 85, 254]} ] } status is unsalted with no assignments, and assigned (salt-split routing active on writes) otherwise.
How writes pick a member # A keyed write of an assigned value picks its member deterministically — hash(<routing value> #hash(<_key>) % splits) — so the same key always lands in the same place; auto-ID writes round-robin the members. Unassigned values keep their single hash(<value>) partition, and searches fan out across every partition either way: salting changes placement, never visibility. Key-addressed reads (GET /<target>/_doc/<key>?routing=<value>) probe the whole partition set.
Inspect the salting state # GET /<target>/_salting Returns the same rendering as the PUT response (without acknowledged).
The salting feed # GET /<target>/_salting/feed?size=10 The operator’s measurement: a terms aggregation over the routing field through the exact search fan-out, each row annotated with the current assignment, values at or above threshold flagged candidate: true:
{ "routing_field": "org_id", "threshold": 4, "size": 10, "values": [ {"value": "org-mega", "doc_count": 6, "candidate": true, "assigned_splits": 4}, {"value": "org-a", "doc_count": 3, "candidate": false, "assigned_splits": null} ] } Query parameters # size (Optional, integer, default: 10) How many top routing values to report. Notes and limits # Assignments are stored in cluster metadata (raft-replicated) and consumed live by the write path; clearing an assignment narrows placement on the very next write. Documents written BEFORE an assignment stay on their old partition until a rehash migration moves them — reads bridge both placements by probing the assigned set (the migration operation ships separately). The bulk keyed fast lane serves field-routed collections through the per-item path (correct placement, no batch grouping) until the lane itself becomes field-aware.
title: Salting (salt-split routing)

content:
Normalize aggregation # A parent pipeline aggregation rescaling a bucket metric into a share or rank — e.g. each bucket’s revenue as a percent of the total (percent_of_sum), a 0..1 position (rescale_0_1), or standard deviations from the mean (z-score).
"share": { "normalize": { "buckets_path": "per_type>revenue", "method": "percent_of_sum" } } How it works # In this engine normalize is evaluated in the sibling placement: declare it next to the bucket aggregation and point buckets_path at the series with the full parent>metric form. The engine collects one value per bucket, applies the chosen method across the whole series, and emits a standalone buckets array (keys 0..n−1) with one value per consumed bucket.
The methods, verified against the engine:
Method Each bucket becomes Edge behavior percent_of_sum v / Σ × 100 Σ ≤ 0 → 0 rescale_0_1 (v − min) / (max − min) flat series → 0 rescale_0_100 the same, × 100 flat series → 0 mean v − mean (centers on 0) — z-score (v − mean) / σ, population σ σ = 0 → 0 softmax exp(v − max) / Σ exp (column sums to 1) — Any other method string passes the original values through unchanged rather than failing the request. Buckets whose metric is missing are skipped — there is no gap_policy parameter.
The nested declaration (normalize inside the terms agg’s aggs, bare buckets_path) parses but is not wired to the nested injection path yet: every bucket’s entry stays null. Use the sibling form above.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The four product types earn 1800, 1800, 1350, 1800 (of 6750 total), so share.buckets answers 26.67, 26.67, 20.0, 26.67 — percentages that sum to exactly 100 and line up, by position, with per_type.buckets.
Use cases # Share of total — percent_of_sum turns per-category revenue into composition: “mug is 20% of sales” survives any change in overall volume a raw total does not. Comparable scales — rescale_0_1 puts series measured in different units (orders, revenue, defects) on one 0..1 axis for side-by-side sparklines. Outlier ranking — z-score expresses each bucket in standard deviations from its own mean: sort by it and the anomalous buckets surface regardless of their raw scale. Attention-style weights — softmax converts the series into positive weights summing to 1, e.g. to allocate quota or traffic proportionally to per-bucket scores. Centering before further math — mean subtracts the series mean, the standard first step before variance-based analysis. Parameters for normalize # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed series: "<bucket_agg>><metric>". method (Required, string) One of percent_of_sum, rescale_0_1, rescale_0_100, mean, z-score, softmax; any other value passes values through unchanged. Related # avg_bucket — the mean of the same series in one number bucket_script — arbitrary per-bucket arithmetic when a fixed method is not enough percentiles_bucket — rank within the series
title: Normalize aggregation

content:
Geohash grid aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation that groups geo_point values into geohash cells — the building block of map clustering. It answers “where are my documents concentrated?” in one request, handing the map a count per cell instead of thousands of individual markers.
How it works # Each document’s point is encoded as a geohash string: base-32 characters produced by interleaving longitude and latitude bits over successively halved intervals. precision is the number of characters kept — 1–12, clamped, default 5 (cells of roughly 4.9 km × 4.9 km). The classic Amsterdam coordinate 52.374081, 4.912350 at precision 3 lands in cell u17.
Every distinct cell becomes one bucket keyed by its geohash string. Buckets are sorted by doc_count descending with a key-ascending tie-break, then truncated to size. Documents whose field carries no parseable point are skipped. Sub-aggregations run per cell over that cell’s documents — a geo_centroid under each bucket gives the map an exact marker position.
Examples # Precision 2 (~1,250 km cells):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Bucket keys are geohash strings (wt, ws, …) — render them on a map tile layer. Over the 15 teaching places, precision 2 yields wt with 4 documents, ws and wx with 2 each, and seven single-document cells:
{ ... "aggregations": { "cells": { "buckets": [ { "key": "wt", "doc_count": 4 }, { "key": "ws", "doc_count": 2 }, { "key": "wx", "doc_count": 2 }, { "key": "tz", "doc_count": 1 }, ... ] } } } Cell sizes per precision (geohash cells shrink by alternately halving longitude and latitude, so even precisions are roughly twice as wide as tall):
Precision Cell size (approx.) 1 5,000 km × 5,000 km 2 1,250 km × 625 km 3 156 km × 156 km 4 39 km × 20 km 5 (default) 4.9 km × 4.9 km 6 1.2 km × 0.6 km 7 153 m × 153 m Use cases # Map heat layers. Feed the bucket keys straight into a geohash overlay; the count per cell drives color intensity. Server-side clustering. At low precision you get continent-scale clusters; raising precision zooms the grid, the standard cluster-on-bounds pattern behind map UIs. Per-cell statistics. Nest metric sub-aggregations to carry the average price or event count of each cell alongside its count. Geo QA. A cell that unexpectedly dominates the counts flags a geotagging bias or a bulk import pinned to one coordinate. Parameters for geohash_grid # field (Required, string) geo_point field you wish to aggregate. precision (Optional, integer, default: 5) Geohash precision 1–12; values outside the range are clamped. size (Optional, integer, default: 10000) Maximum buckets returned. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per cell. Related # geotile_grid — the same grid idea in Web-Mercator z/x/y tile coordinates geo_distance — rings around a point instead of a grid geo_centroid — per-cell center for marker placement composite — paginated grids for dense fields
title: Geohash grid aggregation

content:
Reshard a rolling # Change the number of shards of a rolling, online. Splitting raises the shard count (finer partition ranges, e.g. 1 → 2); merging lowers it (e.g. 2 → 1).
The reshard builds a hidden target rolling while the source keeps serving every read and write. Existing documents are streamed into the target with their _id preserved, the write tail is replayed until the target converges, and a single metadata commit then swaps the target in atomically. Documents stay addressable under the same _id and _key throughout, including for writes issued while the reshard is building.
graph LR W["clients — reads and writescontinue as usual"] --> S("source rolling — 1 shard") S -.->|"1 — stream documents into the target,_id preserved"| T("hidden target rolling — 2 shards") S -.->|"2 — replay the write tailuntil the target converges"| T T -->|"3 — one metadata commit"| SW["atomic swap —the target becomes the rolling"] Start a reshard # POST /my-collection/_rolling/0/_reshard { "number_of_shards": 2 } The API returns as following result:
{ "acknowledged": true, "state": "building", "number_of_shards_before": 1, "number_of_shards_after": 2, ... } Path parameters # <target> (Required, string) Name of the collection to target. <rolling_id> (Required, integer) The rolling to reshard. Request body # number_of_shards (Required, integer) The shard count to change to. Must differ from the current shard count. The request is rejected with 400 when number_of_shards equals the current shard count or is out of range, when another reshard of the same rolling is already in progress, or when the deployment’s WAL configuration does not support resharding. An unknown rolling returns 404.
Get reshard status # GET /my-collection/_rolling/0/_reshard The API returns as following result:
{ "acknowledged": true, "collection": "default:my-collection", "rolling_id": 0, "state": "building", "phase": "catching_up", "shards": [ { "id": "04ffe003da1e4fcab235", "phase": "catching_up", "detail": "..." } ], ... } state is building while the hidden target converges, and committed_draining after the atomic swap, while the final write tail is being drained. phase reports the worst phase across the target’s primaries: waiting_for_engine, bulk_snapshot, catching_up, ready, draining, done, or draining overall once the commit landed. Returns 404 when no reshard is in progress for the rolling.
Get reshard events # The lifecycle event feed (“related log”) of this rolling’s most recent reshard, oldest first:
GET /my-collection/_rolling/0/_reshard/_events The API returns the following result:
{ "acknowledged": true, "collection": "default:my-collection", "rolling_id": 0, "events": [ { "ts_millis": 1700000000123, "shard": "04ffe...", "message": "..." }, ... ] } Events are recorded by the nodes that run the workers (the target’s primaries), the leader (coordinator milestones) and the handling node (user actions); the response merges and orders all of them by timestamp.
The endpoint always answers 200 — an empty list means no reshard ran since startup, and a finished reshard’s event ring survives (it is cleared only when the next reshard of the same rolling starts), so you can keep inspecting what happened after the fact.
Cancel a reshard # POST /my-collection/_rolling/0/_reshard/_cancel The API returns as following result:
{ "acknowledged": true, "state": "cancelled", ... } Cancellation is only possible while the reshard is still building; the source rolling serves traffic untouched and the hidden target is discarded. Once the commit swapped the target in, the reshard is irreversible and cancel returns 400 (as it does when no reshard is running).
title: Reshard a rolling

content:
Geo distance aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation like range, but buckets are distance rings around a geo_point origin. It answers “how many things are near me?” — counts per radius band in a single request, no matter how many rings you declare.
How it works # Every document’s point is measured against the origin with the haversine formula on a spherical Earth (mean radius 6,371,008.8 m — within ~0.5 % of the WGS-84 ellipsoid). The origin accepts either a "lat,lon" string or a { "lat": …, "lon": … } object; an origin that parses to nothing yields zero buckets.
Each range then places the document: from is inclusive, to is exclusive, both in metres. Ranges are checked independently, so overlapping ranges double-count a document, and every declared range produces exactly one bucket — in declaration order, empty ones included. A bucket without an explicit key is named "{from}-{to}" with * for the unbounded side (*-500000, 500000-*). Nested sub-aggregations run per ring over that ring’s documents.
Examples # Ring the Beijing area origin at 500 km:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Two places fall inside 500 km, thirteen beyond — matching the geo_distance query answer:
{ ... "aggregations": { "by_distance": { "buckets": [ { "key": "*-500000", "doc_count": 2 }, { "key": "500000-*", "doc_count": 13 } ] } } } Use cases # Radius reporting. “Stores within 50 km / 50–200 km / beyond” as one request — the classic store-locator bands. Delivery-zone coverage. Ring a warehouse origin and nest a sum per ring to weigh each zone’s demand, not just count it. Local-vs-remote splits. Any near/far comparison around a fixed point: users near an event, sensors near a fault line. Query faceting. Combine with a geo_bounding_box query so the rings summarize only the mapped viewport.
Parameters for geo_distance # field (Required, string) geo_point field you wish to aggregate. origin (Required, object) { "lat": …, "lon": … } center point (a "lat,lon" string is also accepted). ranges (Required, object array) Buckets with optional from / to in metres (from inclusive, to exclusive); key names a bucket. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per ring. Distances are always computed and reported in metres; the unit and distance_type parameters are not accepted.
Related # range — the same bucketing over plain numeric fields geohash_grid, geotile_grid — grid-shaped geo bucketing geo_distance query — filter to one radius instead of counting bands geo_centroid — where inside a ring the points actually sit
title: Geo distance aggregation

content:
Geo centroid aggregation # A metrics aggregation computing the centroid (mean latitude and longitude) of all geo_point values.
How it works # The engine sums latitudes and longitudes across the bucket’s geo_point values and divides by the count:
{ "location": { "lat": .., "lon": .. }, "count": 15 } The mean is arithmetic per axis (a planar average, not spherical) — exact enough at city or country scale, drifting only for extents that cross the 180th meridian or span hemispheres. Every parseable point counts once; there is no weight field. The result is null when the bucket holds no points. Under distributed fan-out the coordinator keeps its own shard’s value (geo metrics have no mergeable intermediate), so single-node results are the exact ones. Like every geo_point consumer, the aggregation sees points normalized at ingestion: {"lat": .., "lon": ..}, [lon, lat] (longitude first) or a "lat,lon" string, all stored as two-dimensional BKD points. Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Returns the count of points and their centroid — the natural center point for map placement. Over the 15 places: count: 15, location about {lat 31.7484, lon 111.2181}.
A centroid per city — the usual bucketed form:
POST /places/_search { "size": 0, "aggs": { "cities": { "terms": { "field": "city" }, "aggs": { "pin": { "geo_centroid": { "field": "location" } } } } } } Beijing’s bucket averages its two stores; every other city has one point and its centroid is that point.
Use cases # Center the map — the initial camera position over a result set, cheaper than fetching every point. Per-city anchors — terms(city) with a geo_centroid inside derives each city’s pin from its own member points (Beijing’s two stores, Shanghai’s two, and so on). Facility siting sketch — the mean point of customer or store locations as a first approximation for a depot. Cluster labels — pair with geohash grid to place each cell’s label at the cell’s own center. Parameters for geo_centroid # field (Required, string) geo_point field you wish to aggregate. Related # geo_bounds — the extent around the same points. geohash grid — cluster first, then centroid each cell. geo_distance buckets — ring buckets around a point.
title: Geo centroid aggregation

content:
Bucket sort aggregation # A parent pipeline aggregation sorting (and paginating) the bucket list by any of the bucket’s metrics — the pipeline counterpart of the request-level sort.
"by_revenue": { "bucket_sort": { "sort": [ { "revenue": { "order": "asc" } } ] } } How it works # Status, verified against the engine: bucket_sort is accepted but not yet active. The request parses — sort, from and size are accepted — but no reordering or truncation is applied: the parent aggregation’s buckets come back in the parent’s own order. A declared bucket_sort evaluates to a null metric, and nested declarations currently leave a "by_revenue": { "value": null } placeholder in each bucket (unlike bucket_selector, it does not clean up after itself).
What is available today for the same goals:
Cap the bucket count — the bucket aggregation’s own size (terms, rare_terms, …) limits how many buckets are produced in the first place (default 10). Filter buckets by metric — bucket_selector keeps exactly the buckets whose script predicate passes. Find the extremes — max_bucket / min_bucket extract the top or bottom bucket as a single value.
Sort client-side — until the pipeline lands, reorder the returned buckets in your application. When the implementation lands, requests written today are already the right shape: sort clauses over any per-bucket metric (or _key / _count), then from skipped, then at most size kept.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The request runs and answers; in the current engine the four type buckets arrive in the terms order (t-shirt, hat, mug, sticker, by document count) rather than by ascending revenue — the intended order would be mug (1350) before the three 1800s.
Use cases # What bucket_sort is for once active — and the working substitute for each today:
Top-N by metric — best-selling categories first: use bucket_selector with a threshold, or max_bucket for the single best. Pagination of buckets — from/size windows over a long bucket list: use the bucket aggregation’s size for a hard cap. Consistent display order — a dashboard that always wants worst-first buckets: sort the returned array client-side for now. Parameters for bucket_sort # sort (Optional, array) Sort clauses over the bucket’s metrics ([{ "revenue": { "order": "desc" } }]). Accepted; not yet applied. from (Optional, integer) Skip this many buckets — pagination offset. Accepted; not yet applied. size (Optional, integer) Keep at most this many buckets. Accepted; not yet applied. gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros. Related # bucket_selector — metric-based bucket filtering that works today bucket_script — derive the metric you want to sort by max_bucket, min_bucket — extract the extreme bucket now terms — size on the bucket aggregation itself
title: Bucket sort aggregation

content:
Partial update a document # Sometimes we may only need to update a portion of the fields of a document. A partial update fetches the stored document, merges the partial doc body, applies the ordered ops operators, and replaces the document in place under its original _id — the new values are visible to search immediately.
Examples # Update the org.id field of the document with system id 0,0 in the collection my-collection:
POST /my-collection/_update/0,0 { "doc": { "org": { "id": "infinilabs" } } } The API returns the following result:
{ "_collection": "default:my-collection", "_id": "0,0", "_key": "news_001", "result": "updated", "_shards": { "total": 1, "successful": 1, "failed": 0 } } For requests that carry ops, the response also reports what was applied: applied_ops (the number of operators) and ops (a one-liner per applied operator, in order).
Atomic-style operators are sent as an ordered ops list; each entry addresses a (dotted) field path and each operator sees the effect of the previous one:
POST /my-collection/_update/0,0 { "ops": [ { "op": "incr", "field": "views", "value": 1 }, { "op": "min", "field": "price", "value": 9.9 }, { "op": "toggle", "field": "active" }, { "op": "append", "field": "tags", "value": ["hot", "new"] }, { "op": "str_append", "field": "title", "value": " (updated)" }, { "op": "unset", "field": "status" } ] } The first failing operator aborts the whole update before any write happens, so the document is never left half-transformed.
The document keeps its _id across partial updates. Fields defined with "inplace": true in the schema (see Field parameters) are applied as O(1) in-place column writes; an update request that mixes inplace fields with regular fields is applied in one atomic step, with every field kind seeing its new value. The O(1) fast lane is operator-dependent — the Fast lane column in the tables below marks exactly which operators qualify.
Request # POST /<target>/_update/<doc_id>?retry_on_conflict=<n> { "doc": {<fields>}, "ops": [<operator>], "doc_as_upsert": false } Query parameters # retry_on_conflict (Optional, integer, default: 3) How many times to retry the update when the document is concurrently modified between this request’s fetch and its write (optimistic concurrency control). Each retry re-fetches the document and re-applies the doc merge and the ops list on the fresh base — safe because the rejected attempt wrote nothing. Set 0 to fail fast: a conflict then answers 409 version_conflict_exception for the client to handle. id_type (Optional, string, default: system id) Address <doc_id> as the user key: ?id_type=key resolves the key to its system id first (probing the key’s home shard). Without the parameter the path carries a system id (rolling,seq). ignore_nulls (Optional, boolean, default: false) Doris REPLACE_IF_NOT_NULL counterpart for sparse CDC rows: a null in the patch means “no data”, not “clear”. Null-valued keys are dropped from the doc merge and set operators with a null value are skipped; unset stays an explicit delete. routing (Required with id_type=key on a routed collection) — the routing VALUE that places the document (hash(<value>) — or its salted partition set, see salting). A bare key has no home partition there and answers 400.
The routing field itself is immutable on the update path: a patch whose doc merge or ops would change or remove it answers 400 — the stored value placed the document, and a drifted value would answer every routing-addressed read (and every relational preflight) with a miss. Omitting the field from the patch is fine (the stored value carries over); moving a document between routing values is a delete and re-create.
Path parameters # <target> (Required, string) Name of the collection to target. <doc_id> (Required, string) The system id of this document, in the <rolling>,<seq> form (e.g. 0,1), as returned in the _id field of index/search responses. Request body # doc (Optional, object) Partial document body, deep-merged into the stored source: nested objects merge recursively, scalars and arrays are replaced. ops (Optional, array) Ordered list of update operators, applied after the doc merge. Operators are applied in order; a field may appear in more than one operator and the effects compose sequentially. Supported operators — the Fast lane column marks the operators that can be applied as O(1) in-place column writes on "inplace": true fields — every unmarked operator, and any request shape the lane rejects, silently takes the read-modify-write path instead (see In-place fast lane eligibility): General
Operator Fields Effect Fast lane set field, value Set the field to value, creating intermediate objects for dotted paths. Yes — top-level inplace field, numeric/boolean value unset field Remove the field. Missing fields are a no-op. Yes — top-level inplace field set_if_absent field, value Set the field to value only when it is currently absent. No rename from, to Move the value from one (dotted) path to another. Fails when from does not exist. No current_date field Set the field to the current Unix time in milliseconds. No Numeric
Operator Fields Effect Fast lane incr field, value Add a numeric value (may be negative). A missing field starts from 0. Yes — integer field, integer value decr field, value Subtract a numeric value (may be negative). A missing field starts from 0. No mul field, value Multiply by a numeric value. A missing field stays 0. Yes — integer field, integer value min field, value Keep the smaller of the current value and value. Yes — value in the field’s family max field, value Keep the larger of the current value and value. Yes — value in the field’s family toggle field Flip a boolean field. A missing field is treated as false. Yes — boolean field Array
Every array operator views the current field the same way: a missing field starts as an empty array, and a scalar value is promoted to a one-element array first. None of the array operators are fast-lane eligible — they always take the read-modify-write path, even on inplace fields.
Operator Fields Effect append field, value Append to the array (an array value appends its elements). add_to_set field, value Append unless an equal element already exists. insert field, index, value Insert the element at index, clamped to the array length. pop field Remove the last element. shift field Remove the first element. clear field Set the field to the empty array []. slice field, value Keep the first value elements (value >= 0), or the last ` remove field, value Remove every element equal to value (an array value removes any of its elements). replace field, value Replace the whole array with value (a scalar becomes a one-element array). String
String operators require a string-typed field; a missing field starts from the empty string. String operators are never fast-lane eligible — they always take the read-modify-write path.
Operator Fields Effect str_append field, value Append value to the end of the string. str_prepend field, value Prepend value to the beginning of the string. str_replace field, value, replacement Replace every occurrence of the value substring with replacement. str_trim field Trim leading and trailing whitespace. doc_as_upsert (Optional, boolean, default: false) When true and the document does not exist, the partial body is indexed as a brand-new document instead of returning 404. When false, a missing document fails the request. In-place fast lane eligibility # Exactly seven operators can take the O(1) in-place fast lane: set, unset, incr, mul, min, max, and toggle. The whole request takes the fast lane only when every condition below holds; otherwise it silently falls back to the read-modify-write path, with the same end result:
the request is ops-only: no doc body and no doc_as_upsert; every field is a top-level field (dotted paths disqualify) declared with "inplace": true in the schema and typed numeric or boolean — see Field parameters for how to declare the parameter and for the column semantics (visibility, missing-field defaults, integer overflow wrapping);
at most one operator per field — a repeated field needs sequential composition; each value matches its field’s family: an integer for integer fields, a non-negative integer for unsigned fields, a number for float fields, a boolean for boolean fields; incr and mul additionally require an integer-typed field and an integer value — float fields and float deltas fall back, and so does a negative delta on an unsigned field; toggle additionally requires a boolean-typed field. decr, set_if_absent, rename, current_date, and every array and string operator never take the fast lane. On the read-modify-write path they still update inplace fields correctly — the merged document’s write-back updates the columns — they just pay the fetch/replace cost and the optimistic- concurrency retries.
Concurrency semantics # The read-modify-write path enforces optimistic concurrency control: the fetch reads the document together with its version, and the write back is a conditional replace the engine rejects when a concurrent write — another partial update, a keyed re-index, or an inplace column update — advanced the version in between. A rejected attempt wrote nothing, so the request retries (re-fetch, re-merge, re-apply) up to retry_on_conflict times; an exhausted conflict answers:
{ "error": { "type": "version_conflict_exception", "reason": "document [0,5] version conflict, expected [7], current [9]: ..." } } Two notes:
Fields declared with "inplace": true and updated through an eligible ops-only request (see In-place fast lane eligibility) take the fast lane instead, which applies its operators atomically inside the engine — no fetch/replace race exists there and no retrying is needed. Inplace values become visible the moment the column write lands — search snapshots pin the document set, not the values. A partial update forwarded to a primary on another node carries the fetched version over the RPC as well — the conditional gate is enforced on the primary’s node either way. (During a mixed-version rolling upgrade, an older primary ignores the version and the update runs ungated there.) Fast-lane inplace updates replicate at the value level: the primary ships each operator’s resulting absolute values to the replicas, which apply them directly to their own columns. Delivery is idempotent — a duplicate replay of the same values is a no-op — and a replica that cannot take the fast lane falls back to applying the update through its own engine.
title: Partial update a document

content:
Geo bounds aggregation # A metrics aggregation computing the bounding box (top-left / bottom-right corners) of all geo_point values — the rectangle that just contains every point in the bucket.
How it works # The engine scans the bucket’s geo_point column, tracks the minimum and maximum latitude and longitude, and emits:
{ "bounds": { "top_left": { "lat": <max lat>, "lon": <min lon> }, "bottom_right": { "lat": <min lat>, "lon": <max lon> } } } null when the bucket holds no parseable point. The column-store fast path and the executor path run the same min/max scan.
