Defaults to false. routing (Required for a key-addressed fetch on a routed collection) — the routing VALUE (?routing=org-a) that places the document. A bare key has no home partition there and answers 400; a value pointing at the wrong partition is an honest 404. On collections without a routing field the parameter addresses nothing and is a 400. You can also use the HEAD method to simply find if the specified document exists or not.
HEAD /<target>/_doc/<doc_id>
title: Fetch a document

content:
Derivative aggregation # A parent pipeline aggregation computing the difference between each bucket’s metric and the previous bucket’s — “how much did it change”. A time series says where you are; the derivative says which way and how fast you are moving, bucket by bucket. The first bucket has no predecessor and answers null.
"delta": { "derivative": { "buckets_path": "revenue" } } How it works # derivative is declared inside the multi-bucket aggregation it decorates (the parent style), next to the metric it consumes. After the buckets are built, the engine walks them in order and attaches current − previous to each bucket under the pipeline’s own name:
"buckets": [ { "key_as_string": "2024-01-01", "doc_count": 1, "revenue": { "value": 15 }, "delta": { "value": null } }, { "key_as_string": "2024-01-05", "doc_count": 1, "revenue": { "value": 30 }, "delta": { "value": 15.0 } } ] Details verified against the engine:
buckets_path addresses a metric in the same bucket: a bare name ("revenue"), optionally with a .value suffix ("revenue.value"). "_count" differences the bucket document counts. A bucket whose metric is missing gets a null derivative, and the next bucket is differenced against the last non-null value — a single gap does not break the chain. Bucket order is the parent’s output order — for a date_histogram that is chronological, which is what makes the differences meaningful. The unit parameter (report the derivative per day/week in a date_histogram) is not implemented: no per-time-unit scaling, and no normalized_value in the response. A derivative over daily buckets is “per bucket”, which is per day only if every bucket is one day wide. gap_policy only takes effect in the sibling placement below; the nested form always answers null for gaps as described above. A second, engine-specific placement also works: declaring derivative next to the bucket aggregation, with buckets_path: "per_day>revenue", returns a standalone buckets array (keys 1..n−1) holding the differences — the same numbers, outside the parent’s response.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Every day in the dataset sells exactly once, so each delta is simply how the day’s amount moved against the previous selling day.
Use cases # Day-over-day change — daily revenue with its derivative: growth days read positive, dips negative, zeros flat. Spike detection — a delta far beyond its neighbors flags the bucket where a series jumped (an outage’s recovery, a campaign’s lift) without fetching the raw series. Growth per period — calendar_interval: "month" buckets and their derivatives give month-over-month deltas of any per-month metric. Volume shifts — buckets_path: "_count" differences document counts: when did traffic itself, not the average, move? Parameters for derivative # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric in the SAME bucket ("revenue"). gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros — effective in the sibling placement; the nested form answers null on gaps. format (Optional, string) Output number format. Accepted for compatibility; not applied to the value in the current engine. unit Not implemented — accepted for compatibility and ignored. Related # cumulative_sum — the running total each bucket feeds into; serial_diff — the difference lag buckets back, for detrending moving_fn — window statistics over the same series
title: Derivative aggregation

content:
Extended stats aggregation # A multi-value metrics aggregation extending stats with squares, variance, standard deviation and their lower/upper bounds. Where stats says what the values are, extended_stats says how tightly they cluster around the mean — the input for outlier bands, quality gates and anything else built on “how unusual is this value”.
How it works # The engine walks the matching documents once, maintaining a running count, sum, sum_of_squares, minimum and maximum — the same single pass as stats, plus one multiply-add for the squares. Everything downstream is derived from these raw moments, and is exact (no sampling, no sketches):
avg = sum / count variance (variance_population) = sum_of_squares / count − avg², clamped at zero to guard against floating-point cancellation variance_sampling = (sum_of_squares − sum² / count) / (count − 1) — 0 when only one value was seen std_deviation (and the _population / _sampling variants) = the square roots of the variances above The population statistics divide by N and describe the matched set itself; the sampling variants divide by N−1 and estimate the underlying distribution — on large matches the two converge.
std_deviation_bounds are avg ± sigma × std_deviation, with sigma defaulting to 2 (the classic 95% band).
Documents missing the field are skipped by default; with missing set, each such document contributes the default to every accumulator. On the column-store fast path (the production executor) each segment’s column is decoded once and walked with for_each_f64. Distributed requests stay exact: per-shard count, sum and sum_of_squares merge by addition, and every variance and deviation is recomputed from the merged moments.
Example # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Returns count, min, max, avg, sum, sum_of_squares, variance, variance_population, variance_sampling, std_deviation, std_deviation_population, std_deviation_sampling plus std_deviation_bounds (upper/lower at ±2σ).
Use cases # Outlier banding. Over the teaching sales, avg = 27.5 and std_deviation ≈ 14.79, so the default bounds are ≈ −2.08..57.08 — the 60-priced stickers are the only sales outside the 2σ band. Spread per segment. Nested under terms, each product type prices uniformly in the teaching data, so every bucket’s variance is 0 — any real pricing drift would light up immediately. Population vs sampling. With 120 values, variance = 218.75 while variance_sampling ≈ 220.59; report the population figure for describing the matched set, the sampling one when estimating beyond it. Adjustable strictness. sigma: 3 widens the band for alert-when-truly-extreme; a fractional sigma tightens it for high-sensitivity monitoring dashboards. Feed downstream math. The moments are the raw material for z-scores ( normalize z-score) and significance tests ( t_test) without re-scanning the field. Parameters for extended_stats # field (Required, string) Numeric field you wish to aggregate. sigma (Optional, float, default: 2) Multiplier for the standard deviation bounds. missing (Optional, number) Value used for documents missing the field; it contributes to every accumulator. Related # stats — the five basic numbers without the moments percentiles — robust spread (medians) when the mean is skewed median_absolute_deviation — a outlier-resistant alternative to σ normalize — z-scores built from these moments
title: Extended stats aggregation

content:
Auto date histogram aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation like date_histogram, but you choose the NUMBER of buckets and the engine picks the interval that best fits. It solves the cold-start problem of time charts: when you do not know whether the data spans minutes or years, you state the resolution you want on screen and let the ladder decide the unit.
How it works # The engine reads every date value (epoch milliseconds), takes the data extent max − min, and divides by the buckets target to get a rough per-bucket width. That width is matched against a fixed ladder, and the smallest interval that covers it wins: 1s, 1m, 5m, 10m, 30m, 1h, 6h, 12h, 1d, 1w as fixed intervals; beyond a week the calendar units month, quarter, year (and multi-year multiples for very long extents). The pick is one closed-form step, not an iterative search.
Fixed-interval grids anchor at the data minimum; calendar picks floor to civil boundaries (month starts, quarter starts, year starts), so bucket keys stay on human dates. Documents are then assigned to the grid points, capped at 100,000 buckets as a runaway guard.
Each bucket reports key (the boundary as epoch milliseconds) and doc_count. The engine does not echo the chosen interval next to the result — infer it from the key spacing, or compare with an explicit date_histogram.
Example # Ask for three buckets over the sales timeline:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The 120 teaching sales span 2024-01-01 to 2025-04-21 — a rough width of ~5.2 months per bucket, which the ladder rounds up to year. The response carries two buckets: 2024-01-01 (92 sales) and 2025-01-01 (28 sales). With the default buckets: 10 the same span picks quarter and returns six buckets (23/23/23/23/22/6).
Use cases # Exploring an unfamiliar date field. First contact with a new dataset: one auto_date_histogram tells you its true timescale before you hand-pick intervals for the real dashboard. Adaptive dashboards. Widgets that render “whatever this filter matches” cannot know the right unit in advance — a bucket-count target keeps the chart readable at any zoom level. Varying retention windows. The same query over “last hour” and “last year” (a date filter plus this agg) rescales from minutes to quarters without per-page interval logic. Parameters for auto_date_histogram # field (Required, string) Date field you wish to aggregate. buckets (Optional, integer, default: 10) Target number of buckets. The ladder rounds up to a coarser unit, so the result often carries fewer buckets than requested. minimum_interval (Optional, string) Smallest interval the picker may choose. Accepted for compatibility; the engine does not currently enforce a floor. format / time_zone (Optional, string) Accepted for compatibility; keys are epoch milliseconds and boundaries are computed in UTC. Related # date_histogram — you name the interval explicitly, including calendar units. histogram — the numeric-field counterpart. composite — paginated date_histogram dimension when the bucket count must be bounded page by page.
title: Auto date histogram aggregation

content:
Stats aggregation # A multi-value metrics aggregation that computes basic statistics (min, max, sum, count, avg) over numeric values extracted from the aggregated documents. It is avg, min, max and sum folded into one request — the five numbers most dashboards put side by side, for the price of one column scan.
How it works # The engine walks the matching documents once, maintaining a running count, sum, minimum and maximum; avg is derived at the end as sum / count. Everything is exact — no sampling, no sketches. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read: integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) contribute, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.
Documents that lack the field are skipped by default, lowering the count. With missing set, every such document contributes the default to the sum, the extremes and the count, exactly as if the field had carried it.
On the column-store fast path (the production executor) the five numbers come out of one fused pass per segment (stats_f64, a full-segment SIMD scan when eligible) instead of three separate sum/min/max walks. The result carries count and sum alongside avg, which is what makes merging exact: distributed requests combine per-shard count/sum by addition, fold min/max pairwise, and recompute avg from the merged totals — identical to a single-node answer.
When no document contributed a value, count is 0, sum is 0.0, and min, max and avg are null.
Examples # The five numbers as one statement on the SQL side — COUNT(*), MIN, MAX, AVG, SUM side by side:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "prices_stats": { "stats": { "field": "price" } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "prices_stats": { "count": 120, "min": 15.0, "max": 60.0, "avg": 27.5, "sum": 3300.0 } } } Use cases # One-request KPI cards. The five numbers every summary header shows — over the teaching sales: count 120, min 15.0, max 60.0, avg 27.5, sum 3300.0 — in a single aggregation instead of five. Per-group profiles. Nested under terms on type, each bucket gets its own five numbers — hats: count 30, min 30, max 30, avg 30, sum 900 — the shape of each product line at a glance. Spread intuition before percentiles. min and max against avg show how wide the distribution runs; when the mean hugs an extreme, reach for percentiles or a histogram. Data sanity on ingest. A count below the match count means missing values; a min or max outside the legal range flags bad writes before anything downstream notices. Cheap composite metrics. Divide sum by count client-side, or feed both into a bucket_script to build ratios per bucket without a second pass. Parameters for stats # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. missing (Optional, value) Value used for documents missing the field. extended_stats takes the same parameters and additionally returns variance, standard deviation and related statistics.
Related # extended_stats — adds sum-of-squares, variance and standard deviation avg / sum / min / max — the individual numbers when you only need one stats_bucket — the same statistics over another aggregation’s buckets
title: Stats aggregation

content:
Exists query # Returns documents that contain an indexed value for a specific field.
A document matches when the field has at least one non-null value — an empty string or an empty array does not count as existing.
Inside a nested query: supported — matches elements that carry the field.
How it works # exists never touches the inverted index. It is answered from the stored-field / column layer, where every document either carries the key or does not:
The field’s value must be present and non-null. An empty string ("") and an empty array ([]) both read as absent. Dotted paths (url.path) resolve in three steps: the flat key first, then descent into object values segment by segment, and finally — for an object parent such as plain url — a prefix rule: the parent exists when any flattened url.* sub-key is present. The check runs identically on the live layer and on built immutable segments (an earlier divergence — exists silently matching everything on built segments — is pinned by a differential test on both layers). Scoring. A match contributes a constant score (the boost), never a relevance signal: the query answers shape, not content. It costs about as much as a filter and composes freely under bool filter, must_not and must.
Examples # The following search returns every log line that carries a url.path — all 150 documents in the logs dataset, since the field is always present there.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The SQL twin quotes the dotted name ("url.path") — unquoted, the dot would parse as part of an expression and the reference is rejected.
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "exists": { "field": "user" } } } Use cases # Data-quality audits. 24 of the 44 articles carry no author; exists on that keyword field returns the other 20 — the starting point of a “fix the missing metadata” ticket. Optional-field gating. Only evaluate a scored clause (or a highlight, or a sort) on documents that actually have the field, by intersecting with exists in a bool.filter. The negated form. bool.must_not.exists is the query twin of the missing aggregation — find the documents a field-based feature will silently skip.
Object-shape probing. exists on the parent (url) answers “does this doc have any URL data at all?” without naming every sub-field. Parameters for exists # field (Required, string) Field you wish to check for presence. Related # missing aggregation — the inverse question, counted per bucket instead of matched per document. term / terms — once presence is settled, match the value. bool — combine with must_not for the not-exists form. nested — per-element existence inside arrays of objects.
title: Exists query

content:
Date histogram aggregation # This multi-bucket aggregation is similar to the normal histogram, but it can only be used with date fields. Dates are represented internally as epoch milliseconds, so the plain histogram can technically run on them too — but calendar intervals are not a fixed length (a month is 28–31 days), which is exactly what this aggregation handles.
How it works # Date fields store epoch milliseconds at ingest, and the aggregation builds its grid on those numbers. calendar_interval and fixed_interval select between two grid types (exactly one must be set):
Calendar intervals (minute, hour, day, week, month, quarter, year, or 1m/1h/1d/1w/1M/1q/1y — single quantities only). Months, quarters, years and weeks floor to civil boundaries: bucket keys are real month starts and Monday weeks, so February is as long as it is. Use these for anything a human reads. Fixed intervals (ms/s/m/h/d units with multiples, like "30m" or "7d"). A fixed number of milliseconds, anchored at the epoch — the grid never bends for the calendar. Each bucket reports key (the boundary as epoch milliseconds) and key_as_string, rendered in UTC as strict_date_optional_time (2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z). The format and time_zone parameters are accepted for compatibility; this engine currently always renders the UTC ISO form and computes boundaries in UTC.
min_doc_count (default 0) drops thin buckets. Unlike the numeric histogram, only buckets that actually received documents are emitted — there is no gap-filling between the data minimum and maximum. Two parameters widen the picture: offset (a duration string like "+1d" or a millisecond number) shifts every boundary — the keys report the shifted boundaries — and hard_bounds ({min, max} as epoch millis) both clips the window and force-materializes every bucket inside it, calendar units stepping real months, up to a 100,000-bucket guard. date_nanos-magnitude values (≥ 10¹⁷) are scaled down to milliseconds so both mappings land on one grid.
Examples # Sales per year — DATE_TRUNC(date, 'year') is the same grouping key on the SQL side:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "sales_over_time": { "date_histogram": { "field": "date", "calendar_interval": "year" } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "sales_over_time": { "buckets": [ { "key_as_string": "2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z", "key": 1704067200000, "doc_count": 92 }, { "key_as_string": "2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z", "key": 1735689600000, "doc_count": 28 } ] } } } Parameters for date_histogram # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate (must be a date / epoch_millis field). min_doc_count (Optional, integer) Minimum number of documents in a bucket to include it. Defaults to 0. format (Optional, string) Date format for the bucket key string. Accepted for compatibility; this engine always renders the strict_date_optional_time UTC form. time_zone (Optional, string) Time zone offset, e.g. +08:00 or -05:00. Accepted for compatibility; bucketing and keys are currently always UTC. offset (Optional, string | number) Shift every bucket boundary by this duration ("+1d", "-2h") or millisecond count; keys report the shifted boundaries. hard_bounds (Optional, object) {min, max} epoch-millis bounds: clip the window and force-materialize every bucket inside it, even at zero documents. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. One of calendar_interval or fixed_interval must be set.
calendar_interval # (Optional, string) Calendar-aware intervals are configured with the calendar_interval parameter. You can specify calendar intervals using the unit name, such as month, or as a single unit quantity, such as 1M. For example, day and 1d are equivalent. Multiple quantities, such as 2d, are not supported.
The accepted calendar intervals are:
minute, 1m All minutes begin at 00 seconds. One minute is the interval between 00 seconds of the first minute and 00 seconds of the following minute in the specified time zone, compensating for any intervening leap seconds, so that the number of minutes and seconds past the hour is the same at the start and end. hour, 1h All hours begin at 00 minutes and 00 seconds. One hour (1h) is the interval between 00:00 minutes of the first hour and 00:00 minutes of the following hour in the specified time zone, compensating for any intervening leap seconds, so that the number of minutes and seconds past the hour is the same at the start and end. day, 1d All days begin at the earliest possible time, which is usually 00:00:00 (midnight). One day (1d) is the interval between the start of the day and the start of the following day in the specified time zone, compensating for any intervening time changes. week, 1w One week is the interval between the start day_of_week:hour:minute:second and the same day of the week and time of the following week in the specified time zone. month, 1M One month is the interval between the start day of the month and time of day and the same day of the month and time of the following month in the specified time zone, so that the day of the month and time of day are the same at the start and end. quarter, 1q One quarter is the interval between the start day of the month and time of day and the same day of the month and time of day three months later, so that the day of the month and time of day are the same at the start and end. year, 1y One year is the interval between the start day of the month and time of day and the same day of the month and time of day the following year in the specified time zone, so that the date and time are the same at the start and end. fixed_interval # Fixed intervals are configured with the fixed_interval parameter.
In contrast to calendar-aware intervals, fixed intervals are a fixed number of SI units and never deviate, regardless of where they fall on the calendar. One second is always composed of 1000ms. This allows fixed intervals to be specified in any multiple of the supported units.
However, it means fixed intervals cannot express other units such as months, since the duration of a month is not a fixed quantity. Attempting to specify a calendar interval like month or quarter will throw an exception.
The accepted units for fixed intervals are:
milliseconds (ms) A single millisecond. This is a very, very small interval. seconds (s) Defined as 1000 milliseconds each. minutes (m) Defined as 60 seconds each (60,000 milliseconds). All minutes begin at 00 seconds. hours (h) Defined as 60 minutes each (3,600,000 milliseconds). All hours begin at 00 minutes and 00 seconds. days (d) Defined as 24 hours (86,400,000 milliseconds). All days begin at the earliest possible time, which is usually 00:00:00 (midnight). Range fields # date_histogram accepts date_range fields: each stored range counts in every calendar bucket it overlaps. offset shifts the bucket grid (keys report the shifted boundaries), and hard_bounds clips the window while force-materializing every in-calendar-window bucket — open-ended stored ranges extend to that window.
Use cases # Log timelines. The teaching logs dataset carries 150 events across one June week; a calendar_interval: "day" histogram returns one bucket per day (24 events each, 6 on the last), exactly the series a monitoring chart plots. Period comparisons. Bucket sales by month or quarter and nest a sum — revenue per period falls out of one query. Over the 120 teaching sales, a year histogram splits them 92 (2024) / 28 (2025). Business-day windows. calendar_interval: "week" floors to Mondays; combined with offset you can slide week boundaries to Sunday starts without changing the data. Fixed-window SLA views. fixed_interval: "1h" gives wall-clock-aligned, never-drifting windows for rate charts, while calendar intervals keep human-readable month edges. Bounded reports. hard_bounds pins a chart to the reporting window (empty in-window buckets included) regardless of when the first and last matching documents happened to arrive. Related # histogram — the same fixed-grid idea over plain numeric fields. auto_date_histogram — pick the bucket count, let the engine choose day/week/month/year. variable_width_histogram — adaptive bucket edges over numeric data. date_range — a handful of named periods instead of a regular grid. composite — paginate a date_histogram dimension with an after cursor.
title: Date histogram aggregation

content:
Weighted average aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that computes the weighted average of numeric values. Each document contributes value × weight, divided by the total weight — e.g. an average price weighted by quantity sold. When documents are not all equally important, avg is the wrong tool and this is the right one.
How it works # The engine walks the matching documents once, accumulating Σ(value × weight) in the numerator and Σ weight in the denominator; the result is their quotient. Both sides are computed in the same pass over two columns, so the pairing of a document’s value with its own weight is never lost.
A document contributes only when both sides resolve: a missing value is substituted with value.missing if given, a missing weight with weight.missing — otherwise the document is dropped entirely, from the numerator and the denominator. Weights of 0 contribute nothing to either side; when the total weight is not positive, the result is null.
value and weight each take a field (scripts are rejected here — use a scripted avg or scripted_metric for computed sources).
Distributed requests carry a caveat: the finalized {"value": …} shape discards the two sums, so the coordinator cannot combine shard results exactly and falls back to the arithmetic mean of the per-shard means. On the teaching single-shard datasets the result is exact; on multi-shard deployments treat the number as an approximation.
Example # Average unit price weighted by qty (larger purchases count more):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The plain avg of price is 27.5; quantity-weighted it is 28.125.
Use cases # True average unit price. Weight price by qty over the 120 sales: 28.125 — exactly sum(amount) / sum(qty) (6750 / 240), the number finance means by “average price actually sold at”. Inventory value per unit. products averages 15.43 on price, but 15.87 when weighted by stock — the stockroom skews toward pricier items, a gap plain avg hides. Why the two diverge. In the teaching data qty is positively correlated with price (sticker sales average 3 units, t-shirts 2), so heavier weights sit on higher values and drag the weighted mean above the plain one; when weights correlate with the value, the gap is the signal. Partial-data tolerance. Sparse weight fields don’t corrupt the mean: documents without a weight drop out of both sums via weight.missing, so an unlogged quantity shrinks the denominator honestly instead of counting as zero. Blended metrics. Any score-times-importance blend — engagement time weighted by session count, rating weighted by review count — is this aggregation with two field names. Parameters for weighted_avg # value (Required, object) field — the numeric field whose values are averaged. weight (Required, object) field — the numeric field used as the per-document weight. value.missing / weight.missing (Optional, number) Value substituted for documents missing the field; a missing weight defaults the document out of the average. Related # avg — the unweighted mean over the same field sum — the numerator without the division stats — count/min/max/avg/sum for context around either mean scripted_metric — computed value or weight sources
title: Weighted average aggregation

content:
Variable width histogram aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation like histogram, but bucket edges adapt to the data so each bucket holds roughly the same number of documents. Fixed grids go blind where data is sparse and waste resolution where it is dense; the variable-width form spends its buckets where the documents actually are.
How it works # The engine collects every numeric value, sorts it, and partitions the sorted run into buckets contiguous segments such that the sum of squared distances to each segment’s mean is minimal — the classic one-dimensional k-segmentation problem, solved exactly with dynamic programming and prefix sums (an O(1) cost function per candidate cut). When n × k exceeds 1,048,576 it falls back to equal-count chunking, a linear-time approximation. buckets is capped at the number of distinct values, so asking for more buckets than there are values simply yields one bucket per value.
Each bucket reports doc_count and a key object with three fields: min and max (the bucket’s data extent) and key (their midpoint). Buckets are returned in ascending order — dense regions come back as narrow [min, max] windows, sparse tails as wide ones.
Example # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The teaching prices take only four distinct values (15/30/45/60), so four buckets means one value per bucket: 60/30/20/10 documents behind min = max edges. Ask for two buckets instead and the optimal split runs [15, 30] with 90 sales against [45, 60] with 30 — the edge moves to where the mass divides, not to a fixed grid line.
Use cases # Equi-populous report rows. “Top decile”, “quintile”, “the 1%” are statements about counts, not value widths — k segments over sorted data is exactly that grouping, with the bucket min/max reporting each band’s actual edges. Skewed numeric fields. Latency, income, view counts: a fixed interval either smears the bulk into one bucket or shreds the tail into thousands. Adaptive edges keep every bucket informative. Pre-histogram reconnaissance. Run it before a histogram to see where the mass sits, then fix the interval where it matters.
Compact distribution summaries. Feed the min/max/doc_count triples straight into a heat strip or a box-style rendering. Parameters for variable_width_histogram # field (Required, string) Numeric field you wish to aggregate. buckets (Optional, integer, default: 10) Target number of buckets; capped at the number of distinct values. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Related # histogram — fixed-width buckets when the grid itself must be stable across queries. percentiles — quantile cut points without committing to a bucket count. auto_date_histogram — the same “target a bucket count” idea over date fields.
title: Variable width histogram aggregation

content:
Range query # Returns documents that contain terms within a provided range.
Use it for intervals: prices between two numbers, events inside a time window, names inside an alphabetical span — anything expressible as “from / to” bounds rather than a list of exact values.
Inside a nested query: supported — the bounds apply per array element.
How it works # The engine picks the index by field type:
Numeric and date fields — the per-field BKD range index (or the column store’s value-sorted region on merged segments without a BKD index). The BKD traversal returns an exact, pre-computed document-id list — no posting verification, no false positives. Date bounds go through the engine’s date parser: epoch numerics parse as epoch milliseconds, and ISO-8601 strings (2024-06-01, 2024-06-01T00:00:00Z) parse to their UTC instant before the traversal. keyword / text fields — a lexicographic term range over the ordered dictionary: every term between the bounds is expanded and their postings unioned, exactly like a should of term queries. Bounds are first run through the field’s normalizer, if one is mapped, so date-descending keys sort as they were indexed. Dual bounds conjoin. When you send both gt and gte (or both lt and lte), the engine applies them conjunctively and keeps the tighter bound — a tie resolves to the exclusive variant, so gt: 100, gte: 150 reads as ≥ 150. At most one bound per side is usually written; the conjoin exists so machine-generated bodies that carry both still behave deterministically.
Scoring. Range matches carry a constant score — the boost (1.0 by default) — with no BM25 input. A range is therefore the natural shape for bool.filter clauses: sliding time windows and price bands constrain the candidate set without touching relevance.
Date knobs. format and time_zone are accepted on the wire for compatibility; today the engine parses bounds with its built-in date parser and does not yet apply these two knobs.
Examples # The following search returns the sales whose price is between 45 and 60 — 20 of the 120 documents in the sales dataset.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. GET /_search { "query": { "range": { "field": "age", "gte": 10, "lte": 20 } } } Use cases # Time windows. sales.date ≥ 2025-01-01 returns the 28 newest sales of 120 — the rolling-window filter behind every “last N months” dashboard. customers.since ≥ 2025-01-01 scopes to the 7 newest customers of 20. Price bands. price ≤ 30 over sales matches the 90 economy sales (60 at 15, 30 at 30); pair one range with a terms on status for segmented funnels.
Lexicographic spans. Over keyword fields the same query slices alphabetically — id ranges, A*–M* name partitions — through the dictionary walk described above. Alerting thresholds. Latency or disk-usage bounds as a must_not.range (the violation detector) inside a monitoring bool. Parameters for range # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. gt (Optional) Greater than. gte (Optional) Greater than or equal to. lt (Optional) Less than. lte (Optional) Less than or equal to. format (Optional, string) Date format for date-field range bounds. Accepted for body compatibility; not yet applied. time_zone (Optional, string) Time zone for date-field range bounds, e.g. +08:00. Accepted for body compatibility; not yet applied. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Decrease or increase the relevance scores of the query. relation (Optional, string) How the range matches range-typed fields: INTERSECTS (default), CONTAINS, or WITHIN. Related # range aggregation — bucket the same field into named intervals; the query filters, the aggregation counts. date_range / date_histogram aggregations — time-bucketed views of the date windows a range query filters on. term — the single-point special case, served by the same BKD index on numeric and date fields. exists — the boundless question: does the field carry any value at all?
title: Range query

content:
Lesson 9 — Operations # Keeping a node healthy: partial updates in place, compaction, the change feed, and reading cluster state. This lesson is server-side — start a node as in Lesson 1 and run the curls against it.
The use case # The features that matter once the node serves real traffic: mutating documents without rewriting them, keeping storage healthy, reacting to every write, and reading cluster state. The questions this lesson answers:
“Decrement stock on a checkout without a read-modify-write race” — partial updates: column-level ops, applied in place. “Settle storage after a big import” — on-demand compaction. “React to every write — invalidate caches, feed downstream systems” — the change feed. “Is the cluster healthy right now?” — health, state, and stats endpoints. Partial updates in place # The document update API takes doc (merge), ops (arithmetic), or both:
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "ops": [ { "op": "incr", "field": "qty", "value": -1 }, { "op": "min", "field": "price", "value": 9.9 } ] }' \ http://localhost:28000/sales/_update/<doc_id> Eleven operators — set, unset, incr, mul, min, max, toggle, append, add_to_set, rename, current_date — each a column-level write, not a read-modify-write of the whole document. Fields mapped with "inplace": true apply as O(1) column writes; the full semantics (visibility, arithmetic, mixed updates) are in the partial update reference and
in-place columns.
No refresh follows: search sees the new values on the next request.
Compaction # Realtime writes land in a mutable layer; background epochs freeze and merge them. When you want that on demand — after a bulk import, before a benchmark:
graph LR W("incoming writes") --> M("mutable layerrealtime, searchable") M -->|"background epochs freeze"| F("frozen epochs") F -->|"_compact: merge on demand"| S("merged segments") curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ http://localhost:28000/sales/_compact The compaction reference covers the response fields; node-level compaction controls live in node settings (pause, tick interval, concurrency).
The change feed # Consume writes as they happen with GET /{collection}/_changes — the cursor format and consumption loop are in the change feed reference:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ 'http://localhost:28000/sales/_changes?limit=10' Reading the cluster # GET /_cluster/health?level=shards — one glance, every level from cluster to shard ( health reference). GET /_cluster/state — the catalog view; filter with /_cluster/state/collections,shards. GET /_node/_local/stats — per-node counters; the full endpoint map is in node observability.
GET /_node/_local/settings — dynamic settings, changeable at runtime ( node settings), including the live log level. Where to go from here # The full search reference, one page per query type, every parameter. Deployment for systemd, NUMA and multi-node joins. The playground to keep experimenting in the browser.
title: Lesson 9 — Operations

content:
Intervals query # The intervals query is a rule language for term positions: it matches documents whose analyzed token stream satisfies proximity rules you express as a tree — fixed token sequences, maximum gaps, required order, unions, multi-term leaves, and positional filters between sibling rules. It covers everything phrase expresses plus the shapes a phrase cannot: unordered combinations with bounded width, disjunctions of positional rules, and prefix/wildcard/fuzzy/regexp leaves inside positional composition.
Requires a position index (text fields analyzed with positions — the default).
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — intervals clauses are rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause. Use phrase with slop for positional logic on nested fields.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. How it works # Evaluation is two-phase. First the rule tree compiles per segment: match texts are tokenized with the field’s analyzer (or the rule’s analyzer), and every multi-term leaf (prefix, wildcard, fuzzy, regexp, range) resolves to the set of dictionary terms its pattern matches. The leaves that sit outside every any_of form the candidate set — a conjunction (bool-must over all of those terms), a cheap inverted-index superset of the answer. Phase two decodes each candidate’s token positions and evaluates the interval grammar exactly: leaves yield one-position spans at every occurrence, all_of picks one span per sub-rule and checks order plus the gap budget, any_of unions, and filter predicates retain or drop spans positionally. Match-ness is exact; only the BM25 frequency is capped (at 1024 combinations per node), so pathological rules cost score resolution, never correctness. The same evaluator runs on every serving path (block producer, realtime segment, disk segment).
Two grammar details worth knowing: a match rule is an implicit all_of whose tokens may never share one position (so "search search" needs two real occurrences), and max_gaps counts the uncovered positions inside the combined span — (end − start + 1) minus the covered positions — not the distance between the outer terms.
Rule family # A rule object sets exactly one of: match, all_of, any_of, prefix, wildcard, fuzzy, regexp, or range — plus its own optional filter.
match # Analyzes query and matches its tokens as one combination:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "intervals": { "message": { "match": { "query": "cluster node restart", "max_gaps": 2, "ordered": true } } } } } query — (Required, string) Text to analyze. max_gaps — (Optional, integer, default -1) Maximum number of positions between the matched tokens; 0 = adjacent (a phrase), -1 = unlimited. ordered — (Optional, boolean, default false) Whether the tokens must appear in the given order. analyzer — (Optional, string) Analyzer override for query; defaults to the field’s analyzer. filter — (Optional, filter object) See filters. all_of / any_of # all_of combines sub-rules conjunctively (all must produce a span); any_of disjunctively (any one suffices):
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "intervals": { "message": { "all_of": { "intervals": [ { "match": { "query": "connection reset" } }, { "any_of": { "intervals": [ { "match": { "query": "peer" } }, { "prefix": { "prefix": "upstream" } } ] } } ], "ordered": true } } } } } intervals — (Required, array of rules) The sub-rules. max_gaps — (all_of only, default -1) Total gap budget between the sub-spans. ordered — (all_of only, default false) Sub-spans must appear in list order and not overlap. prefix / wildcard / regexp # Multi-term leaves: any dictionary term matching the pattern produces a one-position span at every occurrence:
{ "prefix": { "prefix": "rest" } } { "wildcard": { "pattern": "node?1" } } { "regexp": { "pattern": "err(o)?r" } } wildcard supports ? (one character) and * (zero or more). All three accept filter.
fuzzy # Terms within an edit distance of term:
{ "fuzzy": { "term": "recieve", "fuzziness": "AUTO" } } fuzziness — (Optional, default AUTO) AUTO adapts by term length; an integer pins the distance. prefix_length, transpositions — only the default values (0 / true) are accepted; other values are rejected with a named error rather than silently mis-matching. range # Dictionary terms between two analyzed bounds:
{ "range": { "gte": "info", "lte": "warning" } } Both bounds are required; each must be exactly one of the inclusive (gte/lte) or exclusive (gt/lt) form. A bound must analyze to a single term — multi-term bounds are rejected.
Filters # Any rule carries a filter object that keeps only the spans passing positional predicates against another rule’s spans:
"filter": { "containing": { "match": { "query": "username" } } } Predicate Keeps spans that … containing contain a filter span not_containing contain no filter span contained_by are inside a filter span not_contained_by are inside no filter span overlapping overlap a filter span not_overlapping overlap no filter span before lie entirely before a filter span after lie entirely after a filter span The script filter is not supported — rejected with a named error.
Strict gates # Unsupported knobs are rejected with named errors instead of being ignored: use_field pointing at a field other than the query field, filter script, and fuzzy prefix_length/transpositions other than their defaults.
Use cases # Phrases with room. match with max_gaps and ordered is a phrase you can loosen on one axis at a time — the playground’s get search with max_gaps: 0 finds the 25 GET /search lines, exactly what phrase returns, while cluster left with max_gaps: 2 still matches the 25 cluster node left the region unexpectedly lines across the node in between. Unordered co-occurrence in one window. all_of without ordered and with a finite max_gaps bounds how far apart the pieces may drift — “these terms, within a window, any order”, which phrase cannot say. Disjunctions of positional rules. any_of of two match rules is “either wording, positionally” — one clause, not a bool of two phrases that would lose the shared gap budget. Pattern leaves inside proximity. prefix/wildcard/fuzzy/ regexp leaves participate in gap and order logic — upstream* within 2 positions of reset, composed instead of post-filtered. Contextual negation. not_containing / not_contained_by remove matches that sit inside (or around) another rule’s spans — “error near restart, but not inside a stack-trace span”. Related # span — the other positional grammar: clause composition (span_near/span_or/span_multi) instead of a declarative rule tree. Intervals expresses the same shapes more compactly and adds the filter predicates; spans are the older, lower-level family. phrase — the single fixed-sequence special case; its slop corresponds to a match rule’s gap budget. fuzzy, wildcard, regexp, range — the standalone (non-positional) forms of the multi-term leaves.
title: Intervals query

content:
Suffix query # Returns documents that contain terms ending in the provided value. This is the mirror of the prefix query; like a leading wildcard, it is more expensive than a prefix match.
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.
How it works # A term dictionary is sorted by its beginnings, so a prefix can seek directly to its subtree — but a suffix cannot. The engine therefore walks the whole dictionary of the field and keeps the terms that end with the value, then unions their postings lists exactly like a should of term queries. The cost is proportional to the number of distinct terms in the field, not to the number of matches, which is why the suffix query is marked more expensive than prefix.
Matching is per term. On a keyword field the term is the whole value (url.path = "/app.js" ends with .js); on a text field each analyzed token is tested separately. No analysis runs on the suffix itself — it is compared verbatim against stored terms. On fields analyzed with standard, stored tokens are lowercase. Scoring. The expansion rewrites to constant_score: every matching document scores exactly boost (default 1); inside a bool.filter the scores are discarded, leaving a pure set filter. rewrite is accepted on the wire for body compatibility (constant_score default); the engine scores expansions as described above regardless of the setting. Examples # The following search returns the /app.js requests — the 25 documents whose url.path ends in .js.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The SQL twin quotes the dotted name ("url.path") — the dot would otherwise parse as part of an expression.
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "suffix": { "field": "url.path", "value": ".jpg" } } } Use cases # File extensions. .js, .jpg, .png over url.path (keyword) — the canonical suffix query; the logs dataset answers 25 for .js, 25 for .jpg. Domain TLDs. host/referrer values ending in .cn, .io, .com group infrastructure by registry without a wildcard. Naming conventions. Environment suffixes (-prod, -staging), generated ID tails (…-v2) — anything where the meaning lives at the end of the string. Slug routing. Doc slugs ending in -guide / -reference when the head varies too much to enumerate. Parameters for suffix # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. value (Required, string) The suffix terms must end with. case_insensitive (Optional, boolean, default: false) ASCII case-insensitive matching of the value with the indexed field values. rewrite (Optional, string) Method used to rewrite the query (constant_score, scoring_boolean, …). boost (Optional, float, default: 1) Score multiplier — with the constant-score rewrite every matching document scores exactly boost. Related # prefix — the cheap mirror; seeks in the sorted dictionary instead of scanning it. wildcard — *foo is the same leading-anchor idea with more pattern power (and the same cost profile). regexp — suffix anchored patterns like .*\.js as a full regular expression. term — the atom every expansion resolves to.
title: Suffix query

content:
Span queries # Span queries are low-level positional queries that expose and control the positions of terms — the building blocks for phrase-adjacent logic that phrase does not express directly. Most use cases are better served by match_phrase (or its slop); the span family exists for the remaining ones.
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — span clauses are rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause. Use phrase with slop for positional logic.
How it works # The engine rewrites each span query to its fastest equivalent before execution. An in_order span_near whose clauses are all span_term becomes the engine’s native phrase query — reusing the block-max-WAND phrase producer, the fastest position pipeline available; on that path slop carries phrase-slop semantics (swapping two adjacent terms costs 2 slop, so a reversed occurrence matches from slop: 2). A root span_multi becomes its wrapped matcher and a span_or becomes a bool.should. The residual shapes — multi-term leaves inside span_near, unordered span_near — run a native two-phase evaluator: phase one takes the clause AND (each clause’s terms expanded from the dictionary) as the candidate set, phase two decodes each candidate’s positions and counts alignments with a per-pair gap budget (next.start − prev.end, ordered) or a minimal covering window (unordered, the window-minus-widest-span rule). Frequencies cap at 1024 alignments — match-ness is exact, only the BM25 input is capped; the clause idf sum uses each clause’s rarest term. Without a position index the family degrades to the clause AND, exactly like phrase. span_term itself accepts three wire shapes: { "field": "value" }, { "field": { "value": "v" } } and { "field": …, "value": … }.
span_term # Matches documents containing an exact term at any position — the positional unit the other span queries compose.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "span_term": { "field": "message", "value": "search" } } } Parameters: field (required, string), value (required, string), boost (optional, default 1.0).
span_near # Matches documents where the given span clauses occur within slop positions of each other, optionally in order — the span form of a proximity match — get within three positions of search, in order (25 log lines in the dataset):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "span_near": { "clauses": [ { "span_term": { "field": "message", "value": "get" } }, { "span_term": { "field": "message", "value": "search" } } ], "slop": 3, "in_order": true } } } clauses — (Required, array of span queries) The spans to relate. slop — (Optional, integer, default: 0) Maximum positions between the clauses. in_order — (Optional, boolean, default: true) Whether the clauses must appear in the given order. span_or # Matches documents matching any of the given span clauses — the union of spans.
{ "span_or": { "clauses": [ { "span_term": { "field": "message", "value": "get" } }, { "span_term": { "field": "message", "value": "post" } } ] } } clauses — (Required, array of span queries). span_multi # Wraps a multi-term query (such as prefix, wildcard, fuzzy, regexp, term) so it can be used as a span clause inside span_near / span_or. The wrapped query sits under the match key:
{ "span_multi": { "match": { "prefix": { "field": "user", "value": "ki" } } } } match — (Required, query) The multi-term query to wrap. Use cases # Proximity with a budget. The playground’s get…search within slop: 3 keeps all 25 GET /search lines while admitting lines with a word between — the direct sibling of phrase + slop. Positional unions. span_or of get and post matches 125 of the 150 log lines (100 + 25, no overlap) — an OR that stays a span, so it can feed a span_near afterwards. Pattern leaves in proximity. span_multi wrapping prefix: cluster within slop: 2 of left (in order) matches the 25 cluster node left … lines — a wildcard family next to an anchor word, which phrase cannot express at all. Wire compatibility. Span pipelines arriving from existing clients run unchanged — all four clauses take the standard wire forms. Related # intervals — the other positional grammar: a declarative rule tree (all_of/any_of + filter predicates) instead of clause composition. Prefer it for anything richer than near/or; prefer spans for the shapes above. phrase — what an all-span_term span_near becomes internally; its slop documents the shared slop metric. prefix, wildcard, fuzzy, regexp — the queries span_multi wraps.
title: Span queries

content:
Percentiles bucket aggregation # A sibling pipeline aggregation computing percentiles of a metric across buckets — e.g. “the daily-revenue p95”. The mean of the per-bucket values answers “what is typical”; percentiles answer “what the whole ladder of buckets looks like” — including the outlier end that a stats_bucket min/max flattens into two numbers.
"day_pcts": { "percentiles_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } } How it works # percentiles_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, sorts them, and evaluates each requested percentile over the sorted sample, returning a {"values": {...}} object keyed by the percentile:
{ "values": { "1": 15, "5": 15, "25": 30, "50": 45, "75": 75, "95": 180, "99": 180 } } Quantile estimation follows TDigest semantics with every bucket value acting as a weight-1 centroid. For n values the estimate for percentile p is taken at position p / 100 × n in the sorted list: a position landing exactly between two centroids returns their mean, a position inside centroid k returns that centroid’s value, and positions off either end clamp to the minimum or maximum. The median of 100, 200, 300 is 200; their p40 is also 200 (the position 1.2 falls inside the 200 centroid).
The buckets_path and gap rules are the family’s:
"per_day>revenue" (> or . separator) — the sub-metric inside each bucket; it must be single-valued (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality, …). A stats sub-agg contributes its sum. A bare parent name profiles the buckets’ doc_counts. skip (default) leaves buckets with a missing metric — and empty buckets (doc_count 0) whose sum reads 0 — out of the sample; insert_zeros has them contribute 0. With no contributing bucket the result is {"values": {}}.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Half of the 120 selling days bring 45 or less, while the top few percent spike to 180 — a long-tailed distribution an average alone would hide.
Use cases # Typical-vs-tail revenue — p50 versus p95 of daily revenue: the gap between them is the “good day” premium. SLA across groups — p95/p99 of the per-service average latencies of a terms aggregation, the standard way to report tail latency. Spot skewed group totals — percentiles of per-category sums: a p95 close to the max means one category dominates. Robust baseline — the median across buckets resists the outlier days that drag avg_bucket. Parameters for percentiles_bucket # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric. percents (Optional, number array) Percentiles to compute; defaults to [1, 5, 25, 50, 75, 95, 99]. gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros. format Not a parameter of this aggregation in the current engine — accepted for compatibility and ignored; values are returned unformatted. Related # Sibling family: avg_bucket, sum_bucket, min_bucket,
max_bucket, stats_bucket,
extended_stats_bucket
Document-level counterpart: percentiles
title: Percentiles bucket aggregation

content:
Median absolute deviation aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that computes the median absolute deviation — the median of the distances from each value to the median of all values. A robust measure of spread: unlike standard deviation it is not skewed by a few extreme values.
How it works # The aggregation runs in three steps over the collected values of the field:
Compute the median with the same TDigest arithmetic percentiles uses — weight-1 centroids at (i + 0.5) / n, linear interpolation between the two bracketing values.
Take each value’s absolute distance to that median, |v − median|. Return the median of those distances, using the same arithmetic again. Because both medians interpolate, the result can land between observed values (over the 120 teaching sale prices: median 22.5, MAD 7.5 — neither is a price anyone paid). The value is expressed in the same units as the field, so a MAD of 7.5 on prices means “a typical sale is $7.50 away from the median price”.
The robustness comes from the outer median: up to half the values can be arbitrarily wrong (or arbitrarily large) before the MAD moves at all, whereas a single huge value already inflates a standard deviation. If no document has a value for the field, value is null.
Example # Sales prices take only four values (15, 30, 45, 60), so half the documents sit at 15 and the deviation of a typical document is small:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The median price is 22.5; the median distance from that median is 7.5.
Use cases # Outlier-resistant spread for skewed data. Latency, income and price distributions have long tails; quote the MAD when a single spike must not change the “typical variation” story. Robust z-scores. 0.6745 × (x − median) / MAD is the classic robust analogue of “how many standard deviations from the mean” — flag points beyond ±3 as anomalies. With the sales numbers: a 60 sticker price sits at 0.6745 × 37.5 / 7.5 ≈ 3.4 robust sigmas. Comparing variability across groups. Nest MAD under terms to compare how consistent each product type’s prices are, without one expensive outlier dominating a group.
Data-quality gates. A MAD of 0 means at least half the values sit exactly on the median — a cheap “is this field effectively constant?” check before deduplicating or indexing it. Parameters for median_absolute_deviation # field (Required, string) Numeric field you wish to aggregate. missing (Optional, number) Value substituted for documents without the field. Related # percentiles — supplies the median (the 50th percentile) the deviations are measured against. boxplot — the interquartile range (q3 − q1) is the other common robust spread measure; compare the two on the same data. extended_stats — standard deviation and variance, the non-robust counterparts, useful when the contrast itself is the signal (a std-deviation far above MAD means heavy tails).
title: Median absolute deviation aggregation

content:
Lesson 8 — Joins # Traversal (Lesson 5) walks edges inside ONE collection. A join spans TWO: it answers questions a single collection cannot — orders whose customer is gold-tier, where the tier lives in a different collection.
Joins need a running node (the gateway orchestrates the two sides, which is why the wasm playground does not host them), so this lesson is curl against your Lesson 1 node — no live widget. Like traverse, join stays DSL-side outside the SQL M1 subset.
The shape to keep in mind is a semi-join — the SQL intuition is:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE org_id IN (SELECT _key FROM orgs WHERE tier = 'gold') executed as one request, with both sides living in different collections.
The use case # Facts and dimensions live in different collections because they change differently — orders stream in continuously, org tiers trickle. The question spans both. The questions this lesson answers:
“Orders whose org is gold-tier” — the semi-join, Part 1’s walkthrough. “Documents visible only to members of group X” — entitlement filtering: the same shape, the group set lives in another collection. “Can I trust the join to mean what the schema says?” — declared references make contradicting joins fail closed (Part 2). “One tenant dwarfs the others — where do their writes land?” — FK routing and salting (Part 2). Part 1 — the undeclared join # Steps 1–3 build the two collections and run the join with nothing declared — two keyword fields are all a join requires. The sections that follow show what actually executed, where a join may sit, and the guardrails.
Step 1 — create the two collections # Nothing exotic: two keyword fields are enough for a join to work.
PUT /orgs { "schema": { "dynamic": "strict", "properties": { "tier": { "type": "keyword" } }} } PUT /orders { "schema": { "dynamic": "strict", "properties": { "status": { "type": "keyword" }, "org_id": { "type": "keyword" } }} } Step 2 — seed a known answer # Two gold orgs, one silver, and ten orders spread over them:
PUT /orgs/_doc/org-a { "tier": "gold" } PUT /orgs/_doc/org-b { "tier": "silver" } PUT /orgs/_doc/org-mega { "tier": "gold" } PUT /orders/_doc/a-1 { "status": "new", "org_id": "org-a" } # … a-2, a-3 PUT /orders/_doc/b-1 { "status": "new", "org_id": "org-b" } PUT /orders/_doc/m-1 { "status": "new", "org_id": "org-mega" } # … m-2 … m-6 Step 3 — join # The URL stays on the outer collection (orders); the join clause names the inner one:
POST /orders/_search { "size": 10, "track_total_hits": true, "query": { "join": { "target": "orgs", "query": { "term": { "field": "tier", "value": "gold" } }, "join_on": "_key", "field": "org_id" } } } 9 hits — the three a-* orders and the six m-* orders, because org-a and org-mega are gold. b-1 is missing: org-b is silver. Change the inner term to silver and exactly b-1 comes back. The outer side never saw the tier — it only saw the resolved key set.
What actually executed # The work splits in two, and neither half fan-outs blindly:
Gateway — ran the inner term on orgs, distributed across its shards, and collected the matching _keys (org-a, org-mega). These join keys attach to the join node as a prepared payload. Engine — each orders shard received the keys and ran the join as a local membership filter on org_id. graph LR Q["POST /orders/_searchjoin target: orgs"] --> GW("gateway") GW -->|"1. run inner queryterm tier=gold"| O("orgsthe inner side") O -->|"2. extract join keys:org-a, org-mega"| GW GW -->|"3. keys ride the join nodeas a prepared payload"| E("orders shardsthe outer side") E -->|"4. membership filteron org_id"| H["9 hits"] Two collections, one request, no application-side fan-out. Repeated joins amortize: an identical inner request re-issued by auto-fired patterns is served from a dimension cache validated against exact per-shard visibility tokens — any write, failover or restart invalidates it. Never a TTL, never a stale hit.
Joining on values, not keys # join_on names where the keys come from on the inner side — it does not have to be _key. Any inner field works: its values are extracted from each inner hit (scalars verbatim, arrays expand to one key per element) and matched against the outer field:
POST /invoices/_search { "query": { "join": { "target": "orgs", "query": { "term": { "field": "tier", "value": "gold" } }, "join_on": "code", "field": "org_code" } } } orgs.code values (say "A-100") become the key set; invoices matching on their own org_code keyword field survive. This shape cannot ride the fast _ref column path below — that path exists only for joins that follow a declared references (join_on: "_key", field the FK field).
Where a join may sit # Inside bool.must, bool.filter and nested — resolved and executed, composed with ordinary clauses like any filter: POST /orders/_search { "query": { "bool": { "filter": [ { "term": { "field": "status", "value": "new" } }, { "join": { "target": "orgs", "query": { "term": { "field": "tier", "value": "gold" } }, "join_on": "_key", "field": "org_id" }} ] } } } Inside bool.should or bool.must_not — inert. An unresolved join node matches nothing, so a join under should quietly contributes no hits. Put joins in must/filter. Inside another join’s inner query — rejected with a 400 (no join-of-joins). Scoring and guardrails # score_mode controls how inner-query scores reach the outer document: none (the default — pure filter, inner scores discarded), max, sum, or avg. In v1 only the _key rung carries scores; the field-targeted rungs are filter-shaped and reject other values with a 400.
The guardrails are fail-closed, not silent:
inner_hits_cap (default 10 000) bounds the inner query. When the inner hit set reaches the cap the key set may be truncated — the join result is then a lower bound, logged at preflight, never silently complete. Raise the cap if the dimension side is legitimately larger. Point-in-time — a join under a PIT requires the PIT to cover both collections (same pinned snapshot on each side); otherwise a 400, not a pinned outer mixed with a realtime inner. Namespace sharing — the inner query runs in the outer request’s namespace: one tenant’s authorization covers both collections. 400 for a missing target collection, a field absent from the outer schema, a non-keyword field, or a join contradicting a declared references; 503 when the target has no started primary shards. Add "explain": true to a request and the response narrates the join plan — which locality tier it took and, when a better tier was skipped, why.
Part 2 — declaring the relationship # The schema in Step 1 already works. Declaring what org_id means buys three things: joins that are checked (a contradicting request fails instead of silently joining wrong), a faster execution path, and FK-routed placement (an org’s orders colocate on one partition and become addressable by key). This part rebuilds orders with the declaration and walks each consequence — every step runs on your Lesson 1 node, and nothing outside this page is required.
Step 4 — rebuild orders with the declaration # A collection’s schema is fixed at creation, so drop and recreate orders — only ten documents to rewrite:
DELETE /orders PUT /orders { "schema": { "dynamic": "strict", "properties": { "status": { "type": "keyword" }, "org_id": { "type": "keyword", "immutable": true, "references": { "collection": "orgs" }, "routing": true, "ref": true } }} } Then re-run the ten order writes from Step 2 — orgs is untouched. What each parameter buys:
references — declares the foreign key: org_id names a document key in orgs. Writes do not fail when that document is missing (a dangling reference still lands; the join simply does not match it). The declaration also pins the join’s shape — Step 5 shows the 400. immutable — a prerequisite of routing (a mutable routing key would re-route documents), enforced on the update path: an update that re-points or drops the field fails with a 400 — moving a document between routing values is a delete + re-create, never a silent drift. ref — materialize the reference at write time into a hidden _<field>_ref numeric column that joins ride instead of resolving keys. Declare it before ingesting: only documents carrying a materialized _ref match (older documents need a reindex). routing — placement routes by the field’s value: hash(org_id) % partitions picks the home partition, not the document key’s hash. Step 6 makes this visible. Step 5 — the same join, checked and faster # Re-run the Step 3 join verbatim — same 9 hits, different execution. With "ref": true the engine resolves org_id through the hidden _ref column instead of filtering terms. The full rung ladder: a field of "_key" rides the outer key registry; a references field with "ref": true rides the hidden column; any other declared keyword field runs engine-side as an exact terms filter — and a references without "ref": true still joins correctly, degrading to that keyword rung with a warning in the server log saying so. Add "explain": true and the response narrates the join plan — which locality tier it took, and why when a better one was skipped.
The orchestration keeps Part 1’s shape — gateway, then outer shards — but steps 2–4 changed vocabulary:
graph LR Q["POST /orders/_searchthe same join, declared"] --> GW("gateway") GW -->|"1. run inner queryterm tier=gold"| O("orgsthe inner side") O -->|"2. resolve each keyto one packed integer id"| GW GW -->|"3. refs ride the join node:integers, not strings"| E("orders shardsthe outer side") E -->|"4. numeric filter on the hidden_org_id_ref column"| H["same 9 hits"] The declaration is enforced, fail-closed. The join’s target and join_on: "_key" must now match what org_id declares — point the join somewhere else and it is rejected rather than silently joining through a field the schema says means something else:
POST /orders/_search { "size": 10, "query": { "join": { "target": "orders", "query": { "term": { "field": "status", "value": "new" } }, "join_on": "_key", "field": "org_id" } } } 400 — the join contradicts the declared references on org_id.
Step 6 — placement you can see in the write response # Look back at the responses your Step 4 writes returned (or run one again):
{ "result": "created", "_id": "0,17" } The system id is rolling,seq — two numbers; the exact values depend on your node’s write history. The home partition reads straight off the id: seq % partition_count. The routing value is what picks that partition — with routing: true a keyed write lands at hash(org_id) % partitions, and the seq is then allocated on that partition to match — so a-1, a-2, a-3 share one partition, b-1 lands on another, and the six m-* funnel into a third: an org’s orders are colocated, and the hot org’s dominance is already visible in the ids.
graph LR subgraph pa["partition of hash(org-a)"] a1("a-1") a2("a-2") a3("a-3") end subgraph pb["partition of hash(org-b)"] b1("b-1") end subgraph pm["partition of hash(org-mega)"] m1("m-1 … m-6") end The routing field is load-bearing — a write without it has no home partition:
PUT /orders/_doc/bad-1 { "status": "x" } 400 — and null, arrays and objects are refused the same way.
Step 7 — by-key addressing with ?routing= # On a routed collection a key alone has no home partition either: key-addressed operations take the routing value:
GET /orders/_doc/a-1?routing=org-a # 200 — the document GET /orders/_doc/a-1 # 400 — bare key, guidance in the body GET /orders/_doc/a-1?routing=org-b # 404 — honest: org-b's partition was probed HEAD, UPDATE and DELETE take the same parameter:
POST /orders/_update/a-1?id_type=key&routing=org-a { "doc": { "status": "shipped" } } The fetch reference and the partial update reference cover the full key-addressing vocabulary.
Step 8 — salting the hot org # org-mega carries 6 of the 10 orders — all on one partition. Salting splits a hot routing value across a SET of partitions, and it is two-step by design: the feed measures, you assign.
Set a threshold, then read the feed:
PUT /orders/_salting { "threshold": 4, "assignments": {} } GET /orders/_salting/feed?size=10 The feed is a terms aggregation over the routing field: org-mega (6 docs) crosses the threshold and is flagged candidate: true; org-a (3 docs) is not. Nothing is salted yet — candidate flagging is measurement, assignments are intent. Assign four splits:
PUT /orders/_salting { "threshold": 4, "assignments": { "org-mega": 4 } } The response renders the computed partition set — the frozen engine contract hash("org-mega" #i) % partitions, sorted and deduped (the effective spread can land below the requested splits; the response reports what IS):
{ "acknowledged": true, "routing_field": "org_id", "threshold": 4, "status": "assigned (salt-split routing active on writes)", "assignments": [ { "value": "org-mega", "splits": 4, "partitions": [76, 83, 85, 254] } ] } The hot value’s placement, before and after the assignment:
graph LR subgraph before["before — every org-mega write funnels here"] HOT("org-mega's single partitionm-1 … m-6") end subgraph after["after — the assigned SET"] S1("partition 76") S2("partition 83") S3("partition 85") S4("partition 254") end HOT -.->|"new writes pick a member by hash(_key) % 4"| S1 HOT -.-> S2 HOT -.-> S3 HOT -.-> S4 Write six more orders for the hot org:
PUT /orders/_doc/m-7 { "status": "salted", "org_id": "org-mega" } # … m-8 … m-12 The response _ids now spread across the assigned set — each keyed write picks its member deterministically (hash(value #hash(_key) % splits)), so the same key always lands in the same place while the org stops funneling every write into one partition. Unassigned values (org-a, org-b) keep their single partition, and key-addressed reads still work — they probe the whole set:
GET /orders/_doc/m-3?routing=org-mega Step 9 — placement changed, visibility did not # Re-run the Step 3 join: 15 hits now — the three a-* orders plus twelve m-*. Search fans out across every partition, so the split placement is invisible to queries; salting changes placement, never join visibility.
Clearing an assignment narrows placement on the very next write. The PUT is full-replace — restate whatever stays:
PUT /orders/_salting { "threshold": 4, "assignments": {} } Documents written before an assignment stay on their old partitions until a rehash migration moves them — the salting reference covers the contract, the migration story, and the limits.
What you learned # join is a semi-join: the inner query resolves to a key set, the outer collection filters on it — two collections, one request, no application-side fan-out. The inner side is any query; join_on can be _key or any inner field (values, not keys). Joins belong in must/filter; they are inert under should/must_not and cannot nest. Guardrails fail closed: capped joins report lower bounds, PITs must cover both sides, malformed shapes are 400s. Declaring references/immutable/ref/routing buys checked joins (fail-closed 400s), the hidden _ref column path, and FK-routed placement with ?routing= key addressing — and salting splits a hot value across a partition set without touching join visibility. Part 2 walked all of it against your own node. Next: Lesson 9 — operations.
title: Lesson 8 — Joins

content:
Histogram aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation over numeric fields that applies a fixed interval to build the buckets. It answers “how are the values distributed?” — every document lands in exactly one bucket, and the bucket keys form a regular grid over the value axis.
How it works # Each document’s value v is placed by index arithmetic — bucket index floor((v - offset) / interval) — so a bucket covers the half-open window [key, key + interval). Buckets accumulate in a sorted map, and the response lists them by ascending key.
With the default min_doc_count: 0, every bucket between the data minimum and maximum is materialized — gaps inside the data extent come back with doc_count: 0 (the fill is capped at 65,536 buckets). extended_bounds may only widen that fill range, never shrink it; hard_bounds clips it, drops buckets that fall entirely outside [min, max], and force-materializes the full in-window grid even at zero documents. offset slides the whole grid along the value axis (boundaries become k · interval + offset).
Each bucket reports key (the window’s lower bound, a number) and doc_count; the columnar path additionally renders key_as_string by reading the key as epoch milliseconds in strict ISO form — meaningful when the numeric field actually stores dates.
Examples # Prices are 15/30/45/60, so an interval of 25 makes three buckets — HISTOGRAM(price, 25) on the SQL side:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "prices": { "histogram": { "field": "price", "interval": 50 } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "prices": { "buckets": [ { "key": 0.0, "doc_count": 110 }, { "key": 50.0, "doc_count": 10 } ] } } } Parameters for histogram # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate (must be numeric). interval (Required, number) Bucket width. offset (Optional, number, default: 0.0) Shift the bucket boundaries. min_doc_count (Optional, integer, default: 0) Only return buckets with at least this many documents. hard_bounds (Optional, object) Restrict bucket generation to [min, max) — buckets fully outside are dropped even with min_doc_count: 0. extended_bounds (Optional, object) Widen the bucket range beyond the data extent (empty buckets are materialized up to these bounds when min_doc_count is 0). Can only extend, never shrink below the data extent. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Range fields # Histograms (and date histograms) accept _range field types (integer_range, long_range, double_range, date_range, …): a document’s stored range counts in EVERY bucket it overlaps — the bucket window [from, to) and the stored range intersect — rather than in the single bucket holding its midpoint. Open-ended sides ({"lte": 10}, {"gte": 15}) extend to the histogram’s hard_bounds window, which also force-materializes every in-window bucket even at zero documents.
POST /my-collection/_search { "size": 0, "aggs": { "histo": { "histogram": { "field": "range", "interval": 1, "hard_bounds": { "min": 0, "max": 20 } } } } } Use cases # Price-band analysis. Fixed-width bands over a price-style field are the backbone of merchandising reports. Over the teaching dataset’s 120 sales an interval of 50 yields two buckets — 110 sales under 50, 10 at 50 and above. Distribution sketches. Where do values cluster, and how thick is the tail? A histogram with a small interval is the cheapest density estimate the engine offers; follow up with percentiles for exact quantiles.
Time-as-number timelines. Fields stored as epoch milliseconds can be bucketed directly (the fast path renders each key_as_string as an ISO timestamp); for calendar-aware windows prefer the date histogram.
Zero-filled chart axes. min_doc_count: 0 plus extended_bounds produces the contiguous, gap-free bucket series a charting front-end needs, without padding client-side. Related # date_histogram — the same fixed-grid idea over date fields, with calendar-aware intervals. auto_date_histogram — you pick the bucket count, the engine picks the interval. variable_width_histogram — bucket edges adapt to the data instead of staying fixed. range — a handful of hand-named, possibly overlapping bands instead of a regular grid.
title: Histogram aggregation

content:
Value count aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that counts the number of values that are extracted from the aggregated documents. Typically, this aggregator will be used in conjunction with other single-value aggregations. For example, when computing the avg one might be interested in the number of values the average is computed over.
value_count does not de-duplicate values, so even if a field has duplicates each value will be counted individually.
How it works # The engine counts the values a field actually holds across the matching documents — not the documents themselves. A document without the field contributes nothing; a field with a value in every document counts one per document, and a document whose field holds an array also counts once (per element spreading is bucket-aggregation behavior). No numeric coercion is involved: any present value counts, whatever its type.
With missing set, documents that lack the field are treated as carrying the default — one contribution each — so the count then equals the number of matching documents.
On the column-store fast path (the production executor) each segment’s column is decoded once and count_present supplies the per-segment count in a single batch; per-shard counts combine by plain addition, so the result is exact and identical on single-node and distributed requests. Like sum, it never returns null — an empty match is a count of zero.
Examples # Counting the values of type — one number per value present, no de-duplication; COUNT(*) on the SQL side:
