JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs" : { "types_count" : { "value_count" : { "field" : "type" } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "types_count": { "value": 120 } } } The name of the aggregation (types_count above) also serves as the key by which the aggregation result can be retrieved from the returned response.
Use cases # Denominators. sales.value_count(price) = 120 is the N behind avg(price) = 27.5 — display both and a mean never masquerades as a median built on three points. Field completeness audits. Only 20 of the 44 articles docs carry title (the rest are relation edges): value_count(title) = 20 next to places.total-style totals exposes sparse fields at a glance. Coverage rates. Divide the count by the match count to get “share of documents that have this field” — data-quality dashboards in one request. Sparse-field discovery. Run one value_count per field over the same query and sort by the result: fields that come back well below the match count are the ones client code cannot rely on. Distinctness checks. Pair with cardinality: type has 120 values but only 4 distinct ones — high duplication, a candidate for terms instead. Parameters for value_count # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. script (Optional, object) Script evaluated per document as the value source — mutually exclusive with field. missing (Optional, value) Value used for documents missing the field; each such document then counts as one contribution. Related # cardinality — the de-duplicating count stats — count plus min/max/avg/sum in one request terms — count per distinct value
title: Value count aggregation

content:
Script fields # Compute extra values for each hit, at fetch time, from the hit’s own _source — like highlighting, but producing numbers and strings instead of fragments. Scripts run on Pizza’s sandboxed script engine (see the script language reference), only for the hits actually returned on the page.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Every returned hit carries the computed values under fields, as arrays:
{ "_source": { "amount": 30.0, "type": "hat", "...": "..." }, "fields": { "doubled": [60], "with_vat": [36.9] } } The script source goes in either wire form — "script": "<source>" or "script": { "source": ..., "params": ... }. Extra variables arrive as params.<name>.
How it works # script_fields is an engine-native fetch-phase enrich (lib/engine/src/search/aggregator/script.rs, apply_script_fields). The engine compiles each named script once per request, then evaluates it per hit of the RETURNED page — after ranking and truncation, exactly like highlight. A size: 3 request runs each script three times; size: 0 never runs it at all, whatever the match count.
Per hit, the engine builds the doc-values map from the hit’s stored fields — doc.price.value (first value), doc.price.values (all values) — and evaluates with doc and params in scope. The result is coerced to the field shape: a scalar becomes a one-element array, an array stays an array, and a script evaluating to nothing (()) yields an empty array.
Errors are fail-closed by default: a script error fails the whole request rather than returning a silently partial page. ignore_failure: true demotes just that field — omitted for the hits where it errors, computed where it does.
The index.max_script_fields setting (count cap, default 32) is validated by the ES-compatibility layer. The native engine path enforces no count cap; the practical limits are the page size and the sandbox below.
The doc binding # Each script sees the hit’s _source in the doc-values shape — the same binding scripted_metric’s map_script sees:
doc.amount.value — the first value of amount doc.amount.values — all values (multi-value fields) doc['amount'].value — the bracket spelling a field the document doesn’t have has no entry — doc.missing.value errors (guard with "amount" in doc when a field may be absent) ignore_failure # By default a script error fails the whole request — never a silently partial page. Set ignore_failure: true on a field to omit just that field for the hits where its script errors:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. discount does not exist on the sample data, so maybe_discounted is simply absent from every hit while line_total is computed.
Use cases # Derived units on display. Unit prices with VAT, amount × qty line totals, currencies converted with a params rate — computed at read time so the stored document stays the source of truth. Cheap formatting. Bucket labels, display names glued from parts (doc.first + " " + doc.last), or normalization (rounding, string casing) without re-indexing. Conditional annotations. Flag hits whose amount exceeds a params.threshold — an annotation on the page, not a filter (filters belong in the query). Field trimming for wide docs. Emit one compact computed field instead of shipping several raw ones to a thin client. Parameters for script_fields # <name> (Required, object) One entry per computed field; the key is the name under fields in the response. script (Required, string | object) Inline source string, or { "source": ..., "params": ... }. ignore_failure (Optional, boolean, default: false) Omit this field for hits where the script errors instead of failing the request. Notes and limits # Language: Rhai, not Painless — everything in the language reference applies.
Compute-only: script_fields enriches the response; the computed values cannot filter, sort, or score — those need scripted queries (script filters, script_score, the _script sort), which run at query time rather than fetch time.
Page-sized cost: scripts run after truncation, so only the returned page pays — roughly three microseconds per field per hit, native. A size: 0 request never evaluates a script field. Sandboxed: same containment as aggregation scripts — an operation cap stops runaway loops, there is no host or network IO, and string, array and map sizes are bounded. Related # The script language — the shared Rhai reference: syntax, the doc binding, containment. Scripted queries — the query-time siblings: script filters, script_score, the _script sort key. Highlighting — the other page-sized fetch-time enrich. Sort and pagination — the _script sort clause it links to, and why from/size bound what scripts ever see.
title: Script fields

content:
Regexp query # Returns documents that contain terms matching a regular expression.
A regular expression is a way to match patterns in data using placeholder characters, called operators. For a list of operators supported by the regexp query, see Regular expression syntax. Use the regexp query when neither prefix, suffix nor wildcard can express the shape — alternation, character classes, repetition.
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.
How it works # The pattern is compiled and expanded against the inverted index’s term dictionary: the engine walks the field’s terms, keeps those the regex accepts, and unions their postings lists — the same result as a should of term queries over the surviving terms.
Anchored, full-term matching. The pattern must match the entire term, not a substring — every pattern behaves as if wrapped in ^(…)$. web- alone matches only the literal term web-; to reach web-01 write web-.*. Because of the implicit anchoring the explicit ^ / $ assertions (like \b and lazy quantifiers) are not part of the supported grammar. Syntax. The automaton engine supports the constructs of the standard Rust regex grammar (see the syntax link above). On top of that the engine pre-expands the common Perl shorthands so patterns using them behave as written: outside character classes \w \W \d \D \s \S become their ASCII bracket equivalents, and the “any character” idioms [\w\W], [\d\D], [\s\S] collapse to .. Other escapes pass through — an invalid one surfaces a pattern compile error rather than a silent zero-hit query. Cost. Like suffix and leading-wildcard patterns, a regexp cannot seek in the sorted dictionary; the walk is over the field’s full vocabulary. Prefer prefix when the pattern has a literal head. No analysis runs on the pattern — it is compared verbatim against stored terms (lowercase on standard-analyzed fields). case_insensitive lowercases both the pattern and each candidate term instead. Scoring. The expansion is rewritten with ES’s constant_score rule: every matching document scores exactly the boost (1.0 by default), regardless of how many terms matched. Inside a bool.filter the scores are discarded, leaving a pure set filter. Examples # The following search matches hosts like web-01 — the literal web- followed by one or more digits. Every host in the logs dataset has that shape, so all 150 documents match.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. No SQL twin: regular expressions are outside the current SQL subset — this page stays DSL-only.
GET /_search { "query": { "regexp": { "field": "org.id", "value": "in.*i", "case_insensitive": true } } } Use cases # Structured identifier shapes. web-[0-9]+ over logs.host (all 150 lines) — express “two digits at the end” precisely where wildcard’s ? would also admit letters. Alternation classes. .*\\.(js|jpg) over url.path matches the 50 static-asset lines (25 .js + 25 .jpg) in one clause — the pattern terms cannot write and suffix can only express one tail at a time. Path families. /api/v1/.* scopes to the 50 API requests; change the version segment without rewriting the clause. Validation-style sweeps. “Find every SKU that fails the [A-Z]{3}-\\d{4} convention” — a data-quality query over keyword vocabularies, negated with a bool.must_not. Parameters for regexp # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. value (Required, string) Regular expression for terms you wish to find in the provided field. The pattern is matched against whole terms; see the grammar notes above. case_insensitive (Optional, boolean) Allows ASCII case insensitive matching of the value with the indexed field values when set to true. Default is false. flags (Optional, string) Regex flags. Accepted on the wire for body compatibility; not yet interpreted by the engine. max_determinized_states (Optional, integer, default: 1000) Safety cap on automaton complexity. Accepted on the wire for body compatibility. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Multiplier for the clause’s score — with the constant-score rewrite this is the score itself. rewrite (Optional, string) Method used to rewrite the query (constant_score, scoring_boolean, …). Related # wildcard — the */? subset; same dictionary-walk cost model, simpler mental model. prefix — literal-head patterns seek instead of walking; use it whenever the pattern allows. suffix — tail-anchored matching. term — the atom every expansion resolves to. query_string — /regex/ syntax inside a query-string expression routes to the same matching.
title: Regexp query

content:
Match all query # Matches every document. This is the default query used when no query is sent in a search request — relevance-free, constant-scored, and the base every “everything, then narrow” pattern builds on.
How it works # match_all walks every document in the target indexes with a constant score — 1.0 — so _score carries no ranking information and downstream score arithmetic (indices_boost, bool should boosts, cross-engine merges) sees the same baseline everywhere. boost multiplies the constant, and is the only parameter there is.
The producer is the cheapest in the engine: sequential document ids, no postings decode, no I/O. On the block path it enumerates the segment’s real document ids from the stored-docs table rather than a synthetic 0..n range, so segments with id holes (failed writes skip ids) never surface phantom documents. Every block carries the constant score, and downstream collectors skip score comparisons entirely.
Beyond the explicit query form it also serves as the engine’s internal “everything” base — the default query when a search body omits query, the base of a bool whose only clauses are must_not (everything minus the exclusions), and the collection query for aggregation-only requests.
Examples # The query below returns everything — all 120 documents of the sales dataset. The SQL twin is a bare SELECT with no WHERE:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "match_all": {} } } Use cases # Aggregation-only requests. "size": 0 plus aggs with no query: the whole index is the population, and match_all is what the engine runs under the hood. Exclusion-only filters. A bool whose only clauses are must_not is “everything minus the exclusions” — match_all minus a set. Totals and smoke tests. Full scans with track_total_hits are the baseline every other query’s hit count is checked against; the teaching datasets use it to pin totals (120 sales, 150 logs). A score baseline. Constant 1.0 scores make boosting arithmetic visible: wrap match_all in a bool with should boosts and the output score is exactly the boost contribution. Explicit “no query”. Writing match_all out documents intent — “filters and aggregations only” — and gives filters, post_filter and aggs a stated base instead of an implied one. Parameters for match_all # boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Applied to every matched document’s score. Match none query # The counterpart match_none matches no document at all — the empty side of the filter algebra. It is mostly a building block: tests use it as the always-false branch, and it is the neutral occupant wherever a query object is required but no matching is wanted:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "match_none": {} } } Related # bool — match_all is the base under must_not-only bools and the neutral occupant of a scored clause. match — the step up once actual relevance is needed. match_none — the empty counterpart, on this page. API conventions.
title: Match all query

content:
Lesson 7 — Geographic search # From schema to data to queries: filter documents by where they are — a coordinate, a rectangle, an arbitrary polygon, or a full geometric shape.
Pizza has two geographic field types, and picking the right one is the whole design step:
geo_point — a single coordinate. Answers “where is this document?” Distance, box and polygon filters run against it. geo_shape — a full geometry: point, line, polygon, multi-variant, envelope or geometry collection. Answers “what area does this document cover?” and supports the relation vocabulary (intersects, within, contains, disjoint). A store is a geo_point; the district it serves is a geo_shape.
The use case # Location-aware features — the store finder, the delivery-zone picker, the geofence. None of these are text questions: the filter is geometry. The questions this lesson answers:
“Stores within 5 km of me” — geo_point + distance filter. “Everything inside this map rectangle / this city boundary” — box and polygon filters. “Which delivery zones cover this address?” — geo_shape + relation filters (intersects, within, …). “Does this service area overlap that one?” — the shape-relation vocabulary on full geometries. Step 1 — declare the schema # Create a collection whose schema declares both types up front ( create a collection):
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "schema": { "properties": { "name": { "type": "keyword" }, "city": { "type": "keyword" }, "location": { "type": "geo_point" }, "region": { "type": "geo_shape" } } } }' \ http://localhost:28000/geo-lessons geo_point and geo_shape fields always get a column store — exact geometry is verified from it at query time, never guessed from an index approximation. Later schema changes stay additive ( update schema).
Step 2 — index documents # A point is {lat, lon} (or a [lat, lon] array); a shape is GeoJSON — and here is the classic trap: GeoJSON coordinates are [lon, lat], point objects are {lat, lon}. The wire order comes from the GeoJSON standard; the object keys read naturally. Watch it on every shape you write:
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "name": "beijing store", "city": "beijing", "location": { "lat": 39.9042, "lon": 116.4074 }, "region": { "type": "polygon", "coordinates": [[ [116.4074, 39.9542], [116.4574, 39.9042], [116.4074, 39.8542], [116.3574, 39.9042], [116.4074, 39.9542] ]] } }' \ http://localhost:28000/geo-lessons/_doc If JSON objects are not your thing, geo_shape also accepts WKT strings — the same diamond as "POLYGON ((116.4074 39.9542, 116.4574 39.9042, 116.4074 39.8542, 116.3574 39.9042, 116.4074 39.9542))".
The rest of this lesson runs against the teaching dataset’s places collection — 15 Chinese cities, each with a location point and a small diamond region — so every query below is live and has a known answer you can count by hand.
Step 3 — filter points # geo_distance: everything within 200 km of central Beijing — 2 hits, both Beijing rows:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. geo_bounding_box: a rectangle by its corners — the same two Beijing rows:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. geo_polygon: any closed polygon, points as [lat, lon] pairs — a quad around Beijing, again 2:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Over HTTP the nested form ({"geo_polygon": {"location": {"points": …}}}) is accepted too — the gateway normalizes it. Polygons may be concave; they must not self-intersect.
Step 4 — query shapes # geo_shape compares the indexed geometry against a query geometry — any GeoJSON type, or WKT. The relation defaults to intersects; the envelope below clips both Beijing diamonds, so 2:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. within keeps documents whose shape lies entirely inside the query — grow the envelope to swallow the whole diamond and the same 2 remain, everything else drops:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. disjoint inverts intersects — 13 of 15 cities do not touch the Beijing envelope:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. A WKT string works as the query shape as well: "shape": "BBOX (116.1, 40.3, 116.7, 39.6)" — the same envelope in WKT’s minLon, maxLat, maxLon, minLat order, same answers.
Under the hood # Every geo query runs in two phases: a coarse pass over bounding boxes in the BKD index (points are 2-dim trees; shapes index their bounding box as a 4-dim point), then exact geometry verification against the column store. The first phase only nominates candidates — the second decides — so results are exact, with no false negatives. The tradeoffs to know about: coordinates are treated as planar WGS-84 degrees (shapes wrapping the antimeridian are not supported yet), and geo_shape filtering has no dedicated scoring — combine with a match query in a bool when you need ranking.
What you learned # geo_point for where a document is; geo_shape for what it covers. GeoJSON is [lon, lat]; point objects and geo_polygon points are {lat, lon} / [lat, lon]. Mixing them up is the one bug everyone writes once. Points filter by distance, box, polygon; shapes filter by relation — intersects, within, contains, disjoint. Geo filters stay DSL-side — they are demand-gated outside the SQL M1 subset; SQL reaches geo data only through its ordinary columns (a keyword city, a name, a key).
Next: Lesson 8 — joins — one query across two collections, against a live node. Every parameter of the queries in this lesson lives in the geo reference.
title: Lesson 7 — Geographic search

content:
Extended stats bucket aggregation # A sibling pipeline aggregation extending stats_bucket with variance, standard deviation and their sampling variants of the per-bucket metric distribution. Use it when the spread of the per-bucket numbers matters — how uneven the days or categories are — not just their min/avg/max envelope.
"day_xstats": { "extended_stats_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } } How it works # extended_stats_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and emits an extended_stats-shaped result over that sample:
{ "count": 120, "min": 15, "max": 180, "avg": 56.25, "sum": 6750, "sum_of_squares": 614250, "variance": 1954.6875, "variance_population": 1954.6875, "variance_sampling": 1971.11, "std_deviation": 44.21, "std_deviation_population": 44.21, "std_deviation_sampling": 44.4 } variance and std_deviation are the population forms (sum_of_squares / n − mean², clamped at zero); the _sampling variants use the n − 1 denominator (defined from two buckets on). count is the number of buckets that contributed a value — not the sum of their doc_counts.
Two features are not implemented here: there is no sigma parameter (a sigma in the request is accepted and ignored), and the result carries no std_deviation_bounds object — take avg ± k × std_deviation yourself if you need a band.
The buckets_path and gap rules are the family’s:
"per_day>revenue" (> or . separator) — the sub-metric inside each bucket; it must be single-valued (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality, …). A stats sub-agg contributes its sum. A bare parent name profiles the buckets’ doc_counts. skip (default) leaves buckets with a missing metric — and empty buckets (doc_count 0) whose sum reads 0 — out of every statistic; insert_zeros has them contribute 0. With no contributing bucket the numeric fields are null and count is 0.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The 120 daily revenues have a population standard deviation of about 44.2 around the 56.25 mean — days swing widely relative to their average.
Use cases # Volatility of a series — std deviation of daily or monthly revenue buckets: a high std_deviation / avg flags an erratic business rather than a merely small one. Outlier-prone groups — variance of the per-category totals of a terms aggregation to catch one dominant line among many. Anomaly banding — combine avg and std_deviation (population) into a mean ± 2σ envelope for dashboards, computed bucket-side. Small-sample care — with a handful of buckets, read the _sampling variants; the population forms underestimate spread. Parameters for extended_stats_bucket # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric. format (Optional, string) Output number format. Accepted for compatibility; not applied to the value in the current engine. gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros. sigma Not implemented — accepted for compatibility and ignored; the result has no std_deviation_bounds. Related # Sibling family: avg_bucket, sum_bucket, min_bucket,
max_bucket, stats_bucket (the same sample without variance),
percentiles_bucket
Document-level counterpart: extended_stats
title: Extended stats bucket aggregation

content:
Date range aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation like range, but for date fields. Each bucket is a from/to period you name — “before the launch”, “launch week”, “after” — which is the shape reporting questions naturally take, rather than the uniform grid of date_histogram.
How it works # Bounds are epoch milliseconds: from accepts a number (or a numeric string) and is inclusive, to is exclusive, and either may be omitted for an open-ended period. Date strings like "2024-06-04" are not parsed by the aggregation — convert them to epoch millis first (the teaching examples below show the constants).
Every declared range produces exactly one bucket, in declaration order, even when zero documents match. The bucket key is your label verbatim, or — when omitted — the built form "<from>-<to>" with * for unbounded sides and whole numbers rendered without a decimal tail ("*-1717459200000"). Documents missing the field are skipped unless missing supplies a default epoch-millis value, which drops them into whichever period covers it.
Example # Split logs at a mid-June cutoff (epoch millis 1718534400000, i.e. 2024-06-16T10:40:00Z):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The teaching logs dataset ends on June 7, so that cutoff matches no document — the query scope is empty and both buckets return doc_count: 0, which is the point worth noting: declared ranges always materialize. A split inside the data window behaves as you would expect:
POST /logs/_search { "size": 0, "aggs": { "by_period": { "date_range": { "field": "date", "ranges": [ { "key": "early", "to": 1717459200000 }, { "key": "late", "from": 1717459200000 } ] } } } } 1717459200000 is 2024-06-04T00:00:00Z; of the 150 teaching logs, 72 fall before it and 78 from it onward:
{ ... "aggregations": { "by_period": { "buckets": [ { "key": "early", "doc_count": 72 }, { "key": "late", "doc_count": 78 } ] } } } Use cases # Before/after an event. Split at the launch timestamp, the incident time, or the migration cutover, and nest a sum or avg per period to compare behavior across it.
Named reporting periods. Fiscal quarters, holiday windows, retention cohorts — periods with business names, not equal widths. Open-ended cohorts. "before", "between", "ever since" map directly onto omitted from/to sides. Missing-value handling. missing folds documents without the date field into a chosen period instead of silently dropping them from every bucket. Parameters for date_range # field (Required, string) Date field you wish to aggregate. ranges (Required, object array) Buckets with optional from / to (epoch millis numbers or numeric strings; from inclusive, to exclusive). key names a bucket. missing (Optional, number) Epoch-millis value substituted for documents without the field. format (Optional, string) Date format for rendering key_as_string. Accepted for compatibility; the engine builds keys from the bounds as described above. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Related # range — the numeric-field sibling. date_histogram — equal calendar buckets when you want a timeline rather than named periods. ip_range — bands and CIDR masks over IP fields. Range query — filter documents by a date window instead of bucketing them.
title: Date range aggregation

content:
Wildcard query # Returns documents that contain terms matching a wildcard pattern. The pattern supports * (any sequence of characters, including none) and ? (any single character).
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.
How it works # The pattern is expanded against the inverted index’s term dictionary: the engine walks the field’s terms, keeps those matching the pattern, and unions their postings lists — the same result as a should of term queries over the surviving terms. Matching is anchored at both ends: web-1 is the whole term, so web-* matches web-10 and web-1 itself, but web-1 is required for anything with text on both sides.
Cost follows the anchors. A pattern starting with a literal (web-*) can skip most of the dictionary; a pattern starting with * or ? (a leading wildcard) cannot, and degenerates to a full dictionary walk — the same cost class as suffix. Prefer prefix when the pattern is a pure head.
Matching is per term. On a keyword field the term is the whole value; on a text field each analyzed token is tested separately. No analysis runs on the pattern itself — on standard-analyzed fields the stored tokens are lowercase. Scoring. The expansion is rewritten with ES’s constant_score rule: every matching document scores exactly the boost (1.0 by default), regardless of how many terms matched. Inside a bool.filter the scores are discarded, leaving a pure set filter. rewrite is accepted on the wire for body compatibility (constant_score default); the engine scores expansions as described above regardless of the setting. Examples # The pattern below puts the * mid-term — w*b-01 reads “w, anything, then b-01” and matches the host web-01 (50 documents). The SQL twin translates * to % and ? to _.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "wildcard": { "field": "user.id", "value": "ki*y" } } } Use cases # Mid-string holes. Values with a known head and tail but a variable middle (w*b-01 over logs.host → 50 of 150) — the shape neither prefix nor suffix can express. Single-character variation. ? covers ordinal or single-char variation without a full pattern language: web-0? for web-01 to web-03 (all 150 lines). Glob-style file paths. url.path patterns like /api/* (the 50 /api/v1/... lines) or *.js (25 lines) read naturally as globs. Partial IDs from user input. A search box feeding *<input>* over keyword identifiers — convenient, but remember leading wildcards are the expensive case; anchor when the input allows it. Parameters for wildcard # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. value (Required, string) Wildcard pattern to match terms in the provided field against. Note: leading wildcards (*foo) are expensive — prefer the prefix query when possible. case_insensitive (Optional, boolean, default: false) ASCII case-insensitive matching of the value with the indexed field values. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Multiplier for the clause’s score — with the constant-score rewrite this is the score itself. rewrite (Optional, string) Method used to rewrite the expanded terms (constant_score, scoring_boolean, …). Related # prefix — the cheap special case for head-anchored patterns. suffix — tail-anchored matching, same cost class as a leading wildcard. regexp — when */? are not expressive enough. term — the atom every expansion resolves to.
title: Wildcard query

content:
Sum aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that sums up numeric values that are extracted from the aggregated documents. It turns “how much in total” into one number — revenue, bytes, durations, counts of units — without shipping the matching documents anywhere.
How it works # The engine walks the matching documents once, adding each value to a running total. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) contribute, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.
Documents that lack the field are skipped by default. With missing set, every such document adds the default to the total — on the column-store fast path (the production executor) this is computed as missing × absent_count per segment, where the column’s sum_f64 batch reducer supplies the sum of the present values in the same pass.
The sum is exact, and stays exact across shards: per-shard totals combine by plain addition, so distributed and single-node requests return the same number.
sum never returns null — when nothing contributed, the result is 0.0 (an empty bucket is an empty total, not an unknown one).
Examples # Summing the price of every hat — the SQL pill beside the Run button is the same question with a WHERE scoping the sum:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "query": { "term": { "field": "type", "value": "hat" } }, "aggs": { "hat_prices": { "sum": { "field": "price" } } } } Resulting in:
{ ... "aggregations": { "hat_prices": { "value": 900.0 } } } The name of the aggregation (hat_prices above) also serves as the key by which the aggregation result can be retrieved from the returned response.
Use cases # Revenue reporting. sales.sum(amount) = 6750.0 across the 120 teaching sales — total turnover in one request, no matter the match count. Per-group totals. Nested under terms on type, sum(price) returns t-shirt: 900 / hat: 900 / mug: 900 / sticker: 600 — the ranking a leaderboard needs. Stock on hand. products.sum(stock) = 1445 units across the 30 catalog products, and the same aggregation inside a filter drives low-stock alerts. Cross-checking counts. Sum a field that is always 1 to verify a doc_count you distrust; or divide a sum by a value_count for an average computed client-side.
Billing-style rollups. Because shard totals combine by addition, a sum over a date range is safe to fan out and merge — no double counting, no estimates. Parameters for sum # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. script (Optional, object) Script evaluated per document as the value source — mutually exclusive with field. missing (Optional, number) Value used for documents missing the field; each such document adds it to the total. Related # avg — the total divided by how many contributed stats — sum plus count/min/max/avg in one request value_count — how many values went into the sum sum_bucket — sum over another aggregation’s bucket values
title: Sum aggregation

content:
Streaming # Search on Pizza is real-time — documents are visible the moment they are written. The stream block attaches delivery directives to a search request: how the engine should pace and batch the emission of a result that outgrows one response, instead of making the client poll.
POST /my-collection/_search How it works # stream is a native, parsed block of the Pizza request DSL (StreamConfig in lib/engine/src/search/request/mod.rs) — accepted, validated, and carried through the engine with every request. Its knobs describe the emission strategy of the search pipeline:
batch (the default) is the linear pipeline — execute fully, rank, return one JSON answer. progressive paces emission per segment: partial results become available as each segment completes, rather than after all of them. threshold holds hits back until scores drop below score_threshold (or max_wait_ms passes), trading a little latency for a stable top of the list. buffer_size micro-batches whatever is emitted; aggs_priority decides whether aggregations in the same request yield to hit delivery (deferred ships hits first and fills the aggregation results in afterwards). Honest delivery status: over the HTTP gateway every mode currently answers as one complete, buffered JSON body — the block is parsed and executed, but the gateway does not yet translate it into a chunked or event-stream HTTP response, and the in-page widget executes one-shot queries against a WebAssembly engine either way. What is fully real today is the realtime half of the story: there is no refresh interval, so a query re-issued immediately after a write sees that write (see How realtime works) — polling with search_after cursors is an effective stand-in for push delivery while wire-level streaming matures.
Example # This page has no live playground demo: streaming directives shape how a long-running result is paced, while the in-page widget executes one-shot queries against a WebAssembly engine and renders a complete JSON result. Over the gateway today the request below simply returns the usual buffered JSON answer — the block is accepted and executed, wire-level chunked delivery is not switched on yet.
{ "query": { "match": { "field": "message", "query": "error" } }, "size": 0, "stream": { "mode": "progressive", "buffer_size": 4, "max_wait_ms": 250 } } Use cases # Dashboards over big scans. progressive with a generous buffer_size: the first segments’ hits reach the UI while later segments are still being searched, instead of a spinner until the whole corpus is ranked. Alerting-style consumers. threshold mode with a high score_threshold and a small buffer: only strong matches flush early, and max_wait_ms bounds how long a partial buffer waits. Hits before aggregates. A request combining a large hit page with heavy aggregations under aggs_priority: "deferred" ships the hits first and lets the aggregation totals follow. Fresh-as-possible tails. Realtime visibility means a polling loop with search_after over logs sees a freshly written error line on its very next request — no refresh window to wait out. Parameters for stream # mode (Required, batch | progressive | threshold) Delivery mode: batch — normal one-shot search; the block only configures timing. progressive — flush partial results as the query makes progress, then keep pushing newly matching documents. threshold — hold results back until a score threshold or wait budget is met, trading freshness for stability. buffer_size (Optional, integer, default: 4) Micro-batching of pushed hits — more is cheaper per hit, less is lower latency. score_threshold (Optional, float) In threshold mode, the score a hit must reach before the buffer flushes. max_wait_ms (Optional, integer) Upper bound on how long a partially filled buffer may wait before flushing regardless. aggs_priority (Optional, normal | low | deferred, default: normal) Whether aggregations in the same request block streaming delivery. deferred ships hits first and fills in aggregation results later. Notes # Streaming interacts with realtime visibility: a hit can arrive in the same request that indexed it — there is no refresh interval to wait for. Cursors (search_after) combine with streaming for durable consumption; the change feed is the complementary write-path stream (CDC). Keep buffer_size small for alerting-style consumers and large for dashboard-style consumers. Related # API conventions — the request envelope every stream block rides in, and pit snapshots for stable re-queries while data moves. Sort and pagination — search_after cursors: the polling leg of the streaming story. Change feed — the write-path stream (CDC) for consumers that need every change, not every match. How realtime works — the write path (WAL, mutable layer, epoch freeze) that removes the refresh window streaming builds on.
title: Streaming search

content:
Stats bucket aggregation # A sibling pipeline aggregation returning count/min/max/avg/sum of a metric across buckets — the stats of the per-bucket values. One call replaces four: where avg_bucket, min_bucket and max_bucket each reduce the bucket list to a single number, stats_bucket returns the whole summary object beside the aggregation it describes.
"day_stats": { "stats_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } } How it works # stats_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and emits the stats result object over that sample:
{ "count": 120, "min": 15, "max": 180, "avg": 56.25, "sum": 6750 } count is the number of buckets that contributed a value — not the sum of their doc_counts.
The buckets_path names what to collect:
"per_day>revenue" — the > separates the bucket aggregation from the sub-metric inside each bucket; a . separator ("range.v") works identically. The sub-metric must be single-valued (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality, …). A stats sub-agg contributes its sum; multi-value metrics such as percentiles yield nothing. A bare parent name ("per_day") profiles the buckets’ doc_counts. Gaps follow gap_policy:
skip (default) — a bucket whose metric is missing or null is left out of every statistic, and an empty bucket (doc_count 0, e.g. a declared range nothing fell into) is skipped even though its sum reads 0. insert_zeros — such buckets contribute 0 to count, min, and sum. When no bucket contributes, the result is {"count": 0, "min": null, "max": null, "avg": null, "sum": 0.0}.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Each of the 120 single-sale days is one sample, so the daily revenues run from 15 to 180, average 56.25, and total 6750.
Use cases # Per-group spread at a glance — count/min/max/avg of the per-category totals of a terms aggregation: how far the best line is from the worst. Series envelope — a compact min/avg/max band over daily or monthly buckets, ready for a chart’s shaded range. Data-quality check — a suspicious min of 0 (an empty bucket under insert_zeros) or a count smaller than the number of buckets flags gaps in the underlying data. Baseline object for dashboards — one metric the UI can slice into the four numbers it needs. Parameters for stats_bucket # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric. format (Optional, string) Output number format. Accepted for compatibility; not applied to the value in the current engine. gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros. Related # Sibling family: avg_bucket, sum_bucket, min_bucket,
max_bucket,
extended_stats_bucket (adds variance and std deviation),
percentiles_bucket
Document-level counterpart: stats
title: Stats bucket aggregation

content:
Range aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation over numeric fields where each bucket is a user-defined range. It answers “how many documents fall in each band?” — the bands are yours to name and place, unlike the regular grid of histogram.
How it works # Each range is a half-open window: from is inclusive, to is exclusive, and either side may be omitted for unbounded. A document whose value v satisfies from <= v < to counts in that range — and because the test is per range, overlapping definitions put one document in several buckets at once.
Buckets come back in the order the ranges were declared, one per definition even at doc_count: 0. Each bucket reports key and doc_count: the key is your key verbatim when given, otherwise the engine builds it as "<from>-<to>" with * for unbounded sides ("*-50", "50-100", "100-*"). The engine does not echo separate from/to fields on each bucket — the bounds live in the composite key.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "price_ranges": { "range": { "field": "price", "ranges": [ { "to": 50 }, { "from": 50, "to": 100 }, { "from": 100 } ] } } } } Response (the teaching prices are 15/30/45/60 across 120 sales, so the top band is empty but still returned):
{ ... "aggregations": { "price_ranges": { "buckets": [ { "key": "*-50", "doc_count": 110 }, { "key": "50-100", "doc_count": 10 }, { "key": "100-*", "doc_count": 0 } ] } } } Use cases # Price-band reports. low/mid/high labels read better on an executive dashboard than numeric edges — name the ranges with key and let the engine count. Over the teaching sales, under-50 holds 110 of 120 documents. Rating or tier thresholds. Business rules are rarely grid-aligned (“under 3 stars”, “3 to 4.5”, “top”): express the rule once as ranges instead of deriving intervals. Overlapping cohort windows. Ranges may overlap — “under 30”, “under 60”, “all” gives cumulative counts in a single response, something a histogram grid cannot do. Bucketed filters for drill-down. Wrap a range in the query of a filter aggregation (or add sub-aggs per band) to power click-into-band dashboards. Parameters for range # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate (must be numeric). ranges (Required, array) Range definitions; each entry takes: key — (Optional, string) Range label; generated from the bounds when omitted. from — (Optional, number) Lower bound, inclusive. Omit for unbounded below. to — (Optional, number) Upper bound, exclusive. Omit for unbounded above. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Related # date_range — the same band idea over date fields. ip_range — bands and CIDR masks over IP fields. geo_distance — distance rings around a point, the geo sibling of this family. histogram — a regular grid when the bands do not need names. Range query — filter documents by bounds instead of bucketing them.
title: Range aggregation

content:
Lesson 6 — Hybrid search # Most engines hide their fusion behind a magic flag. Pizza exposes the retrieval pipeline as explicit request stages — retrieve runs retrievers in parallel, fuse merges them, and two more stages re-shape scores afterwards:
retrieve → fuse → score_functions → rescore (parallel (merge (function (second pass retrievers) the lists) scoring) on the top window) Every stage is optional and combines with a plain query — you can use score_functions alone on a keyword search, or the full chain for hybrid retrieval.
The dataset for this lesson is the playground’s embeddings collection: 24 documents in three well-separated 8-dim clusters (search, storage, vector) — small enough to stay deterministic, real enough to feel like embeddings.
The use case # Users ask in words; documents answer in different words. “How do I store vectors?” is asked by a human and answered by a page titled dense_vector field options — pure keyword search misses it, and pure vector search misses the exact identifier someone pasted in. Hybrid retrieval runs both legs and merges them; the scoring stages then fix what matching alone cannot. The questions this lesson answers:
“Docs about vector storage that never say ‘vector storage’” — the vector leg, by similarity. “Exact wording AND semantic neighbors, one ranked list” — retrieve + fuse. “BM25 and cosine scores are not comparable — which wins?” — rrf fuses by rank, no score calibration needed. “Boost popular items, demote stale ones” — score_functions. “An expensive second pass, only where it matters” — rescore over the top window. The vector leg, alone # A kNN query with the first cluster’s direction returns exactly that cluster:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Vector search has a direct SQL spelling — KNN(field, vector, k), ranked by SCORE():
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Both return exactly the eight search documents — one pipeline, two front doors.
The lexical leg, alone # The same collection answers BM25 queries — a match on the body text. The words “vector search” appear across all three clusters’ documents, so the lexical leg alone finds all 24:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Two retrievers, two orderings of the same corpus. Neither is the right answer — which is why fusion is a stage you control.
retrieve + fuse: the pipeline itself # Replace the single query with a list of retrievers whose results are fused — the BM25 leg and the vector leg side by side:
graph LR Q["one request"] --> B("bm25 legmatch on text") Q --> V("vector legkNN on embedding") B -->|"ranked list"| F("fuse — rrf") V -->|"ranked list"| F F --> R["one ranked result listthe union of both legs"] JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The fused answer includes every document found by EITHER leg — the match alone finds 24, and the vector leg re-orders the top by similarity. A retriever is bm25 (carrying any query-DSL query) or vector (same options as the vector query).
fuse.method picks how the lists merge:
rrf (reciprocal rank fusion) — ranks by positions alone, no comparable scores needed. The default choice when BM25 and cosine scores must not be compared directly. k (default 60) is the rank constant; larger dampens the influence of top ranks. linear — weighted sum of normalized scores, with per-retriever weights. Use it when the scores are calibrated and comparable. disjmax — keeps each document’s BEST leg score, dedup-like behavior for multi-source retrieval. score_functions: re-shape scores per document # After retrieval (or on a plain query, with no retrieve at all), function scoring re-shapes the score per document — demote stale docs, boost by popularity. Products matching “apparel”, scored by price with a log1p modifier and a constant weight:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Compare _score against the plain match: the price factor lifts expensive products; weight multiplies through. The function vocabulary is field_value_factor, decay (score falls off with distance from an origin — date or numeric), script, and weight; score_mode combines the functions with each other, boost_mode combines the result with the query score.
rescore: an expensive second pass on the top window # When the expensive query only matters for the top candidates, run it as a second pass over a window instead of the whole corpus — text match first, vector re-score over the top 10:
{ "query": { "match": { "field": "text", "query": "vector search" } }, "rescore": { "window": 10, "query": { "vector": { "field": "embedding", "query_vector": [0.98, -0.05, 0.1, 0, -0.1, 0.05, -0.05, 0.1], "k": 10 } }, "query_weight": 0.4, "rescore_query_weight": 0.6 }, "size": 5 } window bounds how many top documents are re-scored (default 10); query_weight / rescore_query_weight blend the original and re-scored scores. This body needs a collection with a dense_vector field — see vector search — run against a live node.
What composes with what # retrieve cannot currently combine with aggs, post_filter, collapse or rescore in the same body — the gateway rejects the mix with a clear 400. score_functions and rescore compose with a plain query — and with each other — without restriction. Of this lesson, the vector half speaks SQL (KNN + SCORE()); the pipeline stages stay DSL in the SQL M1 subset.
Each stage has its own section in the hybrid reference.
What you learned # Hybrid search in Pizza is an explicit retrieve → fuse → score pipeline, not a magic flag — every stage is a request key you can use alone or composed. rrf fuses by rank when scores are incomparable; linear/weights when they are calibrated; disjmax when a document should score by its best leg. score_functions re-shapes scores per document (boost, decay, script); rescore spends an expensive query only on the top window. The vector leg has a SQL twin — KNN(field, vector, k) ranked by SCORE() — one pipeline, two front doors. Next: Lesson 7 — geographic search.
title: Lesson 6 — Hybrid search

content:
Boolean query # A query that matches documents matching boolean combinations of other queries. It is built using one or more boolean clauses.
Inside a nested query: supported — must/filter/should/must_not and minimum_should_match all apply within ONE array element; clauses matched by different elements never combine.
How it works # bool compiles each clause list into iterator algebra: must clauses intersect (AND), must_not clauses subtract, filter clauses intersect without scoring, and should clauses are probed per matched document — a streaming two-pointer walk that adds each matching should score on top of the base hit, with no intermediate materialization.
Matching and scoring rules:
must — every clause must match; each contributes its score, summed. filter — every clause must match; resolved through the unscoring range/BKD/column-store paths, contributing nothing to the score. must_not — no clause may match; unscored. should — optional score boosts while must/filter do the filtering. They become required in exactly two cases: when the bool has should clauses but no must/filter (then at least one must match), or when minimum_should_match is 1 or more, which turns the should group into a required at-least-N-of-M gate alongside the other clauses. When several clauses match the same document their scores add — an OR union sums per-document scores, and a union reduced to a single child passes the child’s score through unchanged, so a one-branch bool never distorts the score below it. score_mode selects how multi-field should scores combine — most_fields (sum, the default) or best_fields (dis_max-style: max + tie_breaker * sum(other_scores), with tie_breaker in [0, 1]). Per-clause boost multiplies into the BM25 chain before the combination. One frozen-segment nuance: when a multi-term expansion (wildcard, regexp, prefix) is a should clause of a same-field bool, its expanded terms merge into the field’s term stream and score per-term BM25 there instead of the constant score a standalone expansion receives.
The optimizer picks the execution shape automatically — filter-led vector evaluation when a filter constrains a vector clause, text-driven scoring with vector boosts when a must text query pairs with a should vector, and reciprocal-rank fusion when independent pipelines sit in a should-only bool. Query::simplify also flattens the tree: a bool whose only content is a single must collapses to that query, and a redundant match_all inside must is dropped when other clauses already restrict the set.
Examples # The query below combines a full-text must with an unscoring range filter — the hats (type = hat) that cost at least 25. All 30 hats are priced 30, so all 30 match:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "bool": { "must": [ { "match": { "field": "title", "query": "search" } } ], "filter": [ { "term": { "field": "status", "value": "published" } } ], "must_not": [ { "range": { "field": "views", "gte": 100000 } } ], "should": [ { "term": { "field": "tags", "value": "featured" } } ], "minimum_should_match": 1 } } } Clause types # must The document must match. Contributes to the score. filter The document must match. Does not contribute to the score — clauses resolve through the unscoring index paths. should The document should match. Contributes to the score; required to match only when no must/filter clauses are present (then at least one should must match) or when minimum_should_match is set. must_not The document must not match. Does not contribute to the score. Use cases # Filter + full text. The workhorse shape: must a match for relevance, filter a range/term for the hard constraints — scored where it matters, unscored where it doesn’t. The example above (hats at price ≥ 25) is exactly this pattern. Exclusion lists. must_not removes archived rows, spam flags or maintenance windows from an otherwise broad query. Optional relevance signals. should boosts featured, recent or vector-similar items without gating admission — and turns into a hard gate via minimum_should_match when the rule demands it. Hybrid retrieval. BM25 text and vector search in one bool: the optimizer fuses the pipelines (text-driven with vector boosts, or RRF for independent shoulds) with no query-side hint. Parameters for bool # must, filter, should, must_not (Optional, array of query objects — a single query object is also accepted as shorthand) The clause lists. At least one clause somewhere is required for the bool to match anything. minimum_should_match (Optional, integer, 0–255) Minimum number of should clauses a document must match. The built-in default is 1 when the query has should clauses but no must/filter, otherwise 0. The percentage and offset string forms ("75%", "-1") are not accepted — the value is a plain integer. score_mode (Optional, string) Multi-field score combination strategy for should clauses: most_fields (sum — the default, for backward compatibility) or best_fields (max, dis_max style). tie_breaker (Optional, float, default: 0) Tie-breaker for best_fields mode. Final score: max_score + tie_breaker * sum(other_scores). Range [0, 1]. Related # match / multi_match — the scored full-text leaves most bools combine; multi_match itself expands into a bool. range — the typical filter occupant: unscoring numeric and date restrictions. match_all — the everything base under must_not-only bools and filter-only aggregations. Analyzers — what the analyzed child queries tokenize with. API conventions — clause shorthand and strict-gate parameter handling.
title: Boolean query

content:
Significant terms aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation returning terms that are unusually frequent in the current scope (foreground) compared with the whole index (background) — the classic “what’s special about this subset” query.
In this engine significant_terms currently approximates that idea by foreground frequency: it ranks the scope’s values by their in-scope doc_count, without computing background statistics. Nest it under a query or a parent bucket to scope the foreground set; the values that dominate that scope come out on top.
How it works # Bucketing follows terms: one bucket per unique value of field, include/exclude filter candidate keys (exact-value arrays or a single wildcard string), and min_doc_count (default 1) drops thin buckets. Buckets are ordered by doc_count descending and truncated to size (default 10).
Two differences from a plain terms are worth knowing:
Buckets carry key and doc_count only — the score and bg_count fields are not part of the response, and there is no background_filter parameter. The significance logic lives in the engine’s significant_text sibling (below), which scores analyzed text foreground-vs-background with the JLH formula; significant_terms over keyword fields ranks by foreground count instead. Because ordering is by in-scope count, the aggregation is most informative when the foreground is skewed: nest it inside a terms bucket (values of a class, category, or status) and compare which inner values lead each outer bucket.
Example # Which merchants over-index inside pending sales?
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. All four merchants sell 10 pending items each in the evenly balanced teaching data, so the ranking is flat; skew your own data and the merchants concentrating in this status surface first.
Use cases # Anomaly-associated values. Inside a logs scope of error messages, which host or url values lead — the suspects for any incident. Per-category fingerprints. Under sales.terms(type), a nested significant_terms on merchant shows which merchant defines each product type. Cohort contrast. Query the cohort (pending customers, gold tier), then let significant_terms list the values that fill it. Sampled significance. On very large scopes, wrap the scope in a sampler first, then rank — the sample-then-signify pattern.
Parameters for significant_terms # field (Required, string) Keyword field you wish to aggregate. size (Optional, integer, default: 10) Maximum number of buckets. min_doc_count (Optional, integer, default: 1) Minimum foreground count per term. include / exclude (Optional) Restrict candidate terms (exact values or wildcard patterns). aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Related # terms — plain frequency ranking rare_terms — the low-frequency tail sampler — cut the foreground down before ranking
title: Significant terms aggregation

content:
Query string query # Returns documents that match a compact query-syntax string, e.g. status:active AND title:search. The same parser powers the URI search parameter ?q=.
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.
How it works # The query string is parsed with the classic query-string grammar and converted to native queries: bare and field-qualified terms become analyzed match queries, quoted phrases become phrase queries, and the boolean operators become bool clauses. Terms without a field: prefix go to default_field (or, when fields is set, the query fans out into a bool.should across those fields with their field^boost weights). The operator subset:
Syntax Meaning field:value term on one field — analyzed for text, exact for keyword AND, OR boolean combination of the surrounding clauses +term, -term required / excluded term (- is the verified exclusion form) "a b" phrase, in order "a b"~N phrase with slop N (a reversed pair matches from N = 2) a*, a?c wildcard against the field’s indexed terms /re/ regular expression against indexed terms term~N fuzzy match, N = 0–2 edits (a bare ~ means 0 edits — exact) [a TO b], {a TO b} term range, inclusive / exclusive field:term^N per-clause boost — multiplies that clause’s score (a b)^N group boost — multiplies every scored clause inside the group Caveats verified against the engine: the per-clause boost field:term^3 binds to that clause and scales its score exactly (3× on term, match, fuzzy, prefix, range and wildcard/regexp expansions alike); the group boost (a b)^2 (also field:(a b)^2) multiplies every scored clause inside the group exactly; a quoted phrase carries no boost slot, so "a b"^N drops the multiplier instead of failing. Also: NOT as an infix keyword does not exclude correctly inside an AND (a AND NOT b) — write a AND -b. Bracketed groups parse, but combining a bracketed group with AND does not constrain correctly for keyword-field groups — flat combinations are the tested path. A query string that fails to parse matches nothing (a warning is logged, never a request failure).
URI search # ?q= on the search and count endpoints feeds the same parser: df becomes default_field, default_operator passes through, and lenient: true turns format errors (a text value against a numeric field) into zero hits instead of a 400. GET /logs/_search?q=level:error is the Kibana-style one-liner form of the example below.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "query_string": { "query": "status:active AND title:search" } } } Across several fields with per-field boosts:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "query_string": { "query": "search engine", "fields": ["title^3", "description"] } } } Use cases # One-line triage. level:error AND message:search — the playground above — narrows 150 log lines to the 25 error lines that mention search, without assembling a bool. Ops URL panes. ?q=host:web-01 (50 of 150 log lines) drives dashboards and curl checks where a JSON body is friction. Exploration by prefix. message:s* widens to every term starting with s (50 lines), the same expansion prefix does — but inline in one string.
Typo tolerance, inline. message:serch~2 still finds the 25 search lines; ~1 tightens, a bare ~ disables fuzziness. Keyword sweeps. level:[error TO warn] walks the dictionary between two terms — all 150 lines, since error < info < warn. Parameters for query_string # query (Required, string) The query-syntax string. default_field (Optional, string, default: *) Field used for bare terms when fields is empty. default_operator (Optional, string, default: or) Default boolean operator between terms: or or and. fields (Optional, array of strings) Multiple fields with optional boost (e.g. ["title^3", "description"]). When non-empty, the query is expanded into a bool.should across these fields; each entry supports the field^boost syntax. type (Optional, string) Multi-field scoring strategy: best_fields (max/dis_max) or most_fields (sum — the default, for backward compatibility). tie_breaker (Optional, float, default: 0) Tie-breaker for best_fields mode: max_score + tie_breaker * sum(other_scores). Range [0, 1]. combination_strategy (Optional, string) Multi-field score combination for fields: best_fields (max/dis_max) or most_fields (sum). Defaults to most_fields. Related # match — what each bare term becomes: one analyzed field query; reach for it when there is no syntax to parse. multi_match — the structured alternative to the fields + type + tie_breaker fan-out. phrase — what a quoted "a b" becomes; it documents the slop semantics the ~N suffix reuses. fuzzy, wildcard, regexp — the standalone forms of the ~, * and /re/ syntax.
title: Query string query

content:
Min aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that keeps track and returns the minimum value among numeric values extracted from the aggregated documents. It answers “how low does this field go” over any query — the floor of a price range, the earliest timestamp in a window, the cheapest item that matches a filter.
How it works # The engine walks the matching documents once, keeping the smallest value seen; any larger value costs one comparison. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) qualify, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.
Documents that lack the field are skipped by default. With missing set, the default is folded into the comparison whenever at least one candidate document lacks the field — a missing document can therefore become the minimum.
On the column-store fast path (the production executor) each segment’s column is decoded once and reduced in a batch (min_f64), with count_present deciding whether the missing default applies; segments and shards combine by pairwise min, so distributed and single-node requests return the same number. Everything is exact — no approximation is involved.
When no document contributed a value, the result is null — unlike sum, an empty set has no meaningful minimum.
Examples # Computing the min price value across all documents — the SQL pill beside the Run button answers the same question with MIN(price):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "min_price": { "min": { "field": "price" } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "min_price": { "value": 15.0 } } } As can be seen, the name of the aggregation (min_price above) also serves as the key by which the aggregation result can be retrieved from the returned response.
Use cases # Price floors. sales.min(price) = 15.0 — the lowest price in the 120 teaching sales; pair it with max to state the full 15..60 range in one response. Cheapest per group. Nested under terms on type, min gives the entry price of each product line for a “starting at” label. Catalogue extremes. products.min(price) = 5.0 across the 30 products — find the loss-leader without sorting the whole index. Bound checks. Alert when min crosses a threshold only a bad value could cross — a negative price, a zero quantity. Framing distributions. Min and max bracket a percentiles report so outliers can’t hide behind the medians.
Parameters for min # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. script (Optional, object) Script evaluated per document as the value source — mutually exclusive with field. missing (Optional, number) Value used for documents missing the field; it takes part in the comparison, so it can become the minimum. Related # max — the mirror image of this aggregation stats — min and max plus count/avg/sum in one request percentiles — the whole distribution, not just the ends min_bucket — min over another aggregation’s bucket values
title: Min aggregation

content:
Max bucket aggregation # A sibling pipeline aggregation identifying the largest per-bucket metric value — e.g. the best-performing group. Bucket aggregations can sort their own output, but only inside one request’s bucket list; max_bucket lifts the winning number out as a single headline metric next to the breakdown.
"best_seller": { "max_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_type>revenue" } } How it works # max_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and returns their maximum as a single-value metric ({"value": 1800}) placed alongside the parent. Only the value is returned — not which bucket produced it; read the parent’s bucket list (or sort it with bucket_sort) when you need the winner’s key.
The buckets_path names what to collect:
"per_type>revenue" — the > separates the bucket aggregation from the sub-metric inside each bucket; a . separator ("range.v") works identically. The sub-metric must be single-valued (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality, …). A stats sub-agg contributes its sum; multi-value metrics such as percentiles yield nothing. A bare parent name ("per_type") takes each bucket’s doc_count — the busiest bucket, not the biggest metric. Gaps follow gap_policy:
skip (default) — a bucket whose metric is missing or null is left out, and an empty bucket (doc_count 0, e.g. a declared range nothing fell into) is skipped even though its sum reads 0. insert_zeros — such buckets contribute 0, which a maximum happily ignores unless every bucket is a gap. If every bucket is missing, the result is {"value": null}.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The four product types bring in 1800, 1800, 1350, 1800, so the largest per-type revenue is 1800 — shared by t-shirt, hat, and sticker.
Use cases # Find the strongest group — the category, merchant, or region with the highest total, as one headline number beside the full breakdown. Peak of a series — the best day in a date_histogram of daily revenue (over the teaching dataset’s 120 single-sale days the daily maximum is 180). Worst-case latency — max of per-service average latencies from a terms over service names: the service to optimize first. Capacity ceiling — max requests-per-minute across time buckets to size a deployment. Parameters for max_bucket # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric. format (Optional, string) Output number format. Accepted for compatibility; not applied to the value in the current engine. gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros. Related # Sibling family: avg_bucket, sum_bucket, min_bucket,
stats_bucket,
extended_stats_bucket,
percentiles_bucket
Document-level counterpart: max
title: Max bucket aggregation

content:
Lesson 5 — Graph traversal # Relations are the first of the two features that most distinguish Pizza from a plain text index: edges as a first-class query target. This lesson walks edges inside one collection — the traversal sections run live in the browser widget, and the modeling section at the end is curl against a live node.
Graph queries are also the one lesson without a SQL pairing: traverse stays DSL-side — it is demand-gated outside the SQL M1 subset, which stops at the single-collection statement.
The use case # “Related to” is everywhere — recommendations, social feeds, GraphRAG context assembly, fraud investigations. When the relationship is the question, a text index makes you assemble the neighborhood in your application; a relation field makes it a query. The questions this lesson answers:
“What is related to this article / user / ticket?” — traverse, one hop out. “Friends of friends — who should I follow next?” — two hops in both directions, ranked by distance for free. “Who points at this node?” — incoming direction: followers, cited-by, who-reports-to. “Start from everything matching X, then expand the neighborhood” — query seeds. “Give me the graph around these hits, for my UI or my RAG pipeline” — the graph projection block. The movie graph at the end models entities and relationships end to end — the same shape as social, hierarchy, citation and fraud domains.
Entities and relationships are both documents # The articles collection (44 documents) carries a related_to field of type relation. The graph lives entirely inside that one collection, in two kinds of documents:
Node documents — the entities. An article carries its attributes (title, body, tags, author). Edge documents — the relationships. A “related to” link is its own document whose relation field names both endpoints by key: { "related_to": { "from": "A01", "to": "A02" } } The dataset is 20 article documents plus 24 edge documents. No side table, no join index to maintain: write an edge document and the adjacency is queryable in the same breath. A traverse query walks those edges.
Your first traversal # Start from two seed articles and walk one hop in either direction:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Two documents are reachable at depth 0 (the seeds themselves), 17 at depth 1 — the known answer for this dataset, 19 hits in total. The walk is a ring at a time, and the score falls with each ring:
graph LR S("seeds — depth 0score 1.0") -->|"one hop along related_to"| R1("depth 1 — 17 documentsscore 0.5") R1 -->|"the circle grows"| R2("depth 2score 0.33") Three knobs did the work:
field — the edge field to walk, declared relation in the schema. seed — where the walk starts. Here: two document _keys. max_depth — the hop budget. Seeds sit at depth 0, so max_depth: 0 returns just the seeds; change it to 2 and watch the circle grow. direction — edges are directed: outgoing follows what a node points at, incoming finds who points at it, both (the default) walks either way. Edit the widget and flip it. Every reached node comes back as a hit, and the score encodes the distance: 1.0 / (1.0 + depth). Seeds score 1.0, one-hop neighbors 0.5, two-hop neighbors 0.33 — the closer a document is to the seed, the higher it ranks.
Seeds do not have to be keys # Any query can select the seeds. Instead of naming articles, start from everything a given author wrote, and walk one hop out from there:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The seed selector takes three forms: keys (as above), query (any sub-query, resolved before the traversal dispatches), or ids (pre-resolved internal ids — the programmatic form). On a live server keys also accepts system ids in "rolling,seq" form; keys that do not exist are simply dropped.
Traversal plus a query seed is the graph-search workhorse: find the documents matching X, then expand the neighborhood — related articles, referenced tickets, upstream dependencies — in one request.
Keep a graph collection on one shard # Edge endpoints resolve against the key map of the shard that stores the edge document. An endpoint living on a different shard cannot be resolved there — that edge is dropped with a warning, not silently half-walked. So keep a graph collection (or at least its edge documents and the nodes they reference) on a single shard:
{ "settings": { "rolling": { "partitions_sharding_strategy": { "hash": { "number_of_shards": 1 } } } }, "schema": { "properties": { "related_to": { "type": "relation" } } } } That is exactly how the articles teaching dataset is declared. The traverse reference covers the placement rules in detail.
Rendering: the graph block # traverse searches by walking edges. The graph block renders: add it to any search request and the response carries a graph object — nodes and edges — built from the hit set, alongside the normal hits. A term query picks the seeds, the graph block projects everything they reach:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The projection works in two tiers:
Relation fields (adjacency). On a relation-typed field it walks the same adjacency structure traverse uses, emitting document-to-document edges for every recorded edge whose endpoints are in the hit set. Ad-hoc column projection. On an ordinary keyword field, every distinct value on the hit documents becomes a synthetic entity node, and each document links to its values. No relation schema needed — any faceting-style column turns into a bipartite graph: JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. In the response, node ids are stable (doc:<key> for documents, ent:<field>:<value> for entities), edges carry from/to/via, and a short plan line summarizes which tier executed. A UI — or a GraphRAG pipeline — consumes the structure directly, no client-side adjacency assembly. label_field and extra_fields attach titles and metadata to the nodes so rendering needs no second round trip; the graph reference has the full parameter list.
Modeling entities and relationships # related_to is one edge type over one node type. Real domains have several of each — and the model is always the same three moves:
Entities are node documents, with a discriminator field saying which is which (node_type below). Relationships are edge documents — {from, to} naming endpoint keys. One relation field per relationship type — acted_in, directed and has_genre are three fields, three edge sets, queryable independently. This section builds a small movie graph against your Lesson 1 node and asks it real questions — the same shape as the engine’s own graph_movies example. It is curl, not a widget: the playground ships fixed datasets.
The model # One collection holds people, movies and genres, plus three edge types:
PUT /movies { "schema": { "dynamic": "strict", "properties": { "node_type": { "type": "keyword" }, "name": { "type": "text" }, "title": { "type": "text" }, "year": { "type": "integer" }, "acted_in": { "type": "relation", "relation": { "from_type": "person", "to_type": "movie" } }, "directed": { "type": "relation", "relation": { "from_type": "person", "to_type": "movie" } }, "has_genre": { "type": "relation", "relation": { "from_type": "movie", "to_type": "genre" } } }} } (The relation meta is descriptive — documentation for humans and the traversal planner; the engine does not enforce it.)
Node documents — four people, three movies, two genres, keys as slugs:
PUT /movies/_doc/leonardo { "node_type": "person", "name": "Leonardo DiCaprio" } PUT /movies/_doc/nolan { "node_type": "person", "name": "Christopher Nolan" } PUT /movies/_doc/gordon { "node_type": "person", "name": "Joseph Gordon-Levitt" } PUT /movies/_doc/page { "node_type": "person", "name": "Ellen Page" } PUT /movies/_doc/inception { "node_type": "movie", "title": "Inception", "year": 2010 } PUT /movies/_doc/knight { "node_type": "movie", "title": "The Dark Knight", "year": 2008 } PUT /movies/_doc/star { "node_type": "movie", "title": "Interstellar", "year": 2014 } PUT /movies/_doc/scifi { "node_type": "genre", "name": "sci-fi" } PUT /movies/_doc/thriller { "node_type": "genre", "name": "thriller" } Edge documents — one per relationship, endpoints by key:
PUT /movies/_doc/e1 { "acted_in": { "from": "leonardo", "to": "inception" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e2 { "acted_in": { "from": "gordon", "to": "inception" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e3 { "acted_in": { "from": "page", "to": "inception" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e4 { "acted_in": { "from": "leonardo", "to": "knight" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e5 { "directed": { "from": "nolan", "to": "inception" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e6 { "directed": { "from": "nolan", "to": "knight" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e7 { "directed": { "from": "nolan", "to": "star" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e8 { "has_genre": { "from": "inception", "to": "scifi" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e9 { "has_genre": { "from": "inception", "to": "thriller" } } PUT /movies/_doc/e10 { "has_genre": { "from": "knight", "to": "thriller" } } The graph those documents build — three node types, three edge types, one collection:
graph LR subgraph people["person nodes"] L("leonardo") N("nolan") G("gordon") P("page") end subgraph movies["movie nodes"] I("inception") K("knight") T("star") end subgraph genres["genre nodes"] SC("scifi") TH("thriller") end L -->|"acted_in"| I G -->|"acted_in"| I P -->|"acted_in"| I L -->|"acted_in"| K N -->|"directed"| I N -->|"directed"| K N -->|"directed"| T I -->|"has_genre"| SC I -->|"has_genre"| TH K -->|"has_genre"| TH Order matters: endpoints resolve by key at write time, and an edge whose endpoint does not exist yet is silently dropped (a warn in the node log). Write the nodes first — the same bulk request is fine — then the edges. Beyond that, an edge document is ordinary: it can carry attributes (a role, a since date) that are searchable like any field, and deleting it removes the edge.
The questions the graph answers # Who acted in Inception? Walk acted_in backwards from the movie — incoming finds everyone pointing at it:
POST /movies/_search { "size": 10, "track_total_hits": true, "query": { "traverse": { "field": "acted_in", "seed": { "keys": ["inception"] }, "max_depth": 1, "direction": "incoming" } } } 4 hits: inception at depth 0, and at depth 1 exactly the three actors — leonardo, gordon, page. The depth-1 tier is the answer; the seed is just the anchor.
Which movies has DiCaprio been in? Same edge field, forward:
"seed": { "keys": ["leonardo"] }, "max_depth": 1, "direction": "outgoing" 3 hits: leonardo, inception, knight — one hop out along acted_in.
Who are DiCaprio’s co-actors? Two hops, both directions:
