"seed": { "keys": ["leonardo"] }, "max_depth": 2, "direction": "both" 5 hits: leonardo (1.0), his two movies (0.5), and at 0.333 exactly the co-actors — gordon and page, reached through inception. This is the recommendation pattern: people two hops out through a shared movie, and the depth-scored ranking already orders them.
Query seeds: the cast of the 2010s movies. Seeds do not have to be keys — any query selects them. All movies from 2010 on, then everyone who acted in one:
POST /movies/_search { "size": 10, "track_total_hits": true, "query": { "traverse": { "field": "acted_in", "seed": { "query": { "range": { "field": "year", "gte": 2010, "lt": 2015 } } }, "max_depth": 1, "direction": "incoming" } } } The range matches inception (2010) and star (2014); one hop in on acted_in reaches the inception cast — 5 hits, the two movies at depth 0 and the three actors at depth 1.
What genres is Inception? A third relationship type, same mechanics — has_genre, outgoing from the movie: 3 hits, scifi and thriller one hop out.
Render the whole neighborhood # The graph block merges several edge types into one picture — all people, linked through both their acting and directing edges:
POST /movies/_search { "size": 4, "track_total_hits": true, "query": { "term": { "field": "node_type", "value": "person" } }, "graph": { "relations": [ { "field": "acted_in" }, { "field": "directed" } ], "max_seeds": 4 } } The response’s graph.nodes/graph.edges carry the four people, the movies, and every acted_in/directed edge between them (edge documents render as doc nodes the endpoints link through) — ready for a UI, or as the context assembly step of a GraphRAG pipeline.
The same shape, other domains # Social — users + a follows edge. incoming = followers, both at depth 2 = friends-of-friends, ranked as follow suggestions. Hierarchy — employees + a reports_to edge. outgoing climbs the management chain, incoming collects the org below. Citations — papers + a cites edge. incoming is cited-by (impact), outgoing is the reference list. Fraud rings — accounts + shared keyword columns (email, phone, device). No relation schema at all: the graph block’s ad-hoc tier turns shared values into entity nodes, and a ring shows up as one connected cluster — the tags widget above is exactly this shape. One boundary to keep in mind: edges live inside ONE collection — the endpoint keys resolve against that collection’s key map. When the relationship points into another collection (orders → orgs), it is not an edge: declare a keyword foreign key with references and query it with a join — Lesson 8. Rule of thumb: same collection, walk it; across collections, join it.
What you learned # Entities and relationships are both documents: nodes carry the attributes, an edge document carries {from, to} by key — graph queries without a graph database, and without a second index to maintain. Seeds can be _keys, system ids, or an arbitrary sub-query; non-existent keys drop out quietly. max_depth bounds the hops, direction picks the edge orientation, and scores fall off with distance (1 / (1 + depth)) — which makes two-hop walks a ranked suggestion list for free. One relation field per relationship type; endpoints resolve at write time, so write nodes before edges. Edge resolution is shard-local: keep graph collections on one shard. The graph block renders any hit set as nodes and edges — adjacency tier for relation fields, ad-hoc entity tier for plain keyword columns. The modeling boundary: same collection, walk it (traverse); across collections, join it (references FK + join). Next: Lesson 6 — hybrid search. The two-collection sibling of these edges — joins — is Lesson 8.
title: Lesson 5 — Graph traversal

content:
Graph projection block # Add a graph block to any search request and the response carries a graph — nodes and edges — built from the hit set, alongside the normal hits. Where the traverse query searches by walking edges, the graph block renders: it takes the documents a query already found and projects them into a node/edge structure a UI (or a GraphRAG pipeline) can consume directly.
graph LR subgraph walk["traverse — searches by walking"] S("seeds") -->|"walk edgesup to max_depth"| H1["hits — every reached node,scored by distance"] end subgraph render["graph — renders what was found"] Q("any query") --> H2("hit set") H2 -->|"project the relation field"| G["nodes + edgesfor a UI or GraphRAG"] end Live over the articles teaching dataset (44 documents with a related_to relation field) — a term query picks the seeds, the graph block renders everything they reach:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. And the ad-hoc form over a plain keyword field — no relation schema, every tags value on the hit documents becomes an entity node:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /articles/_search { "size": 20, "query": { "match_all": {} }, "graph": { "field": "related_to" } } How it works # The block runs after the query: whatever the request selected — the hit page, capped at max_seeds — is the seed set, and each slice (one entry of relations, or the field shorthand) projects over it.
Adjacency tier. A relation field’s edges are stored as their own documents ({"related_to": {"from": "A01", "to": "A02"}}). At write time a writer hook resolves both endpoints through the key map to internal ids and records the pair in an in-memory adjacency index that keeps both directions; an unresolvable endpoint drops the adjacency entry, never the edge document. The projection walks that adjacency from the seed documents and emits one doc → doc edge per recorded edge whose endpoints it reached. Column tier. For an ordinary field the projection reads each seed document’s values for the field (stored fields first, columnar storage as fallback), deduplicates them, and emits one entity node per distinct value plus a doc → ent:<field>:<value> edge — capped at max_values_per_doc values per document. Slices merge into one graph: doc nodes are deduplicated across slices by key, entity nodes stay per-field, and the plan string records what actually executed per slice.
The adjacency walk inherits the same shard-local endpoint resolution as traverse — see Notes and traverse — shard placement.
Two projection tiers # The engine picks a tier per relation slice:
Relation fields (adjacency). When the field is declared type: relation in the schema (or you pass the relation hint), the projection walks the field’s adjacency index — the same structure traverse uses — and emits document-to-document edges for every recorded edge whose endpoints are in the hit set. Ad-hoc column projection. For an ordinary keyword field, every distinct value on the hit documents becomes a synthetic entity node and each document links to its values (doc → ent:<field>:<value>). This turns any faceting-style column into a bipartite graph — no relation schema needed. Shapes # Single relation (the shorthand):
{ "query": { "term": { "field": "author", "value": "medcl" } }, "graph": { "field": "genres", "max_values_per_doc": 8 } } Multiple relations in one round trip — each slice merges into one graph; doc nodes are deduplicated across slices, entity nodes stay per-field. Live: one projection over both the related_to edges and the tags column:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The equivalent request as JSON:
{ "query": { "match_all": {} }, "graph": { "relations": [ { "field": "related_to" }, { "field": "tags", "max_values_per_doc": 4 } ], "max_seeds": 100 } } Response # The response gains a graph object as a peer of hits and aggregations:
{ "hits": { … }, "graph": { "nodes": [ { "id": "doc:A01", "kind": "doc", "key": "A01", "degree": 3 }, { "id": "ent:tags:search", "kind": "ent", "field": "tags", "value": "search" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "doc:A01", "to": "doc:A09", "via": "related_to" }, { "from": "doc:A01", "to": "ent:tags:search", "via": "tags" } ], "plan": "slices=2 seeds=3 [tier=edge field=related_to reached=10, tier=column field=tags]" } } Node ids are stable identifiers for consumers to dedupe on: "doc:<key>" for document nodes, "ent:<field>:<value>" for entity nodes. Internal numeric document ids are never exposed — documents without a _key render as doc:<id>. kind is "doc" or "ent"; doc nodes carry their key and a degree (edges touching the node), entity nodes carry the field they were derived from and its stringified value. With a relation field, edge documents appear as doc nodes too — the endpoints they connect link through them, mirroring how the edges are stored. Edges carry from, to (node ids) and via (the field the edge was derived from). plan is a short human-readable summary of what actually executed (tier chosen per slice, field, seed count, reach). Use cases # GraphRAG context assembly. Retrieve candidate documents by text or vector similarity, then project the related_to edges among them so the prompt receives structure — which candidates cite which — not a flat list. Over the articles teaching set (20 nodes, 24 citation edges) one block renders both layers. Knowledge-graph UIs. Render a hit set as a node-link diagram without standing up a graph database: doc nodes carry stable ids, optional labels (label_field) and metadata (extra_fields) for immediate rendering; entity nodes carry the shared values. Facet exploration. The ad-hoc tier turns any keyword column into a bipartite doc-value graph — project articles.tags to see which topics co-occur inside one hit set, at facet-query cost. One round trip, two views. The relations array renders citation edges and tag entities in a single response, so a UI paginates hits and graph together instead of issuing a second graph request. Parameters for graph # field (string) Single-relation shorthand — the field to project. Set this or relations, not both. relation (Optional, string) Explicit hint naming a schema relation field, routing the slice through the adjacency tier even when field alone would be ambiguous. relations (array) Multi-relation form — one entry per slice, each with field, optional relation hint and max_values_per_doc. max_values_per_doc (Optional, integer, default: 16) Cap on distinct values projected per source document (ad-hoc tier) — keeps a long array field from blowing up the node set. In the relations form, set it per entry. max_seeds (Optional, integer, default: the request’s size) Cap on how many hit documents feed the projection — prevents accidental projections over million-hit baselines. seed_kind (Optional, string, default: "doc") Kind label for document nodes — set it to the collection name (e.g. "movie") for more semantic rendering. key_field (Optional, string) _source field used to key document nodes that are NOT part of the returned hit page (reached only through edges) — the engine looks the value up from the document store so their ids carry a business key instead of the internal ordinal. Nodes in the hit page always use their _key. label_field (Optional, string) _source field populating each doc node’s human-readable value (e.g. the title) — verified live: works for in-page and edge-reached nodes alike. extra_fields (array of strings) Additional _source fields attached to each doc node under extras (e.g. ["author"]) so a UI can render metadata without a second round trip. Notes # The block composes with any query, sort, and size — the graph is derived from whatever the query selected. Like traverse, relation-field projection resolves endpoints within the shard that stores the edge document — keep graph collections on a single shard (see traverse — shard placement).
Related # traverse — the searching sibling: walks the same adjacency to decide which documents match, where this block renders documents a query already found. join — cross-collection membership (semi-join) rather than in-collection edge walking. nested — correlation within one document’s array elements, the intra-document counterpart of relation edges. Relational parameters — declaring the relation field type these projections execute over. Nested aggregation and children aggregation — bucket-side analytics over nested and parent/child structures.
title: Graph projection block

content:
Geo-shape query # Matches documents whose geo_shape field relates to a query geometry by a spatial relation. The query geometry is a GeoJSON geometry object or a WKT string; the indexed shape was written the same way.
Where the geo_point queries ask “is this point inside my region?”, geo_shape asks it of whole geometries — the document carries a polygon, line or envelope (a delivery zone, a pipeline route, a parcel) and the query tests it against another geometry.
How it works # A geo_shape field owns a dedicated field store with two structures per field:
a 4-dimensional BKD tree holding each document’s shape bounding box as one point [min_lat, min_lon, max_lat, max_lon]; the exact geometry per document, stored alongside. Execution is two-phase:
Bounding-box overlap. “My bbox overlaps the query’s bbox” is itself expressible as one range in the 4-dim space, so the tree walk yields a candidate superset — every true spatial relation implies overlapping bounding boxes, so nothing is missed. Exact relation. Each candidate’s stored geometry is tested with exact planar predicates: intersects (a vertex inside the other shape, a boundary touch, or a segment crossing), within (every exterior vertex inside plus no edge properly crossing the boundary — touching from inside still counts), contains (the same test with both sides swapped). disjoint runs differently: disjoint shapes usually have non-overlapping boxes and never enter the overlap range, so it evaluates NOT intersects over the stored geometries directly. All predicates work in planar WGS-84 degree space: edges are straight in latitude/longitude (no great-circle interpolation), boundaries count as intersecting/inside within a 1e-9-degree tolerance (~0.1 mm), and antimeridian wrapping is not applied.
On the fifteen-place teaching dataset — each document carries a small diamond region around its point — the Beijing envelope in the example below answers intersects: 2, within: 2, disjoint: 13.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The live example matches the two Beijing places — each document carries a small polygon region around its point. The same query as a curl request:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "geo_shape": { "field": "region", "shape": { "type": "polygon", "coordinates": [[ [-73.96, 40.78], [-73.90, 40.78], [-73.90, 40.72], [-73.96, 40.72] ]] }, "relation": "intersects" } } } A WKT string works too (BBOX takes minLon, maxLat, maxLon, minLat):
{ "query": { "geo_shape": { "field": "region", "shape": "BBOX (-74.1, 40.9, -73.8, 40.6)", "relation": "within" } } } The nested form also works, with relation defaulting to intersects:
{ "query": { "geo_shape": { "region": { "shape": {"type": "envelope", "coordinates": [[-0.20, 51.60], [0.05, 51.45]]}, "relation": "within" } } } } Parameters for geo_shape # field (Required, string) The geo_shape field to filter on. shape (Required, object|string) The query geometry: a GeoJSON object (point, multi_point, line_string, multi_line_string, polygon, multi_polygon, envelope, geometry_collection) or a WKT string. GeoJSON coordinates are [lon, lat] as in the standard. relation (Optional, string) How the indexed shape must relate to the query geometry. One of: intersects (default) — the shapes share at least one point. disjoint — the shapes share nothing. within — the indexed shape lies entirely inside the query geometry. contains — the indexed shape contains the query geometry. Matching is exact: candidates are narrowed by a bounding-box index and then verified against the full stored geometry, so there are no misses and no false positives. Shapes are treated as plain latitude/longitude geometry on WGS-84; antimeridian wrapping is not supported.
Use cases # Indexed service regions. Each document owns its zone (a store’s delivery polygon) and the query is a rectangle or point of interest — intersects finds every zone covering that spot. Boundary containment. “Which parcels lie entirely inside this planning area?” is within; “which planning area fully contains this parcel?” is contains — the same test from either side. Linear assets. Routes, pipelines and power lines indexed as linestrings, matched against a region they cross — the exact phase handles line-through-polygon with no vertex inside. Everything-but filtering. disjoint excludes the shapes that touch a zone — keep results outside a hazard area or an excluded district. Related # geo_bounding_box, geo_distance,
geo_polygon — the point-side family: the document carries a geo_point, the query the region.
geo-centroid aggregation — mean centre of the matched documents. geohash-grid and geotile-grid aggregations — grid the matches onto map tiles.
title: Geo-shape query

content:
Fuzzy query # Returns documents that contain terms similar to the search term, within the maximum edit distance (Levenshtein — with transpositions counting as a single edit by default).
Use it when the indexed terms are only approximately known: typos in identifiers, OCR noise, or human-entered names.
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.
How it works # The value is expanded against the inverted index’s term dictionary by edit distance, then the survivors’ postings are unioned like a should of term queries. The engine takes the union of three resolution passes — the value recorded as an exact term, a whole-value fuzzy walk, and (on non-keyword fields) a per-token walk after running the field’s search analyzer over the value — so the query works on keyword fields and on analyzed text alike (the per-token pass matters for CJK and multi-word input). On keyword fields the raw value is used, with the field’s normalizer applied first and no tokenization.
The four knobs — prefix_length, max_expansions, transpositions and case_insensitive — are wired end-to-end across the engine’s execution layers (live, built and frozen segments; the count path honours them exactly like the hits path so totals and results agree):
prefix_length requires the first N characters of every expansion term to match the value exactly — a cheap relevance and cost filter. max_expansions (default 50) truncates the candidate set best-distance-first. transpositions (default true) counts an adjacent-character swap (ab → ba) as one edit (Damerau/OSA, the engine’s native distance); false re-checks every candidate with strict Levenshtein, which can drop swap-only matches. case_insensitive lowercases both sides before matching. Scoring. Each hit scores BM25 × a distance-derived boost of (max_edits + 1 − distance) — exact matches outrank one-edit matches outrank two-edit matches, before BM25 breaks ties.
Examples # The search below misspells search by one character — serch is a single insertion away, well within 2 edits, so the 25 GET /search lines still match:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. "AUTO" picks the budget from the value’s length — serch is 5 characters, so AUTO grants a single edit, which is exactly the insertion needed to reach search:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "fuzzy": { "field": "user.id", "value": "kiiby", "fuzziness": 2 } } } Use cases # Typo-tolerant lookups. serch over logs.message still finds the 25 GET /search lines — the single-edit case every search box needs. Identity resolution. Customer or host names typed by humans (medcl / medic / mecl) — AUTO with a prefix_length of 1–2 keeps expansions sane on large vocabularies. OCR and sensor noise. Machine-generated text where single-character substitutions are common; transpositions additionally catches the swapped-pair class. Vocabulary suggestion. Run fuzzy over a keyword field with fuzziness: 1 to propose “did you mean” terms before running the real query. Parameters for fuzzy # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. value (Required, string) Term you wish to find in the provided field. fuzziness (Optional) Maximum edit distance allowed for matching: an integer 0–2, "AUTO", or "AUTO:low,high". "AUTO" picks the budget from the value’s length at query time — shorter than low characters (default 3): 0 edits; shorter than high characters (default 6): 1 edit; otherwise 2. Values above 2 clamp to 2 (Levenshtein automata are only implemented up to distance 2). Default 0 (exact) — write "AUTO" explicitly for auto-scaling. prefix_length (Optional, integer, default: 0) The first N characters of every expansion term must match the query value exactly. max_expansions (Optional, integer, default: 50) Cap on the number of expansion terms considered, best-distance-first. transpositions (Optional, boolean, default: true) An adjacent-character transposition (ab → ba) counts as one edit. false re-checks each candidate with strict Levenshtein distance. case_insensitive (Optional, boolean, default: false) Fold case on both the query value and candidate terms before matching. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Decrease or increase the relevance scores of the query. Related # term — the exact-match original; fuzzy with fuzziness: 0 degenerates to it. match — analyzed full-text matching. Note match rejects a fuzziness parameter with HTTP 400; fuzzy matching on analyzed text is this query’s job. query_string — the ~ operator is fuzzy matching inside a query-string expression.
title: Fuzzy query

content:
Field collapsing # Collapse the result list so each distinct value of a field appears at most once — “best product per merchant”, “best article per author” — without a terms aggregation, keeping full hit semantics (scores, source, highlight).
POST /my-collection/_search How it works # Collapse is engine-native and runs as a post-retrieval step. The collector normally stops at from + size, but collapse pages over GROUPS, so the engine first gathers a wider window — max(1000, from + size) hits (COLLAPSE_WINDOW in lib/engine/src/search/mod.rs) — in request sort order, then:
Groups the hits by the collapse field’s value, preserving first-seen order. Documents missing the field form their own group. Keeps the FIRST hit of each group as its representative — with no sort that is the highest-scoring member; with a sort it is the first under that order. Pages from/size over the representatives (groups, not raw docs). Leaves hits.total at the FULL match count — collapse deduplicates the result list, never the count. inner_hits asks for each group’s runner-ups. The engine gives every inner-hits request its own sort clause (numeric compare first, text fallback, missing values always last regardless of direction, doc-id ascending as the tie-break), an optional second-level collapse that deduplicates the runner-ups, and a total counted before size truncation. Default inner-hits name is inner_hits, default size 3; the wire form accepts a single object or an array.
Delivery status of inner_hits today: the engine assembles the blocks, but the distributed transport currently drops them at the RPC boundary (collapse_inner_hits is a named TODO in the transport conversion), and the in-page widget executes the wasm engine, which also collapses without runner-ups — over the HTTP API, treat inner_hits as pending.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. One best-selling hit per product type (the dataset has four: hat, t-shirt, mug, sticker); the plain match-all total stays 120 — collapse deduplicates the RESULT list, not the count.
Collapse composes with sort: sort by price descending and collapse by type, and each representative is that type’s most expensive sale — the group order follows the same sort.
Use cases # One hit per owner. Deduplicate search results per user, per host, or per merchant so a single noisy owner cannot fill the first page — classic “best X per Y” result lists. Grouped browsing. Collapse logs by host (or level) to see one representative log per group while hits.total still reports how many logs matched overall. Cheaper distinct lists. A small distinct-value list with full hit bodies (source, highlights) — what a terms aggregation cannot give you, since buckets carry counts, not documents. Two-level grouping shape. Outer collapse for the group, inner collapse inside inner_hits for a secondary key when rendering grouped result cards (conformance-suite path today). Parameters for collapse # field (Required, string) The field to collapse on. Keyword-like fields with doc values give the cheapest collapse. inner_hits (Optional, object | array of objects) Also return the top runner-up documents of each group: name (Optional, string, default: inner_hits) Key under which the inner hits appear. size (Optional, integer, default: 3) Runner-ups per group. sort (Optional, array) Sort clause for the runner-ups; equal keys tie-break by internal doc id ascending. collapse (Optional, object) Nested collapse for a second-level grouping of the runner-ups. max_concurrent_group_searches (Optional, integer) Accepted for wire compatibility; the engine’s group assembly is not parallelized today, so the value is unused. Notes # Collapse runs after scoring, so the top hit per group is the best match, not the newest document (unless you sort by date). Pagination applies to collapsed groups, not raw documents. rescore and collapse in one request: the ES-compat layer rejects the mix; the native gateway path currently executes both — do not rely on that combination. For full per-group analytics (counts, aggregations over group members) use a terms aggregation with sub-aggs instead; collapse is for result-list shape. Related # Sort and pagination — the other half of result-list shape: which group leads, and where missing values land. Rescore — re-rank the window before (or instead of) collapsing; the third member of the result-shaping family. terms aggregation — per-group counts and sub-aggregations when you need analytics, not hits. Hybrid search — retrieve (hybrid) requests cannot carry a collapse block; the gateway rejects the mix.
title: Field collapsing

content:
Traverse query # Term and full-text queries match document content; none of them can ask “what is connected to these documents?” — the question citation graphs, reference data and knowledge graphs are made of. The traverse query answers it: a bounded graph traversal over a relation-typed edge field — starting from seed documents, walk the edges up to max_depth hops and emit every reached node as a hit.
Scores encode distance — 1.0 / (1.0 + depth) — so seeds outrank 1-hop neighbors, which outrank 2-hop neighbors, and the standard top-K collector orders the results.
How it works # Edges live in the collection itself: a relation-typed field is written as its own document — {"related_to": {"from": "A01", "to": "A02"}} — and a writer-side hook resolves both endpoints (string keys through the key map, numbers as ids) into an in-memory adjacency index that stores every edge in both directions, so incoming and both cost the same per step as outgoing. An endpoint that cannot be resolved is dropped with a warning; the edge document itself is still stored.
The walk is breadth-first: the seed frontier expands level by level, and each node is recorded at the depth it was first reached — its shortest hop from any seed. Every reached node becomes an ordinary hit scored 1.0 / (1.0 + depth).
Seeds resolve before the walk dispatches: a query seed runs first and its hits become the id list; keys go through the store’s key map (missing keys drop — the same semantics the writer applies to edge endpoints). On Pizza server the gateway rewrites a mixed seed list per shard: system ids in "rolling,seq" form de-roll on the rolling that owns them and drop everywhere else, user keys pass through untouched.
Live numbers over the articles teaching graph (20 article nodes, 24 citation edges): seeding with author = medcl matches 5 documents, max_depth: 0 returns exactly those 5, and one undirected hop reaches 17 — the seeds plus every article they cite or are cited by.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "traverse": { "field": "related_to", "seed": { "query": { "term": { "field": "topic", "value": "search-engines" } } }, "max_depth": 2, "direction": "outgoing" } } } Seeds by document _key (the string ids you index with):
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "traverse": { "field": "related_to", "seed": { "keys": ["A01", "A05"] }, "max_depth": 1 } } } Shard placement # Edge endpoints resolve against the key map of the shard that stores the edge document. Endpoints living on a different shard cannot be resolved there, and the edge is dropped with a warning — so keep a graph collection (or at least its edge documents and the nodes they reference) on a single shard:
{ "settings": { "rolling": { "partitions_sharding_strategy": { "hash": { "number_of_shards": 1 } } } }, "schema": { "properties": { "related_to": { "type": "relation" } } } } Use cases # “Read these too.” One or two hops over related_to from the articles a search already returned — citation-neighborhood expansion with no co-occurrence index to maintain. Structural recommendation. Walk curated relation edges instead of vector similarity when the relationship is editorial — related products, co-authored papers, linked issues. The edges you wrote define the candidates; distance ranks them. GraphRAG retrieval. Seed with an ordinary query, then traverse to pull the structured neighborhood into the prompt — the retrieved set and its context arrive scored in one request. Impact analysis. “Which entities sit within two hops of this flagged one?” — reachability over a graph you already store, without exporting it to a graph database. Parameters for traverse # field (Required, string) Edge field to traverse; must be declared in the schema with the relation type. seed (Required) Seed selector, one of: query — a sub-Query resolved before the traversal dispatches. keys — document _keys; resolved through the store’s key map, keys that do not exist are dropped. On Pizza server, keys may also be system ids in "rolling,seq" form (the same mixed-id convention as GET/DELETE) — the gateway routes them to the owning shard and de-rolls them; keys containing , are reserved and rejected at ingest, so the two forms never conflict. ids — pre-resolved internal _ids (u32). max_depth (Required, integer) Maximum hop count. Seeds are at depth 0, so max_depth: 0 returns just the seeds. direction (Optional, string) Traversal direction along the edges: outgoing, incoming or both (the default). Related # graph — the rendering counterpart: project the hit set as nodes and edges instead of searching by walking them. join — cross-collection membership when the relationship lives in another collection’s keys rather than edge documents. nested — same-element correlation inside one document’s array, the intra-document counterpart of edges. Relational parameters — the schema side of relation fields and the references they declare. Nested aggregation and children aggregation — bucket-side analytics over nested and parent/child structures.
title: Traverse query

content:
Semantic query # Semantic search with zero field knowledge: the vector field and the embedding model resolve from the collection schema, and the request is plain text — the retrieval question asked without naming a field, a model, or a vector.
Examples # POST /my-collection/_search {"query": {"semantic": "find documents about search engines"}} The clause composes inside bool like any other leaf — the text is embedded and the clause rewritten before execution:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "bool": { "should": [ { "semantic": "search engines" }, { "match": { "field": "title", "query": "engines" } } ] } } } How it works # semantic is sugar over the native vector query, resolved and rewritten at the gateway in three steps:
graph LR Q["semantic: 'search engines'plain text, no field"] --> G("gateway") G -->|"resolve from the schema:the vector field + its model"| E("embed server-side") E --> R["the clause rewrites intoa native vector query"] Field resolution. The collection’s schema is scanned for semantic fields (a semantic_text field, a semantic multi-field, or a dense_vector with source + model). Exactly one makes it the default; several require the query’s field to name one. Embedding. The text goes through the field’s configured model — the same inference path (and the same model) that derived the documents’ vectors at write time, so both sides of the search live in one embedding space. Rewrite. The clause becomes a vector query on the resolved field, with k, num_candidates, similarity and min_score passed straight through. From there the standard kNN machinery executes: index type, quantization overrides and filters all behave exactly as on an explicit vector query. Because the field and model live in the mapping, the query never names them — and the search must target exactly one collection (see Notes).
Enable semantic search # Three steps, server config first:
1. Configure an embedding endpoint — the server embeds through external OpenAI-compatible services (OpenAI, vLLM, Ollama, TEI, …), declared in pizza.yml under node.embedding:
node: embedding: endpoints: - name: openai url: https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings api_key: sk-… models: ["text-embedding-3-small"] timeout_ms: 30000 max_batch_texts: 64 A model id routes to the endpoint that lists it as an embedding model; with exactly one endpoint configured, every model routes there (default_endpoint overrides) — that lenient routing serves ad-hoc /_embedding calls. Schema declarations are stricter: the model must be listed as an embedding model by exactly one service, or the mapping names service explicitly (see AI Services). Endpoints behind self-signed TLS set insecure_skip_verify: true (per endpoint). The registry can also be re-managed at runtime — see AI Services — and every node.embedding key is in the
configuration reference.
2. Map a semantic field — the simplest form is the semantic_text type, which collapses field + wiring into one declaration (pure semantic — the field is not inverted-indexed):
PUT /my-collection { "schema": { "properties": { "body": { "type": "semantic_text", "service": "openai", "model": "text-embedding-3-small", "dims": 1536 } } } } Two explicit forms count as semantic fields too — a dense_vector sub-field on a top-level text/keyword field (the parent is the source, and stays BM25-searchable — hybrid out of the box), or a standalone dense_vector whose vector_options declare source (the document’s text field to embed) and model:
PUT /my-collection { "schema": { "properties": { "title": { "type": "text" }, "embedding": { "type": "dense_vector", "vector_options": { "dims": 768, "similarity": "cosine", "source": "title", "model": "text-embedding-3-small" } } } } } 3. Write and search — documents indexed into the collection get their embedding derived automatically at write time for the field’s model (you don’t supply vectors); the semantic query embeds its text through the same path at search time. The /_embedding API exposes the inference directly.
Wire forms # String shorthand — just the text:
{ "semantic": "find documents about search engines" } Object form — any subset of the parameters:
{ "semantic": { "query": "search engines", "k": 10, "similarity": "cosine" } } Parameters for semantic # query (Required, string) The natural-language text to embed and search with. field (Optional, string) The semantic field to search. Resolved from the schema when omitted: with exactly one semantic field it is the default; with several, the request must name one (a 400 lists the candidates otherwise). k (Optional, integer, default: 10) Nearest neighbors to return. num_candidates (Optional, integer) Graph beam width for the query (HNSW ef); see vector. similarity (Optional, string) cosine (default), l2 or dot_product — must match the field schema. min_score (Optional, float) Return everything above this similarity instead of a fixed top-k — useful when the semantic clause feeds a hybrid intersection. Use cases # Plain-text search over meaning. Synonyms and paraphrases match where keywords fail — “cheap flights” finds “affordable travel” — with no embedding code on the client. Hybrid retrieval without the retriever DSL. A semantic should clause beside match inside one bool gives lexical + vector fusion in the plainest possible request (the retrieve/fuse pipeline is the heavier, stage-by-stage counterpart).
Zero-boilerplate prototyping. Map one semantic_text field, write plain documents, search with plain strings — the embedding pipeline is entirely server-side, so demos and MVPs skip the embedding client altogether. Cross-lingual retrieval. With a multilingual model, documents and queries in different languages share one embedding space — the query stays a plain string either way. Notes # The search must target exactly one collection — the schema is where the field and model live; multi-collection targets answer 400. A collection whose schema declares no semantic field answers 400 with instructions to map a semantic_text field (or a dense_vector with vector_options.source and model). The query never names a service or model — the binding lives in the mapping, and query-time inference uses the same one (writes and searches stay consistent). The full vector parameter surface (vector_options overrides, quantization, sparse vectors) is on the vector query page. Related # vector — the native query underneath: full parameter reference, index types, quantization, sparse vectors. multi_vector — several semantic fields searched and fused in one request. Hybrid search pipeline — retrieve / fuse / rescore stages for full hybrid control. Hybrid search tutorial — a walkthrough mixing text and vector legs on the embeddings dataset.
title: Semantic query

content:
Sandboxed scripting — scripted_metric, script_fields, script_score # Scripts landed across the whole request path — the engine runs the examples from the Elasticsearch docs unmodified. The engine is Rhai rather than Painless, but doc['x'].value, _score and params.<name> mean what they mean there.
Aggregations. scripted_metric runs your own four-phase map/reduce — init_script, map_script, combine_script, reduce_script — with per-segment states folded at the end. The single-value metric aggs (sum, avg, min, max, cardinality) accept a script in place of a field ( details), and pipeline aggregations keep their buckets_path arithmetic.
The hits themselves. script_fields computes extra values per returned hit at fetch time — nothing indexed, _source untouched, results under fields as arrays:
POST /sales/_search { "size": 3, "query": { "match_all": {} }, "script_fields": { "doubled": { "script": "doc['amount'].value * 2" } } } Scoring, filtering, sorting. The scripted queries wrap a query and replace its score, filter by predicate, or re-sort the page by a computed key:
POST /sales/_search { "query": { "script_score": { "query": { "match": { "field": "type", "query": "hat" } }, "script": "_score * doc['qty'].value" } } } script_score ranks the real candidate window — a high-scoring hit outside the first page still wins — and _script sort re-sorts the returned page, with the computed keys echoed per hit.
Everything runs in a sandbox: a per-script operation cap (a runaway loop is cut off with a named error), no host IO — no filesystem, network, or clock — and score tampering inside a script (_score = 99) stays local to that evaluation. Builds without the scripting feature reject script nodes explicitly rather than ignoring them. The full language reference — scoping, params, the MovingFunctions.* spellings in pipelines — is here.
title: Sandboxed scripting — scripted_metric, script_fields, script_score

content:
Rare terms aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation that keeps only RARE terms — bucket keys whose document count is at or below max_doc_count. The mirror image of terms for finding the long tail: instead of the top-N most frequent values, it returns every low-frequency value.
How it works # Bucketing works exactly like terms: one bucket per unique value of field, multi-valued fields counted per element, and documents without the field either skipped or folded into a missing bucket. include/exclude filter candidate keys up front (exact-value arrays or a single wildcard string prefix* / *suffix).
The difference is the cut: after counting, buckets with doc_count <= max_doc_count (default 1) survive and the rest are dropped — the inverse of terms’ min_doc_count. Surviving buckets are ordered by doc_count ASCENDING (rarest first). There is no size truncation: every rare term is returned, because the interesting population is by definition small.
For the example below the response is a single bucket:
"rare_types": { "buckets": [ { "key": "sticker", "doc_count": 10 } ] } terms could approximate this with a small size and luck, but it would still rank by descending count and truncate; rare_terms expresses “everything at or below this frequency” directly.
Example # Every product type sells ≥10 times; raise the bar to 15 and only sticker (10 sales) survives:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Use cases # Long-tail tag inventory. Of the 30 distinct tags on the teaching articles, 25 appear on exactly one article — rare_terms on tags lists them all in one shot. Singleton detection for data quality. Values occurring once are often typos: rare terms on customers.city surfaces mis-entered cities for cleanup. One-off events. Hosts, URLs or error codes seen a single time in logs — the prefix of any anomaly hunt. Complement of a leaderboard. Pair a terms (top values) with a rare_terms (everything rare) to describe a field’s full shape in one request. Frequency-band filtering. max_doc_count: 2 on articles.tags widens the net to the handful of tags used twice (optimizer, search, sharding, storage, vector) while ignoring the workhorse tags entirely. Parameters for rare_terms # field (Required, string) Keyword field you wish to aggregate. max_doc_count (Optional, integer, default: 1) Maximum document count for a term to be considered rare. missing (Optional, value) Value substituted for documents without the field; they land in one bucket keyed by it. include / exclude (Optional) Restrict candidate terms (exact values or wildcard patterns). aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Related # terms — the frequent side of the same field significant_terms — rare AND unusually concentrated in a scope
title: Rare terms aggregation

content:
Prefix query # Returns documents that contain a specific prefix in a provided field.
Use it when the values share a known beginning — a hostname family, an ID scheme, a URL section — and you want every term that starts with it.
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause.
How it works # The prefix is expanded against the inverted index’s term dictionary. Because the dictionary is kept in sorted order, the expansion is an ordered seek to the first term greater than or equal to the prefix, followed by reading the subtree of terms that start with it — no scan of the whole dictionary. Each expanded term’s postings are then unioned (OR semantics), exactly as if you had written a should of term queries.
Matching is per term, not per field value. On a keyword field the term is the whole value, so the prefix must match the value’s beginning. On a text field each analyzed token counts separately — web- matches the token web-01 wherever the analyzer left it intact. No analysis runs on the prefix itself. It is compared verbatim against the stored terms; on text fields analyzed with standard, stored tokens are lowercase, so a capitalized prefix (Web-) finds nothing unless case_insensitive folds it. Scoring. The expansion rewrites to constant_score: every matching document scores exactly boost (default 1), on the realtime buffer and on frozen segments alike. In a bool.filter context the scores are simply discarded. rewrite is accepted on the wire (constant_score by default, plus the scoring_boolean / top_terms_N family) for body compatibility; the engine currently scores expansions as described above regardless of the setting. Examples # Every host in the logs dataset is one of web-01, web-02, web-03 — so the web- prefix below matches all 150 documents.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. GET /_search { "query": { "prefix": { "field": "org.id", "value": "inf" } } } Use cases # Hostname / shard families. host: "web-" over the logs dataset (all 150 lines) — the classic fleet-scoping filter, cheaper than a terms list because you need not enumerate the hosts.
URL sections. url.path: "/api" matches the 50 lines whose path is /api/v1/products or /api/v1/orders. ID schemes. Key spaces like L00… or order numbers with a fixed date prefix (2024-06-…) slice by construction, without ranges. Typeahead on keyword fields. For exact-vocabulary completion over keyword terms; for analyzed free text prefer the match family, which analyzes the input the same way the field was indexed. Parameters for prefix # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. value (Required, string) Beginning characters of terms you wish to find in the provided field. case_insensitive (Optional, boolean) Allows ASCII case insensitive matching of the value with the indexed field values when set to true. Default is false. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Decrease or increase the relevance scores of the query. rewrite (Optional, string) Method used to rewrite the expanded terms (constant_score, scoring_boolean, top_terms_N, …). Related # wildcard — patterns anywhere in the term, not just the head. suffix — the mirror image; matches term endings. regexp — the fully general pattern over dictionary terms. term — the atom every expansion eventually resolves to. intervals — a prefix rule also exists inside interval queries for positional matching.
title: Prefix query

content:
Multi-match query # Returns documents that match a provided text across several fields — like the match query, with per-field boosts and multi-field scoring strategies.
Inside a nested query: supported — fields under the nested path are matched per array element.
How it works # multi_match is expanded before execution (Query::simplify) into a tree the segment executors already know:
Each entry in fields — after splitting off a ^boost suffix — becomes one match query over that field, carrying the query-level boost multiplied by the field boost ("title^3" → per-field boost 3). For type: "phrase" and type: "phrase_prefix" each field instead becomes a phrase query with slop: 0. The prefix part is not implemented: phrase_prefix currently behaves as an exact phrase and does not expand its last term as a prefix. Two or more fields are wrapped in a bool whose should clauses are the per-field queries, with at least one field required; a single field collapses to that field’s query — a plain match. Scores: should clauses add their per-document scores (the bool default). The type additionally picks the combination used when one field name resolves to several indexed sub-fields — best_fields keeps the maximum, most_fields and cross_fields sum. cross_fields does not blend term statistics across fields; each field scores independently and the results merge.
operator and analyzer are forwarded to every per-field match unchanged. tie_breaker and the string form of minimum_should_match are accepted on the wire but not yet applied by the expansion — it always requires at least one field and combines by sum.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "multi_match": { "query": "search engine", "fields": ["title^3", "description"] } } } Use cases # One search box, several fields. title^3 plus body is the classic relevance shape: matches in the title outrank the same words in the body, without excluding body-only matches. Log triage across columns. "search error" over ["message", "level"] matches lines whose message mentions search or whose level is error — 25 of the 150 logs documents (the same 25: every /search line is an error-level line). Analyzed plus keyword variants. Listing both a text field and its keyword sub-field catches prose matches and exact-label matches with one query. Phrases everywhere. type: "phrase" with several fields runs the same exact-phrase constraint over each field independently. Parameters for multi_match # query (Required, string) The query text to search for. fields (Required, array of strings) Fields to search, with optional per-field boosts via the field^boost syntax (e.g. "title^3"). type (Optional, string) Match type / multi-field scoring strategy: best_fields (default), most_fields, cross_fields, phrase or phrase_prefix. See How it works for what each strategy actually computes here. operator (Optional, string, default: or) Boolean operator joining terms within each field: or or and. Forwarded to every per-field match. minimum_should_match (Optional, string) Accepted but not yet applied: the expansion always requires at least one field to match. analyzer (Optional, string) Analyzer override forwarded to the per-field match queries. tie_breaker (Optional, float, default: 0) Accepted but not yet applied by the expansion — per-field scores currently combine by sum. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Boost applied to the overall query; multiplied with each field’s ^boost (carried by the per-field match queries — the phrase types carry no boost). Related # match — the per-field query that multi_match expands into. phrase — type: "phrase" runs one phrase query per field. bool — the should-clause skeleton the expansion targets. Analyzers — per-field analysis of the query text. API conventions.
title: Multi-match query

content:
Min bucket aggregation # A sibling pipeline aggregation identifying the smallest per-bucket metric value. Bucket aggregations rank groups by their own key or doc_count; min_bucket answers the orthogonal question — which of the per-bucket numbers (a revenue, a latency, a rate) is the lowest, and how low.
"worst_seller": { "min_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_type>revenue" } } How it works # min_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and returns their minimum as a single-value metric ({"value": 1350}) placed alongside the parent. Only the value is returned — not which bucket produced it; read the parent’s bucket list when you need the winner’s key.
The buckets_path names what to collect:
"per_type>revenue" — the > separates the bucket aggregation from the sub-metric inside each bucket; a . separator ("range.v") works identically. The sub-metric must be single-valued (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality, …). A stats sub-agg contributes its sum; multi-value metrics such as percentiles yield nothing. A bare parent name ("per_type") takes each bucket’s doc_count. Gaps follow gap_policy:
skip (default) — a bucket whose metric is missing or null is left out, and an empty bucket (doc_count 0, e.g. a declared range nothing fell into) is skipped even though its sum reads 0 — so it can never win the minimum. insert_zeros — such buckets contribute 0 and will typically become the new minimum. If every bucket is missing, the result is {"value": null}.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The four product types bring in 1800, 1800, 1350, 1800, so the smallest per-type revenue is 1350 — the mug line.
Use cases # Find the weakest group — the category, merchant, or region with the lowest total, as one headline number beside the full breakdown. Floor of a series — the slowest day in a date_histogram of daily revenue (over the teaching dataset’s 120 single-sale days the daily minimum is 15). Best-case latency — min of per-service average latencies from a terms over service names. Sanity check — a min_bucket of 0 usually means an empty bucket slipped in under insert_zeros, not a real measurement. Parameters for min_bucket # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric. format (Optional, string) Output number format. Accepted for compatibility; not applied to the value in the current engine. gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros. Related # Sibling family: avg_bucket, sum_bucket, max_bucket,
stats_bucket,
extended_stats_bucket,
percentiles_bucket
Document-level counterpart: min
title: Min bucket aggregation

content:
Max aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that keeps track and returns the maximum value among the numeric values extracted from the aggregated documents. It answers “how high does this field go” over any query — the top of a price range, the latest timestamp in a window, the biggest order that matches a filter.
How it works # The engine walks the matching documents once, keeping the largest value seen; any smaller value costs one comparison. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) qualify, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.
Documents that lack the field are skipped by default. With missing set, the default is folded into the comparison whenever at least one candidate document lacks the field — a missing document can therefore become the maximum.
On the column-store fast path (the production executor) each segment’s column is decoded once and reduced in a batch (max_f64), with count_present deciding whether the missing default applies; segments and shards combine by pairwise max, so distributed and single-node requests return the same number. Everything is exact — no approximation is involved.
When no document contributed a value, the result is null — an empty set has no meaningful maximum.
Examples # Computing the max price value across all documents — the SQL pill beside the Run button answers the same question with MAX(price):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "max_price": { "max": { "field": "price" } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "max_price": { "value": 60.0 } } } As can be seen, the name of the aggregation (max_price above) also serves as the key by which the aggregation result can be retrieved from the returned response.
Use cases # Price ceilings. sales.max(price) = 60.0 — the highest price in the 120 teaching sales; together with min it states the full 15..60 range in one response. Outlier spotting. Avg price is 27.5 and the max is more than twice that — the few expensive orders pull the mean, a first hint before reaching for percentiles. Capacity planning. On telemetry-style data, max over a time window gives the peak you must provision for, not the typical load. Per-group extremes. Nested under terms, max(price) per product type finds the premium item in each line. Freshness checks. The highest value of a monotonically increasing field (sequence numbers, timestamps) tells you how far ingestion has progressed for any slice of the data. Parameters for max # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. script (Optional, object) Script evaluated per document as the value source — mutually exclusive with field. missing (Optional, number) Value used for documents missing the field; it takes part in the comparison, so it can become the maximum. Related # min — the mirror image of this aggregation stats — min and max plus count/avg/sum in one request percentiles — the whole distribution, not just the ends max_bucket — max over another aggregation’s bucket values
title: Max aggregation

content:
Lesson 4 — Aggregations # From counts to histograms to composite paging — over sales and logs, with known answers you can verify by hand.
The use case # Dashboards, reports, and faceted navigation — wherever the deliverable is not a page of hits but an answer. The questions this lesson answers:
“What is the average / min / max price?” — metric aggregations. “How is revenue split by status?” — terms buckets. “Volume per week / per price band” — histograms. “Every (merchant, day) pair, complete — not just the top N” — composite aggregations with after cursors. “Just the number, skip the hits” — size: 0. Metric aggregations # One number out: sum, avg, min, max,
stats (all of them at once),
cardinality (distinct values):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Four distinct product types; stats gives you min/max/sum/avg/count in one round trip.
The same question as SQL — global aggregates are the M1 subset’s scalar lane (see the SQL reference):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. 120 sales, prices 15–60, four distinct types — one row, no size: 0 to remember.

Sub-aggregations # Every bucket runs its own aggs — revenue per type as sum of price inside a terms bucket:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. A sub-aggregation is just another column in SQL — the metric aggregates over each group:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Filtered aggregations # filter scopes an aggregation to a query; filters builds named buckets — the logs level split (error 25 / warn 25 / info 100):

Paging through buckets # composite pages through multi-dimensional buckets with an after cursor — for dashboards, not top-10 lists:

What you learned # Metric aggs summarize; bucket aggs group; sub-aggs nest. size: 0 skips hit assembly — the aggregations ARE the result. composite + after cursors for complete bucket walks.
