title: Lesson 4 — Aggregations

content:
Keys query # Returns documents whose key is in the provided set. There is no field argument — the match is against the document identity itself, and values that do not exist in the collection are skipped.
The query’s native name is keys: it speaks Pizza’s _key vocabulary, the same word the REST API uses for by-key addressing. The ids spelling deserializes to the same query — an accepted alias, not a different feature.
On Pizza server the same mixed-id convention as GET/DELETE/UPDATE applies to every value: a value containing a comma ("0,17") addresses a document by its system id (rolling,seq — the same id hits echo as _id); any other value is a user key. Query and response therefore speak the same ids both ways.
The convention is unambiguous because user keys are not allowed to contain commas — , is reserved as the system-id separator and is rejected at ingest (keys must not contain ',' (reserved for system IDs)).
In the playground / engine (single rolling context) values are document keys; a numeric value that matches no key addresses its system doc id.
How it works # keys is a Pizza-native query, not an inverted-index lookup. At the search entry point the key set is rewritten into a store-level document-set query: each value is resolved through the store’s document-key index — a point lookup per key, not a term scan — and the resulting document ids become the match set. Consequences:
It runs identically on every layer (live, built and frozen segments) — the key index exists before and after segment builds, so results never shift at build boundaries. Unknown values are skipped, not errors — only existing documents can match; an empty (or fully unknown) values array rewrites to match_none. Numbers are accepted and stringified (1 → "1"); on the engine a numeric value that resolves to no key addresses its system doc id, so keyless documents stay reachable. Scoring is constant: every hit scores 1.0, scaled by boost. There is no term frequency to rank by — identity is binary. Unlike a term query, nothing about the document’s content is consulted: term matches a field’s indexed value (dictionary or BKD, BM25-scored on text), keys matches the document’s name in the store.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. No SQL twin: the SQL subset can project _key (SELECT _key …) but cannot filter on it yet — WHERE _key … matches nothing. Use the DSL form above.
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "keys": { "values": ["L001", "L002", "NOPE"] } } } Unknown values (NOPE above) are skipped; an empty values array matches nothing. Numbers are accepted and stringified:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "keys": { "values": [1, 4] } } } The ids spelling in a full request:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "ids": { "values": ["L001", "L002"] } } } Use cases # Two-phase retrieval. Collect keys from a first pass (an aggregation, a collapse, a join) and re-fetch exactly those documents — a stable anchor when scores would otherwise reorder results. ids bodies carried over. Migrated requests using {"ids": {...}} run unchanged; the response speaks _key back. Spot-checking ingestion. “Did L001, L002 and the retried L150 land?” — unknown keys drop out silently, so the hit list is the answer. Addressing keyless documents. On the engine, numeric values that match no key fall back to system doc ids — the way to select documents indexed without a key at all. Parameters for keys # values (Required, array of strings or numbers) Document keys to match. A document matches if its key is any of these values. Unknown keys are ignored; an empty array matches nothing. Server mixed-id values ("rolling,seq") route to the owning shard and resolve by system id; keys resolve on every shard holding them. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Decrease or increase the relevance scores of the query. Notes # The query is executed natively: keys are resolved through the store’s document-key index on every layer (live, built and frozen segments), so it works the same before and after segment builds, and inside bool filter clauses. An explicit type parameter is rejected.
Related # term — the content-side counterpart: match a field’s indexed value instead of the document’s identity. join — key-based correlation between collections; join rewrites produce exactly the key/doc sets this query consumes. bool — combine a keys selection with content filters (e.g. keys of a batch AND an error-level term).
title: Keys query

content:
Hybrid search and scoring pipeline # Pizza runs lexical (BM25) and vector retrieval side by side and gives you explicit, composable stages to combine and re-shape scores:
graph LR B("bm25 leg") --> F("fuserrf / linear / disjmax") V("vector leg") --> F F --> SC("score_functionsper-document function scoring") P["a plain query,no retrieve"] --> SC SC --> RS("rescoresecond pass on the top window") RS --> H["one ranked list"] Every stage is optional and combines with a plain query: use score_functions alone on a keyword search, or the full chain for hybrid retrieval.
POST /<collection>/_search Stage 1: retrieve — parallel retrievers # Replace the single query with a list of retrievers whose results are fused. BM25 and vector legs side by side over the embeddings dataset:
{ "retrieve": [ { "bm25": { "query": { "match": { "field": "text", "query": "vector search" } } } }, { "vector": { "field": "embedding", "query_vector": [0.98, -0.05, 0.1, 0, -0.1, 0.05, -0.05, 0.1], "k": 5 } } ], "fuse": { "method": "rrf", "k": 60 }, "size": 5 } JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The fused answer includes every document found by EITHER leg (the match alone finds 24; the vector leg re-orders the top by similarity).
When both a bm25 and a vector retriever are present together with a pre_filter, the engine’s strategy optimizer picks the execution plan from the filter’s selectivity instead of always running the legs blindly: no filter (or an unselective one) runs the legs in parallel and fuses; a filter under ~5% pre-filters and runs the vector leg only on survivors; mid-selectivity filters on an HNSW field lead the text leg and re-rank; a filter matching over ~80% leads with the vector leg. You do not choose this — the planner estimates and decides (lib/engine/src/search/mod.rs, hybrid strategy table).
Retriever types # bm25 (object) Carries a query in the normal query DSL — any leaf or boolean query. vector (object) Carries field, query_vector (or query text / query_sparse), k, num_candidates — same options as the vector query.
Stage 2: fuse — combine the result lists # method (Required, rrf | linear | disjmax) How lists are merged. rrf (reciprocal rank fusion) needs no comparable scores — it ranks by positions; linear takes a weighted sum of normalized scores; disjmax keeps the max score per document. k (Optional, integer, default: 60) RRF rank constant — larger dampens the influence of top ranks. weights (Optional, array of floats) Per-retriever weights for linear. The three methods are exact, not approximate (lib/engine/src/search/pipeline/mod.rs, built-in Fuser set):
rrf — score(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_r(d)) over every retriever r, with rank counted from 1. Purely rank-based: BM25 and cosine scores never meet, only their positions do. A document found high on both legs outranks a document found first on one leg only. linear — each leg’s scores are min-max normalized to [0, 1] independently, then summed per document as Σ weight_r × score_r(d). A document absent from a leg contributes nothing from that leg. disjmax — score(d) = max over legs of score_r(d), no normalization; ties keep the single best leg’s score. For per-document multi-vector fusion inside one query see multi_vector; the gateway also translates the Elasticsearch top-level knn and retriever forms into these stages (see
API conventions).
Stage 3: score_functions — function scoring # Re-shape the score per document (demote stale docs, boost by popularity). Composes with a plain query — no retrieve needed: products matching “apparel”, scored by price with a log1p modifier and a constant weight:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Compare _score against the plain match (≈1.4 per hit): the price factor lifts expensive products; weight multiplies through.
Function types # functions (Required, array) One or more of: field_value_factor — {field, factor, modifier (none|log1p|log2p|sqrt|reciprocal|ln|square), missing} decay — {origin, scale, decay, offset, function (linear|exp|gauss)} — score falls off with distance from origin (date or numeric distance) script — {source, params} weight — constant multiplier score_mode (Optional, multiply|sum|avg|first|max|min, default: multiply) How the functions’ values combine with each other. boost_mode (Optional, multiply|replace|sum|avg|max|min, default: multiply) How the combined function value combines with the query score. A script_score function form is available too — it nests the source under "script", and the script sees doc, _score and params (see scripted queries):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Stage 4: rescore — second pass on the top window # Re-score only the top candidates with an expensive query (typically a vector or phrase pass over the top-K). Text match first, vector re-score over the top 10:
{ "query": { "match": { "field": "text", "query": "vector search" } }, "rescore": { "window": 10, "query": { "vector": { "field": "embedding", "query_vector": [0.98, -0.05, 0.1, 0, -0.1, 0.05, -0.05, 0.1], "k": 10 } }, "query_weight": 0.4, "rescore_query_weight": 0.6 }, "size": 5 } window (Optional, integer, default: 10) Number of top documents re-scored. query (Required, object) The rescoring query. query_weight / rescore_query_weight (Optional, float) Blend weights of original and rescored scores. What composes with what # retrieve cannot currently combine with aggs, post_filter, collapse or rescore in the same body — the gateway rejects the mix with a clear 400 (verified live). score_functions and rescore compose with a plain query — and with each other — without restriction. rerank (cross-encoder style re-ranking) is recognized but not implemented: requests fail fast with an explicit error naming the missing reranker-model serving layer. Use cases # Lexical + semantic recall. Exact-match reliability (BM25 on keywords, SKUs, hostnames) plus meaning-match recall (vector on prose) in one ranked list — the embeddings dataset’s search / storage / vector topics fuse cleanly with RRF. Cheap two-stage relevance. Skip retrieve entirely: a plain query plus score_functions (freshness decay, popularity field_value_factor) covers most “boost good documents” needs with one stage. Precision pass on the top window. Broad text match, then a vector or phrase rescore over the top 10 — expensive similarity computed only where it changes the answer (Stage 4). Multi-source retrieval without score wars. When the legs' scores are not comparable (different models, different scales), RRF sidesteps calibration entirely; disjmax when a document should rank by its best single source. Choosing a fusion method # Prefer rrf when BM25 and cosine scores must not be compared directly — it works from ranks alone. Prefer linear/weights when you have calibrated, comparable scores. disjmax when a document should score by its BEST leg (dedup-like behavior for multi-source retrieval). Related # vector query — the vector leg’s full parameter surface (k, num_candidates, similarity); a standalone vector query composes like any leaf for hybrid search without the retriever DSL. multi_vector — per-document multi-vector fusion inside one query, the query-level counterpart of request-level fuse. Rescore — Stage 4 in depth: window semantics, blend weights, and where the re-scored list meets from/size. Script fields — _script sorts and script score functions share the same sandboxed script engine and doc binding. API conventions — request envelope and wire-form tolerance at the gateway.
title: Hybrid search and scoring pipeline

content:
Geo-polygon query # Matches documents whose geo_point field lies inside an arbitrary polygon. The ring is given as points in (lat, lon) order; vertices on the boundary count as inside, and holes can be modelled with a concave ring.
Real regions are rarely rectangular. City limits, districts, service areas and lakes have corners everywhere — this query filters points by an exact ring instead of the four edges of a bounding box.
How it works # The field is the standard two-dimensional (lat, lon) BKD tree (any of the three ingest forms — object, [lon, lat] array, "lat,lon" string — normalizes to the same pair). Execution is two-phase:
Bounding-box prefilter. The polygon’s own extents (the min/max latitude and longitude over its vertices) become one BKD tree range. Only leaves overlapping that rectangle are visited. Exact point-in-polygon check. Each surviving point is tested with ray casting (the even-odd rule): a ray fired from the point toggles inside/outside at every ring edge it crosses, and an odd count means inside. The closing segment between the last and first vertex is implied. Points lying exactly on an edge or vertex count as inside (a tolerance of 1e-9 degrees, about 0.1 mm at the equator). The second phase is what makes the query exact: a point inside the ring’s bounding box but in a concave notch is correctly rejected — the coverage suite pins this with a “C”-shaped ring whose box covers a point that the ring itself excludes.
The ring is a single latitude/longitude loop on the plane: edges are straight in degrees (no great-circle bulge), holes need a concave ring rather than a second loop, and rings that wrap the antimeridian are not supported (split them into two queries joined by a bool should instead).
Examples # The live example matches the two Beijing places (beijing store, beijing north):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. As a curl request the same query reads:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "geo_polygon": { "field": "location", "points": [ [40.85, -74.05], [40.85, -73.85], [40.70, -73.85], [40.70, -74.05] ] } } } The nested form also works — points may use any of the three point forms ({"lat": .., "lon": ..}, [lon, lat], "lat,lon"), and options such as validation_method are accepted for compatibility and ignored:
{ "query": { "geo_polygon": { "location": { "points": [ {"lat": 40.85, "lon": -74.05}, {"lat": 40.85, "lon": -73.85}, {"lat": 40.70, "lon": -73.85}, {"lat": 40.70, "lon": -74.05} ], "validation_method": "ignore_malformed" } } } } Use cases # City and district boundaries. Filter stores or users by the actual administrative polygon — over the teaching places dataset, a four-vertex quad around Beijing picks exactly the two Beijing places out of fifteen. Service and delivery areas. Zones drawn by hand (a peninsula delivery route, an area bounded by two rivers) whose shape only a ring expresses; concave rings behave exactly as drawn. Exclusion zones. The same ring under bool must_not keeps results out of a no-go area — the exact phase makes both the inclusion and the exclusion trustworthy. Corridor checks. Routes, coastlines or borders approximated by a many-vertex ring, used as a coarse “inside the corridor” filter before finer tools such as geo_shape match against the line itself. Parameters for geo_polygon # field (Required, string) The geo_point field to filter on. points (Required, array) Three or more ring vertices. In Pizza’s flat form each vertex is [lat, lon]; in the nested form every point form is accepted. Polygons are interpreted as plain latitude/longitude rings; rings that wrap the antimeridian are not supported (split them into two queries joined by a bool should instead).
Related # geo_bounding_box — the cheaper special case when four edges are enough. geo_distance — round regions around one centre. geo_shape — the indexed side is a full geometry, not a point: match regions against a query region. geohash-grid aggregation and geotile-grid aggregation — grid the matched points onto map tiles. geo-centroid aggregation — the mean position of the matched points.
title: Geo-polygon query

content:
Credits # Pizza stands on the shoulders of the Rust and information-retrieval communities. This page credits the software we build on — and the projects whose ideas we learn from.
Reference points # Lucene — decades of query semantics and scoring design that the DSL and scoring model learn from. Elasticsearch — the JSON query DSL and REST API surface (_search, _doc, _bulk) the gateway is modeled on. tantivy — the Rust search library our inverted-index benchmarks measure against, on the corpus and golden queries of the search-benchmark-game. No tantivy code runs inside Pizza — the engine is written from scratch, a different engine end to end, built to go far beyond it.
Engine core # The search engine (lib/engine) is a no_std-capable crate that compiles from server to browser; these crates make that possible:
roaring — Roaring bitmaps carry every doc-id set: postings, filters, deletions. fst-no-std and fst-regex — our no_std forks of BurntSushi’s fst: finite-state term dictionaries, with regex and Levenshtein automata running directly over them. cedarwood — double-array tries for dictionary-driven analysis and suggestions (forked to drop its std dependency). hashbrown — the hash map that works everywhere, including the wasm builds. memmap2 — immutable segments are memory-mapped, never copied. bitpacking — SIMD-packed posting lists. zstd (with lz4 and flate2) — segment, column, and stored-source compression; a single .fire segment stacks all three where they win. rayon and crossbeam — parallel query execution across segments and workers. rhai — scripting for scripted aggregations and pipelines. turbovec — TurboQuant 4-bit vector quantization for approximate kNN. Apache Arrow (parquet, arrow-array, arrow-schema) — mounting Parquet files directly as searchable segments. moka — segment cache, ureq — remote segment fetching, and fs4 — advisory file locks for the KV store. nom — parser combinators behind the query_string mini-language. wildmatch — wildcard query and route matching. crc32fast and crc32c — CRC checksums over segments, WAL frames, and manifests; corruption is detected, never guessed around. Distributed layer # openraft — the Raft consensus that keeps cluster state and the catalog in agreement; we vendor it with openraft-rt-monoio, a runtime binding that lets Raft’s timers and heartbeats run on our monoio reactor instead of tokio. capnp (with capnp-rpc) — the inter-node transport wire format; zero-copy both ways. monoio — the thread-per-core, io_uring-based runtime the gateway and replication build on, with signalfut handling OS signals inside that runtime. tokio — the async runtime for the pieces whose ecosystems assume it: the capnp-rpc transport endpoints and the actix-based modules. The split is deliberate — monoio owns the data path, tokio sits at the edges. rskafka — the client behind the Kafka WAL backend, via our monoio-compatible fork.
sled — the embedded KV store holding Raft log and catalog state on disk. Formal methods # TLA+ / TLC — the protocols we built on top of Raft are specified and model-checked in contrib/formal-models before being trusted in code: promotion and WAL handover, shard allocation, online rolling reshard, doc-id reservation, inplace-column seeding, layered deletion visibility, and the membership fence. The TLC counterexamples have caught 18+ real bugs along the way. Gateway and operations # actix-web — HTTP types and client plumbing in the gateway. serde and serde_json — every byte of the JSON surface, schema included. prqlc — the PRQL compiler behind POST /_prql, used as a black box: pipeline text compiles to SQL that runs through the /_sql frontend. Pinned exact, because the emitted SQL shape shifts across prqlc minor versions. clap — the CLI. tracing — structured logs and the per-request trace tree. jemallocator — the global allocator, with profiling and stats enabled. sysinfo — host and disk facts behind node stats. flatten-json-object — flattening nested JSON documents into dot-pathed fields. arc-swap — lock-free swapping of routing tables and security snapshots: readers never pause while a new cluster state publishes. Text analysis # The per-language analyzer family (contrib/analysis-*, 40+ languages) is a Lucene-lineage port with embedded dictionaries, leaning on the best Unicode infrastructure available:
ICU4X — Unicode segmentation, normalization, casing, and collation. jieba-rs — Chinese segmentation, alongside the SmartCN, IK, simplified↔traditional (stconvert), and pinyin analyzers. lindera — Japanese morphological analysis with the ipadic dictionary (the kuromoji analyzer), and Korean via nori (ko-dic). Stempel and Morfologik — Polish stemming and morphology, straight out of the Lucene contrib family. The European stemmer set (analysis-english, -french, -german, …) and the Indic, Thai, Turkish, and Vietnamese analyzers round out the family. Bindings and this site # pyo3 — native Python bindings for the engine (lib/engine/bindings/python): the same segments and query engine, importable from Python. meilisearch-docsearch — the search box in these docs is pizza-searchbox, our fork of the docsearch component that the Meilisearch and Tauri ecosystems use. Browser builds # wasm-bindgen (with js-sys and web-sys) — the engine compiled to WebAssembly, the same segment format mounted read-only in the docs playground. serde-wasm-bindgen — zero-copy search results from wasm into JS. Maintainers and contributors are listed in the repository and on the community page. Thank you all.
title: Credits

content:
Terms query # Returns documents that contain one or more exact terms in a provided field. Equivalent to a boolean should of individual term queries — a document matches if it contains any of the values.
Inside a nested query: not supported yet — the clause is rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause. Expand into a bool should of term clauses instead.
How it works # The planner expands the query before execution: each value becomes a term clause inside a BooleanQuery with minimum_should_match: 1, and a single-value terms collapses straight into one bare term query. Everything said on the term page about verbatim lookup, index routing (dictionary for keyword/text, BKD for numeric/date, Bool column for boolean) and BM25 scoring therefore applies per value here, with the per-value scores OR-ed together.
Like term, the values are matched as exact terms — no analysis is applied. Note the engine’s terms has no case_insensitive knob (its term sibling does); fold case yourself before sending if you need it.
One internal fast path is worth knowing about: when a terms set was produced by a join rewrite (the _ref payload) rather than hand-written, the executor may run it as a sorted-intersect over the value-sorted doc-values column instead of one iterator per value. Scores are irrelevant on that path; hand-written queries keep the per-term scoring semantics described above.
Examples # The following search matches the two noisiest levels together — 50 of the 150 documents in the logs dataset (25 error + 25 warn).
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "terms": { "field": "status", "values": ["published", "pending"] } } } Use cases # Multi-select facets. A dashboard checkbox set (“error + warn”, three of four sales statuses) maps one-to-one onto a values array — the SQL twin is an IN (...) list. Cohort sets. terms on customers.tier = ["gold","silver"] returns 12 of the 20 customers; on articles.tags = ["search","storage"] it returns the 4 articles carrying either tag. Host shards. terms on logs.host = ["web-01","web-02"] scopes an investigation to 100 of the 150 log lines. Filter step of a two-phase search. A bool.filter terms narrowing candidates before a scored full-text clause — the cheapest possible shape since per-value scoring is discarded anyway. Parameters for terms # field (Required, string) The field to match. values (Required, array) List of terms to match. A document matches if it contains any of these values. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Decrease or increase the relevance scores of the query. Notes # The values are matched as exact terms — no analysis is applied. To match analyzed text, use the match query.
Related # term — the single-value original this expands into. bool — what the expansion becomes; write it by hand when you need must_not or per-clause boosts around the values. range — the contiguous-family alternative when the values form an interval. terms aggregation — count documents per value of the same keyword field a terms query filters on; the pair powers faceted navigation.
title: Terms query

content:
Sum bucket aggregation # A sibling pipeline aggregation computing the sum of a metric across another aggregation’s buckets — e.g. “total of the daily totals”. Where avg_bucket characterizes the typical bucket, sum_bucket re-totals the per-bucket values, which is how you grand-total a figure that was only computed per group.
"grand_total": { "sum_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } } How it works # sum_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes and runs after every regular aggregation — including the distributed merge — has finished. It walks the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and adds them up into a single-value metric ({"value": 6750}) placed alongside the parent.
The buckets_path names what to collect:
"per_day>revenue" — the > separates the bucket aggregation from the sub-metric inside each bucket; a . separator ("str_terms.v") works identically. The sub-metric must be single-valued (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality, …). A stats sub-agg contributes its sum; multi-value metrics such as percentiles yield nothing. A bare parent name ("per_day") totals the buckets’ doc_counts. Gaps follow gap_policy:
skip (default) — a bucket whose metric is missing or null is left out, and an empty bucket (doc_count 0, e.g. a declared range nothing fell into) is skipped even though its sum reads 0. insert_zeros — such buckets contribute 0; with all-numeric buckets the total is unchanged, the difference only shows with null metrics. If every bucket is missing, the result is {"value": null}.
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The result equals the plain sum over all documents (6750).
Use cases # Grand total of a grouped report — total the per-category sums of a terms aggregation to append an “all categories” line without re-running the query. Total across a filtered slice — when the search already filters to a subset, sum_bucket re-totals the per-bucket figures of just that subset. Total of a derived metric — sum per-bucket averages or rates (over buckets holding equal document counts, e.g. per-day counts) where a document-level sum is meaningless. Count the buckets’ documents — buckets_path: "per_day" (bare) totals doc_count across buckets, a quick cross-check against hits.total. Parameters for sum_bucket # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric: "<bucket_agg>><metric>". format (Optional, string) Output number format. Accepted for compatibility; not applied to the value in the current engine. gap_policy (Optional, string) skip (default) or insert_zeros. Related # Sibling family: avg_bucket, min_bucket, max_bucket,
stats_bucket,
extended_stats_bucket,
percentiles_bucket
Document-level counterpart: sum
title: Sum bucket aggregation

content:
Phrase query # Returns documents that contain the exact sequence of terms, in order, with no other terms in between (modulo slop). The text is analyzed before matching, like the match query.
The query’s native name is phrase; the match_phrase spelling deserializes to the same query — an accepted alias, not a different feature.
Inside a nested query: supported — the phrase, including its slop, must be satisfied by ONE array element; terms keep query order.
How it works # The text is analyzed — the field’s search analyzer (index analyzer as fallback, then standard), or analyzer when given — and every term must be present in the field’s dictionary: one unknown term and the phrase matches nothing, like an AND.
Order is verified against the position index. At slop 0 a start position is a hit only when every term sits exactly at its query offset from the lead — strict adjacency, no intervening terms. With slop > 0 the engine runs sloppy phrase scoring semantics: each term’s positions are adjusted by its query offset (an exact, in-order match collapses to a zero-width window), and a window holding one position per term matches when its spread max − min is within the slop budget. Reversed order matches too, but pays for the reversal out of the same budget — every position a term moves costs 1.
The match frequency — how many windows satisfy the budget — feeds a BM25-style phrase score:
score = idf_sum * (k1 + 1) * pf / (pf + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl / avgdl)) with k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75, idf_sum the sum of the per-term IDFs, and pf the window count. Term cursors are driven rarest-first under block-max WAND pruning, which makes the phrase pipeline one of the engine’s fastest.
Two fallbacks matter: a field indexed without positions degrades the phrase to a plain AND of its terms (no order constraint), and on a keyword field the whole phrase text is resolved as one exact term.
Examples # The following search returns the lines whose message carries the phrase HTTP/1.1 200 — 75 of the 150 documents, the successful responses:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "phrase": { "field": "message", "query": "this is a test" } } } Allow words in between with slop:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "phrase": { "field": "message", "query": "this test", "slop": 3 } } } Use cases # Exact signatures. HTTP/1.1 200 in logs.message picks out the successful responses — 75 of 150 — where a match on the same text would also admit documents carrying the fragments in any order. Error templates. Operational messages follow fixed templates (“node left the region”); the phrase pins the template while slop absorbs minor wording drift. Word-order-sensitive data. Titles, names and commands, where “restore backup” and “backup restore” mean different things. Controlled proximity. slop turns a phrase into a near-phrase: allow a word or two of insertion without falling back to a bag of terms. Parameters for phrase # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. query (Required, string) The phrase you wish to find in the provided field; analyzed before matching. analyzer (Optional, string) Analyzer used to convert the text into terms. Defaults to the field’s search analyzer. slop (Optional, float, default: 0) Maximum number of positions the terms may be shifted to match the phrase; 0 requires strict adjacency. Related # match — same analysis, but treats the tokens as an unordered bag. multi_match — one phrase per field via type: "phrase". span — position-level rules (order, gaps, proximity) when a slop budget is not expressive enough. Analyzers — the token stream whose positions the phrase verifies. API conventions.
title: Phrase query

content:
Multi-vector query # Executes several vector queries — each targeting a (potentially different) vector field — and fuses their results into one ranking.
One document often has more than one useful representation: a title embedding and a body embedding, a dense vector and a learned-sparse vector, an image embedding beside its caption. A single vector query can read only one of them; this query runs them all and merges the rankings.
How it works # Each leg executes independently — the same per-segment path a standalone vector query takes (brute-force on the realtime store, graph or quantized scan on flushed segments, per the leg field’s index_type). Every leg produces its own top-k list, sorted by similarity and truncated to the leg’s own k; fusion then combines the lists per document:
weighted_sum — fused(d) = Σ wᵢ · scoreᵢ(d), summing each leg’s similarity score times its weight. The scores are the legs' raw similarity values (no cross-leg normalization), so when the legs use different metrics or scales, prefer RRF. rrf — fused(d) = Σ wᵢ / (k_rrf + rankᵢ(d)), where rankᵢ is the document’s 1-based rank in leg i’s list. Ranks, not scores, are combined, which makes it robust to incomparable score scales; k_rrf (default 60) dampens the influence of top ranks. Omitting fusion defaults to RRF with k = 60; omitting weights weights every leg 1.0. The fused ranking is truncated to the query-level k.
Legs may carry "query" text instead of a vector — each is embedded server-side through its own field’s configured model before execution (batched per model), so the request stays plain text. Like all text-embedded queries, the search must target exactly one collection.
Examples # POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "multi_vector": { "queries": [ { "field": "title_embedding", "query": "search engines", "k": 50 }, { "field": "body_embedding", "query": "search engines", "k": 50 } ], "fusion": "weighted_sum", "weights": [2.0, 1.0], "k": 10 } } } The same two legs under RRF — rank-based, no weights needed when the two fields’ score scales differ:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "multi_vector": { "queries": [ { "field": "title_embedding", "query": "search engines", "k": 50 }, { "field": "body_embedding", "query": "search engines", "k": 50 } ], "fusion": { "rrf": { "k": 60 } }, "k": 10 } } } A document found by both legs outranks one found by only one — RRF rewards the agreement even though it never looks at the scores themselves.
Use cases # Multi-channel semantic retrieval. Title matches the gist, body matches the detail — weight the title higher with weighted_sum, or let RRF balance them without tuning. Dense + sparse fusion. A dense_vector leg for meaning plus a sparse_vector (SPLADE-style) leg for exact term evidence, fused by rank in a single request. Multi-representation documents. Image embedding, caption embedding and keyword vector on the same document, searched together for cross-modal recall. Candidate union. Several specialized embeddings each recall part of the answer set; fusion merges them into one stable ranking without any leg’s score scale dominating. Parameters for multi_vector # queries (Required, array of vector queries) The individual vector queries to execute. Each may target its own field, carry query_vector / query_sparse / query text, and set its own k (the leg’s candidate depth).
fusion (Optional) Fusion strategy for combining results; defaults to {"rrf": {"k": 60}}: "weighted_sum" — weighted sum of the per-leg similarity scores; each query’s score is multiplied by its weight (from weights) before summing. {"rrf": {"k": 60}} — Reciprocal Rank Fusion: combines rankings rather than raw scores, with k as the RRF smoothing constant (default 60). weights (Optional, array of numbers) Per-query weights, must match queries.len() if provided. For weighted_sum: score multipliers; for rrf: rank contribution multipliers. Defaults to equal weight (1.0) per query. k (Optional, integer, default: 10) Final top-k to return after fusion. Related # vector — the leg query: parameters, index types, sparse vectors, text embedding. semantic — schema-resolved semantic search when a single field suffices. Hybrid search pipeline — the request-level counterpart: retrieve + fuse merges BM25 and vector legs (and other retrievers) with the same RRF/linear options.
title: Multi-vector query

content:
Multi terms aggregation # A multi-bucket aggregation like terms, but the bucket key is a TUPLE of values from several fields — e.g. every (merchant, status) combination. It answers cross-tab questions — “rows by column” tables — that a single-field terms aggregation cannot express without chaining requests.
How it works # Each entry in the terms array contributes one component of the composite key. A document is placed in the bucket keyed by the tuple of its values, and the response reports each bucket’s key as an array — ["infini-store", "pending"].
A document contributes only when EVERY listed field has a value: a document missing any component field is skipped entirely (there is no missing fallback here, unlike terms). Multi-valued fields are not expanded per element on this aggregation — a document whose field holds an array is skipped as well.
Buckets are ordered by doc_count descending (ties in arbitrary order) and truncated to size (default 10). Nested sub-aggregations run per composite bucket exactly as they do under terms.
Over the teaching data, merchant × status produces twelve buckets of 10 sales each; the response reports each key as an array:
"pairs": { "buckets": [ { "key": [ "infini-store", "delivered" ], "doc_count": 10 }, { "key": [ "infini-store", "pending" ], "doc_count": 10 }, { "key": [ "infini-store", "shipped" ], "doc_count": 10 }, ... ] } Example # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Each bucket’s key is an array [merchant, status].
Use cases # Cross-tab grids. merchant × status over the teaching sales covers 12 combinations of 10 documents each — the skeleton of a pivot table, in one request. Revenue per cell. Nest a sum on amount to turn the count grid into a revenue matrix (type × status, merchant × type, …). Compound dimension drill-down. When a report needs “per (category, tier)” figures, one multi_terms replaces two chained terms aggregations and a client-side join. Slice matrices for reporting. type × status with a nested avg on price fills a spreadsheet-shaped result directly — each cell self-describing via its array key. Parameters for multi_terms # terms (Required, object array) Two or more field entries forming the composite key. size (Optional, integer, default: 10) Maximum number of buckets. aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Buckets always sort by doc_count descending; the order and min_doc_count parameters are not accepted.
Related # terms — single-field version rare_terms, significant_terms — filtered views of the value space
composite — paginates large key sets (also multi-field)
title: Multi terms aggregation

content:
Lesson 3 — Structure and numbers # Ranges, sorts, and cursor pagination over the sales collection (120 documents: type, price, qty, amount, merchant, status, date).
The use case # Most queries are not about words — they are filters and ordering over the structured half of the document: prices, quantities, timestamps. And real interfaces page through result sets, sometimes deeply. The questions this lesson answers:
“Sales priced $45 to $60” / “everything from 2024” — range over a typed field. “Top 5 by amount” — the canonical sort clause. “Page 3000 of a big result set, without re-ranking the world” — cursor pagination (search_after), where from+size breaks down. “Why did my filter miss the row with 45?” — the field-type system: 45 the number and "45" the keyword are different values. The types behind the data # Numbers are indexed as their real types (float for price, integers for qty), dates as epoch millis. That is what makes the queries below precise — see the field types reference for the full catalog.
Ranges # A range query takes any combination of gt/gte/lt/lte:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. SQL spells a range with the operators you already know (BETWEEN for inclusive bounds):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Dates work the same way — 92 sales in 2024, 28 in 2025:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Sorting # The canonical sort clause names the field, direction, and where missing values land ( sort reference):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The SQL spelling is ORDER BY … DESC LIMIT n — same order, same page size:

Cursor pagination # from+size re-ranks everything before the offset — fine for page 3, wrong for page 3000. Cursors (search_after) jump straight to the position after a sort-key tuple. Take sort values from the last hit of the page above and feed them back:

Exact sets and existence # terms matches a set of values; exists checks presence:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. 50 — the 30 hats plus the 20 mugs you will meet again in the aggregation lesson.
IN is the SQL set; IS NULL / IS NOT NULL cover exists:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. What you learned # Ranges on numbers and dates, with explicit epoch millis. Canonical sort clauses and the cheap pseudo-fields. search_after/search_before cursors beat deep from. terms for sets, exists for presence. The SQL lane mirrors all of it: comparison operators for ranges, ORDER BY … LIMIT for sorts, IN/IS NULL for sets and presence — see the SQL syntax page. Next: Lesson 4 — aggregations.
title: Lesson 3 — Structure and numbers

content:
Join query # Status: functional (semi-join). Joins need a running node — the gateway orchestrates and the engine executes, which is why the wasm playground does not host them. The
joins tutorial walks the complete relational sequence — references → join → FK-routed writes → salting → ?routing= addressing — step by step against a live node.
Matches documents in the outer collection — the one in the request URL — whose field values intersect the join_on values of documents matching a query on the inner collection — the one named by target. The result is a semi-join: outer documents that have at least one matching inner document, each reported once. It is the moral equivalent of SQL’s
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE org_id IN (SELECT _key FROM orgs WHERE tier = 'gold') except the two sides live in different collections and the engine runs them in one request.
Naming the target # target names the inner collection — either a bare string or the explicit object form, mirroring the schema language’s references object:
"target": "orgs" "target": { "collection": "orgs" } The object form also carries an optional index key for addressing an index within the collection — reserved vocabulary: the serving layer resolves joins at collection granularity today, and a request that sets index is rejected with a 400 saying so, not silently approximated.
How it executes # The work splits in two, and neither half fan-outs blindly:
Gateway (orchestration) — runs the inner query on the target collection, distributed across its shards, and extracts the join_on values from every hit. These values — the join keys — attach to the join node as a prepared payload. Engine (execution) — each outer shard receives the keys and runs the join as a local membership filter. The gateway never joins data itself, and the outer side never re-queries the inner collection. graph LR Q["join requeston orders"] --> GW("gateway") GW -->|"run the inner queryon orgs"| K["join keysorg-a, org-mega"] K -->|"keys ride the join node"| E("each orders shard —local membership filter") E --> H["outer hits, each reported once"] The outer side routes keys per shard, not per request: when the outer collection routes by _key (no hash-routing field) and field is "_key", the preflight licenses each outer shard to drop the batch keys whose routing partition cannot live on it before resolving them — exact by the routing invariant, never more than skipped impossible lookups.
How the engine resolves the keys depends on field:
field Execution path Requirement "_key" Outer key registry — keys resolved to outer document ids none a field declaring references with "ref": true Hidden _<field>_ref numeric column over pre-resolved global ids — the fastest path declare before ingesting: only documents carrying a materialized _ref value match (older documents need a reindex) any declared keyword field Engine-side exact terms filter over the field’s values field declared keyword in the schema A field that declares references without "ref": true still joins correctly — it degrades to the keyword rung, and the gateway logs a warning saying so ("ref": true + reindex promotes it to the column path).
A declared references also pins the join’s shape: the join’s target and join_on: "_key" must match what the field declares, or the request fails with a 400 rather than executing a value join through a field the schema says means something else.
Repeated joins amortize: an identical inner request re-issued by auto-fired patterns is served from a dimension cache validated against exact per-shard visibility tokens (any write, failover or restart invalidates it) — never a TTL, never a stale hit.
Walkthrough: orders of gold-tier orgs # Two collections — a dimension (orgs) and a fact (orders) whose org_id declares the full relationship (see relational parameters for what each part costs and buys):
PUT /orgs { "schema": { "dynamic": "strict", "properties": { "tier": { "type": "keyword" } } } } PUT /orders { "schema": { "dynamic": "strict", "properties": { "status": { "type": "keyword" }, "org_id": { "type": "keyword", "immutable": true, "references": { "collection": "orgs" }, "routing": true, "ref": true } } } } Seed one silver org and two gold ones, then ten orders — three for org-a, one for org-b, six for org-mega:
PUT /orgs/_doc/org-a { "tier": "gold" } PUT /orgs/_doc/org-b { "tier": "silver" } PUT /orgs/_doc/org-mega { "tier": "gold" } PUT /orders/_doc/a-1 { "status": "new", "org_id": "org-a" } # …a-2, a-3 PUT /orders/_doc/b-1 { "status": "new", "org_id": "org-b" } PUT /orders/_doc/m-1 { "status": "new", "org_id": "org-mega" } # …m-2 … m-6 Now the join — orders (outer, in the URL) whose org matches a query on orgs (inner, named by target):
POST /orders/_search { "size": 10, "track_total_hits": true, "query": { "join": { "target": "orgs", "query": { "term": { "field": "tier", "value": "gold" } }, "join_on": "_key", "field": "org_id" } } } The inner term matches org-a and org-mega (gold), their _keys become the membership filter, and the answer is 9 orders — the three a-* plus the six m-*. b-1 is absent: its org is silver. Flip the inner value to silver and exactly b-1 comes back.
The inner query is any leaf or bool — a full-text match works the same way:
POST /orders/_search { "query": { "join": { "target": "orgs", "query": { "match": { "field": "name", "query": "infini" } }, "join_on": "_key", "field": "org_id" } } } Joining on values, not keys # join_on names where the keys come from on the inner side — it does not have to be _key. Any inner field works: its values are extracted from each inner hit (scalars verbatim, arrays expand to one key per element, objects and nulls are skipped) and matched against the outer field:
POST /invoices/_search { "query": { "join": { "target": "orgs", "query": { "term": { "field": "tier", "value": "gold" } }, "join_on": "code", "field": "org_code" } } } orgs.code values (say "A-100") become the key set; invoices matching on their own org_code keyword field survive. This shape cannot ride the _ref column path — the fast column path exists only for joins that follow a declared references (join_on: "_key", field the FK field).
Where a join may sit # Inside bool.must, bool.filter and nested — resolved and executed.
Inside bool.should or bool.must_not — inert: an unresolved join node matches nothing, so a join under should quietly contributes no hits (v1). Put joins in must/filter. Inside another join’s inner query — rejected with a 400 (no join-of-joins). Compose it with ordinary clauses like any filter:
POST /orders/_search { "query": { "bool": { "filter": [ { "term": { "field": "status", "value": "new" } }, { "join": { "target": "orgs", "query": { "term": { "field": "tier", "value": "gold" } }, "join_on": "_key", "field": "org_id" }} ] } } } Add "explain": true to the request and the response narrates the join plan — which locality tier it took (colocate or key-directed) and, when a better tier was skipped, why.
Scoring # score_mode controls how inner-query scores reach the outer document:
none (default) — pure filter; inner scores are discarded and the outer document keeps its ordinary query score. max / sum / avg — combine the scores of the matching inner documents into the outer score. In v1 only the _key rung carries scores — both field-targeted rungs (_ref column, keyword terms) are filter-shaped and reject score_mode values other than none with a 400.
Guardrails # inner_hits_cap (default 10 000) bounds the inner query. When the inner hit set reaches the cap the key set may be truncated — the join result is then a lower bound, never silently complete, and the gateway logs the truncation at preflight. Raise the cap if the dimension side is legitimately larger. Namespace sharing — the inner query runs in the outer request’s namespace, so one tenant’s authorization covers both collections. Point-in-time — a join under a PIT requires the PIT to cover both collections (same pinned snapshot on each side); a PIT that does not cover the join target is rejected with a 400 instead of silently mixing a pinned outer with a realtime inner. Fail-closed errors — 400 for a missing target collection, an index-level target (the index key inside target is reserved vocabulary — rejected until index-level joins exist), a field absent from the outer schema, a non-keyword field, a join contradicting a declared references, a join inside a join, or a scoring rung mismatch; 503 when the target has no started primary shards. Placement features compose with joins but are declared separately: routing: true colocates an org’s facts on one partition (by-key reads then take ?routing=), and salting splits a hot value across a partition set — salting changes placement, never join visibility. The
joins tutorial walks the whole story against a live node, and
traverse covers the graph-shaped sibling of this query.
Use cases # Dimension-filtered facts. “Orders of gold-tier orgs” without copying tier onto every order: the dimension stays small and editable, the facts stay big, and each request re-derives membership. The teaching customers collection is the same shape at toy scale — a 20-document dimension split gold 4 / silver 8 / bronze 8 that a fact collection could join against. Business-key scoping. Facts that carry a natural code (org_code, sku) rather than a foreign key: join_on: "code" matches values, not keys, so reference data keyed by its own code joins without a reindex — the keyword rung, no _ref fast path. Continuously re-fired filters. Dashboards that auto-refresh the same inner query are exactly what the dimension cache amortizes: one validated version read per shard instead of a distributed inner search, invalidated by any write, failover or restart. Placement-composed reads. Declare routing: true on the FK and one org’s facts colocate on a partition, so by-key reads take ?routing= after the join narrows the candidates — placement composes with join visibility.
Parameters for join # target (Required, string or object) The inner (foreign) side to query: a bare collection name, or {"collection": ...} with an optional reserved index (rejected today — see Naming the target).
query (Required, query) Query to execute on the inner collection. Any leaf or bool composes here — except another join. join_on (Required, string) Field in the inner collection whose values become the join keys. Use "_key" to join on the inner document primary key; any field name extracts that field’s values (arrays expand, scalars verbatim). field (Required, string) Field in the outer (current) collection matched against the inner join keys. "_key" matches the outer primary key; a declared keyword field executes engine-side; a references field with "ref": true rides the fast _ref column path. score_mode (Optional, string) How inner-query scores affect the outer document score: none (default — pure filter, inner scores are discarded), max, sum or avg. Field-targeted paths accept none only in v1. inner_hits_cap (Optional, integer, default: 10000) Maximum number of inner hits to collect — protects against runaway inner queries. A join that hits the cap is a lower bound and is logged. Related # nested — the intra-document counterpart: key membership across collections vs same-element correlation inside one document. traverse and graph — the graph-shaped siblings over a relation edge field within one collection. Relational parameters — references, ref and routing: what the schema side of a join costs and buys. Nested aggregation and children aggregation — bucket-side analytics over nested and parent/child structures.
title: Join query

content:
Intervals and more-like-this queries # Two Elasticsearch-compatible queries landed natively in the engine — no more shape-shifting through match_phrase compositions.
intervals is a rule language over term positions. Say “these two phrases within two positions of each other, but only if neither overlaps this third one”:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "intervals": { "body": { "all_of": { "ordered": true, "intervals": [ { "match": { "query": "search engine", "max_gaps": 0, "ordered": true } }, { "match": { "query": "ranking", "max_gaps": 2 } } ], "filter": { "not_overlapping": { "match": { "query": "deprecated" } } } } } } } } Eight rule shapes (match, all_of, any_of, prefix, wildcard, fuzzy, regexp, range) and eight positional filter predicates (containing, before, not_overlapping, …) compose into one tree. Unsupported knobs are rejected with named errors instead of silently ignored — ask for a script filter and you will be told no.
more_like_this is the classic similarity query: give it text or documents and it expands the significant terms into a disjunctive query — “find more of this” without an embedding model:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "more_like_this": { "fields": ["title", "body"], "like": [{ "_id": "42" }], "unlike": "clearance sale", "min_term_freq": 1 } } } Liked documents are excluded from their own results by default (include: false), minimum_should_match defaults to "30%" with the same truncating resolution, and unlike drops the terms the result should steer away from.
Both queries execute across every segment kind — frozen blocks, realtime mutable segments, and legacy immutable segments — with one shared interval evaluator, and participate in BM25 scoring, count pushdown, and highlighting like any native query.
title: Intervals and more-like-this queries

content:
Highlighting # Ask for matched fragments of your text fields back alongside each hit, with the matched terms wrapped in tags — ready to render as a search result list.
POST /my-collection/_search How it works # Highlighting is an engine-native enrich step that runs on the returned page only — after ranking and truncation, exactly like script fields. It has two phases (lib/engine/src/search/highlight/):
1. Term extraction. The engine walks the query tree and collects (field, term) pairs worth highlighting: term, terms, fuzzy, span_term, intervals, match, multi_match, match_phrase, and bool clauses. Text queries (match, multi_match, phrase) are re-tokenized through the field’s search analyzer (or the query’s explicit analyzer override), so the highlighted terms mirror what the query scored. must_not clauses never contribute — documents excluded by them get no tags from them. match_all, range, geo and vector queries carry nothing to highlight.
2. Substring marking. For each requested field the stored text of the hit is scanned case-insensitively (ASCII) with word-boundary checks on both edges — cat matches “cat” but not “category”. When several terms match at the same spot the longest wins, and matches never overlap. Fragments are byte windows of about fragment_size centered on a match, snapped to UTF-8 character boundaries (multibyte text is never split mid-character, though a fragment may end mid-word); the walk pivots on the first match, then on the next match beyond the previous window, so fragments cover matches in document order without overlapping repeats. Multi-value fields fan out their fragments across the array values.
The result lands on each hit under highlight (serialized as _highlight), keyed by field name. Fields with no matches emit nothing unless no_match_size is set — and no_match_size applies to any highlighted field without matches, including fields the query never touched. The leading snippet it returns is trimmed back to the last whitespace, so no partial word is shown.
Verified on logs: highlighting message for the query cluster node with fragment_size: 60 returns "<em>cluster</em> <em>node</em> left the region unex" — two tagged terms, a 60-byte window, and a mid-word cut at the boundary.
Examples # { "query": { "match": { "field": "message", "query": "search" } }, "highlight": { "fields": { "message": { "fragment_size": 100, "number_of_fragments": 3 } } }, "size": 5 } JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Each returned hit carries a highlight object whose keys are the requested fields; values are fragment strings with matched terms wrapped in the tags (default <em> … </em>). Custom tags — same idea with <b> wrapping:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Use cases # Result-list snippets. Show why each hit matched without shipping the whole document — the bread and butter of every search UI. Tag-rendered summaries. pre_tags/post_tags emit whatever your frontend consumes (<mark>, ** for Markdown, [h]…[/h]), so no post-processing is needed on the client. Whole-value flagging. number_of_fragments: 0 tags every match in the full field value — useful for short fields (titles, names, single log lines) where cutting context away hurts. Fallback lead-ins. no_match_size keeps a uniform result-card height: matched hits show a snippet, unmatched ones show the start of the field instead of a hole. Bandwidth trimming. Combine with fields/_source filtering to return highlights without the full source when lines are long (the logs messages are short; production log lines usually are not). Parameters for highlight # Top level:
fields (Required, object) Map of field name (or "*" for every field in the schema that the query collected terms for) to per-field options below. pre_tags (Optional, array of strings, default: ["<em>"]) Tag(s) emitted before a matched term. The first tag is used. post_tags (Optional, array of strings, default: ["</em>"]) Tag(s) emitted after a matched term. The first tag is used. Per field:
fragment_size (Optional, integer, default: 100) Target length of each fragment in characters. 0 returns the whole field value instead of fragments. number_of_fragments (Optional, integer, default: 5) Maximum fragments returned per field. 0 returns the whole field. pre_tags / post_tags (Optional, array of strings) Per-field tag override; falls back to the request-level tags. no_match_size (Optional, integer) When the document has the field but nothing matched, return this many leading characters of the value (whitespace-trimmed) instead of nothing. Notes # Matching runs on the stored text of the hit, so it works for stored-only fields too — no positions index is consulted. fuzzy highlights the query term as typed, not the variants the query expanded to. Fragments follow match order (first match first), not score; tag every occurrence by choosing number_of_fragments: 0. The conformance suite pins this behavior (search.highlight family). Related # Analysis — the analyzers that decide which terms a match produces, and therefore which terms get tagged. Script fields — the sibling fetch-time enrich: computed values instead of tagged fragments, same page-sized cost. Sort and pagination — highlight runs on the final page, so sorting changes which hits get tagged, not how. Hybrid search — vector-only legs carry no highlightable terms; a bm25 leg does.
title: Highlighting

content:
Geo-distance query # Matches documents whose geo_point field lies within a great-circle distance of a centre point. Distances are in metres.
This is the “find me things nearby” query: given one centre and one radius, it returns exactly the documents inside that disc on the sphere — the shape behind store locators, delivery zones and proximity alerts.
How it works # The field is the same two-dimensional (lat, lon) BKD tree the other geo queries use (points indexed in any of the three ingest forms — object, [lon, lat] array, "lat,lon" string). Execution is two-phase:
Bounding-box prefilter. The disc is approximated by the rectangle that contains it: latitude span d / R degrees either side of the centre, longitude span divided by cos(lat) to account for meridians converging toward the poles. The BKD tree is range- walked over that rectangle. When the disc touches a pole or would wrap the antimeridian, the longitude span saturates to the full [-180, 180] range — the prefilter then over-selects but never misses a hit.
Exact haversine check. Each surviving point is measured with the haversine formula on a spherical Earth of mean radius R = 6 371 008.8 m:
a = sin²(Δlat / 2) + cos(lat₁) · cos(lat₂) · sin²(Δlon / 2) d = 2R · atan2(√a, √(1 − a)) A document matches when d <= distance_meters — a point exactly on the circle counts as inside.
The spherical model is about 0.5 % off the WGS-84 ellipsoid — plenty for city- and region-scale search, but not for surveying.
The gateway also accepts a unit-suffixed distance key: {"geo_distance": {"distance": "100km", "location": {"lat": .., "lon": ..}}} understands km, m, cm, mm, mi, yd, ft, in and nmi; options such as distance_type are accepted for compatibility and ignored.
Examples # Five hundred kilometres around central Beijing (39.9, 116.4) matches the two Beijing places — beijing store at ~0.8 km and beijing north at ~11.4 km. The next nearest place in the dataset (Xi’an) is over 900 km away.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "geo_distance": { "field": "location", "lat": 40.73, "lon": -74.1, "distance_meters": 200000 } } } Use cases # Store locator / nearby search. The user’s coordinate as the centre, a walk- or drive-distance radius as the bound; sort the matches by an ascending geo-distance bucket to build “within 1 km / 5 km / 20 km” facets.
Delivery and service geofences. “Is this order address inside a 5 km delivery disc?” is a distance query with the zone’s radius as the bound; combine several with bool should for multi-centre coverage. Proximity alerting. Streams of events (a vehicle, an IoT fix) filtered against fixed centres — the bounding-box prefilter keeps the per-event cost to one tree range plus a handful of haversines. Local ranking. Use it as a bool filter clause under a text or vector query, so relevance ranks only what is geographically eligible. Parameters for geo_distance # field (Required, string) The geo_point field to filter on. lat (Required, number) Centre latitude in WGS-84 degrees ([-90, 90]). lon (Required, number) Centre longitude in WGS-84 degrees ([-180, 180]). distance_meters (Required, number) Maximum great-circle distance from the centre, in metres (>= 0). Related # geo_bounding_box — the rectangular counterpart; cheaper when the region is a box. geo_polygon — irregular service areas with straight-edge boundaries. geo_shape — geometry-on-geometry matching. geo-distance aggregation — distance rings as buckets over any query’s results. geo-centroid aggregation — the mean position of the matched points.
title: Geo-distance query

content:
Cardinality aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that counts the number of distinct values of a field — how many different types were sold, how many different hosts logged, how many different authors wrote.
How it works # The engine counts with a HyperLogLog++ sketch — tuned so that small counts stay exact:
Values are hashed (MurmurHash3, 64-bit) into a sketch that keeps an exact set while the number of distinct values stays at or below precision_threshold; those counts are returned verbatim. Above the threshold the sketch promotes to dense HyperLogLog registers, so memory stops growing with the data: roughly 1.6% relative error at the default threshold of 3000, tightening to about 0.4% at the maximum of 40000. The returned value is always a rounded whole number. When documents lack the field and missing is set, they all count as one additional distinct value; without missing they are simply not counted. Distributed queries ship the sketch itself with each shard’s partial result and the coordinating node unions the sketches before estimating — the same number a single-node execution over all shards' documents would produce. (Cardinality nested inside bucket sub-aggregations still merges its per-shard finalized counts by maximum, a lower bound, when no sketch travels with them.)
Examples # Distinct values — COUNT(DISTINCT …) on the SQL side (the pill beside the Run button):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "type_count": { "cardinality": { "field": "type" } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "type_count": { "value": 4 } } } Four product types (t-shirt, hat, mug, sticker), and the same shape of question over the other teaching datasets gives 4 merchants in sales, 3 hosts and 3 log levels in logs, and 4 authors across the 44 articles.
Use cases # Unique counts. Distinct users, hosts, sessions or SKUs — the canonical cardinality question. Over logs, cardinality on host is “how many servers am I actually hearing from” (3: web-01 … web-03). Gauging dimensionality before faceting. Run cardinality on a field before you build a terms aggregation on it: 4 distinct types is a clean facet, 4 million is a dashboard that will not load. Data-quality checks. A field expected to be nearly unique (_id-like) should return cardinality ≈ value_count; a gap means duplicates. Compare with value_count, which counts values without de-duplicating. Funnel and coverage metrics. “In how many distinct days did each customer buy” is a cardinality nested per customer under terms. Parameters for cardinality # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. precision_threshold (Optional, integer) Counts are exact at or below this many distinct values; above it, the HyperLogLog++ estimate takes over (default 3000, maximum 40000 — larger requests clamp to 40000). Higher thresholds cost more memory, not more time. missing (Optional, value) Value used for documents missing the field; all such documents count as one distinct value. Related # value_count — total values, no de-duplication; the ratio cardinality / value_count measures repetition. terms — not just how many distinct values, but which ones, with per-value counts. cumulative_cardinality — the running distinct count across date_histogram buckets.
title: Cardinality aggregation

content:
Built-in analysis components # The server ships 83 analyzers, 50 tokenizers, 15 normalizers and 327 token filters, registered at startup. The authoritative, always-current list on YOUR node is:
GET /_analysis/components Components are referenced by name — in a field’s schema ("analyzer": "english"), in a custom analyzer definition, or in an ad-hoc _analysis/analyze pipeline.
How it works # The catalog is assembled in two layers. The engine core registers the minimal set that is always present: the standard and whitespace tokenizers, the lowercase normalizer, the lowercase/uppercase/ stopwords token filters, and the two named analyzers composed from them (standard, whitespace). Every other name below comes from the ~40 analysis plugin crates under contrib/analysis-*, registered at startup in one pass — foundation plugins first (core, stemmers, icu), then the CJK and per-language plugins, which intentionally override the basic analyzers from core with richer pipelines (language stop words, normalization, stemming).
Dictionary-backed components (kuromoji, nori, jieba, ik, smartcn) are registered lazily: they are built on first use, so a node whose schemas never reference them never pays the dictionary-load cost. Components are plain names in a registry — a schema, a custom analyzer definition and an _analysis/analyze request all resolve through the same one, which is what the workbench page relies on.
Examples # The three places a component name can appear:
"history": { "type": "text", "analyzer": "english" } "analysis": { "analyzer": { "custom": { "my_analyzer": { "normalizers": ["lowercase"], "tokenizer": "standard", "token_filters": ["asciifolding"] } } } } POST /_analysis/analyze { "text": "The Quick Foxes", "analyzer": "english" } Analyzers # General purpose:
fingerprint, keyword, pattern, simple, standard, stop, whitespace
CJK and transliteration:
cjk, ik_max_word, ik_smart, jieba, kuromoji, nori, pinyin, smartcn stconvert_s2t, stconvert_t2s
Language analyzers (stop words + stemming per language):
afrikaans, amharic, arabic, armenian, aymara, azerbaijani, basque, bengali brazilian, bulgarian, catalan, cherokee, croatian, czech, danish, dutch english, estonian, filipino, finnish, french, galician, georgian, german greek, guarani, hebrew, hindi, hungarian, indonesian, irish, italian khmer, latvian, lithuanian, malay, marathi, mongolian, nahuatl, navajo nepali, norwegian, persian, polish, portuguese, quechua, romanian, russian scottish_gaelic, serbian, slovak, slovenian, sorani, spanish, swahili, swedish tagalog, tamil, thai, tibetan, turkish, ukrainian, urdu, vietnamese welsh, yiddish
The CJK tokenizers (ik_max_word/ik_smart, jieba, smartcn, kuromoji, nori) load their dictionaries at runtime from the external <config>/analysis/ directory (make init-analysis-dicts); without the dictionary files the analyzers answer but degrade to simpler segmentation.
Tokenizers # burmese, camel_case, char_group, chinese_char, classic, code, compound_word, edge_ngram elision, email, emoji, fingerprint, hyphenated, icu_tokenizer, ik_max_word, ik_smart jieba, json_field, keyword, kuromoji_tokenizer, letter, log, lowercase, markdown microblog, ngram, nori_tokenizer, path_hierarchy, pattern, phone_number, pinyin, punctuation reverse, script_boundary, sentence, simple_pattern, simple_pattern_split, sliding_window, smartcn_tokenizer, standard stconvert_s2t, stconvert_t2s, structured_id, tab_separated, thai, truncate, uax_url_email, url whitespace, wildcard
standard is Unicode-aware word segmentation: maximal alphanumeric runs, CJK ideographs as single-character tokens. whitespace splits on whitespace only.
Normalizers # Applied to raw text BEFORE tokenization (keyword fields use them at index time via the field’s normalizer schema parameter):
collapse_whitespace, html_strip, lowercase, mapping, pattern_replace, pinyin, pinyin_first_letter, stconvert_s2t stconvert_t2s, trim, unicode_nfc, unicode_nfd, unicode_nfkc, unicode_nfkd, uppercase
Token filters # 327 filters covering stemming (33 snowball_* variants plus per-language light stemmers), stop words (per-language *_stop lists), case and folding (asciifolding, cjk_width, decimal_digit, icu_folding), n-grams and shingles (edge_ngram, ngram, fixed_shingle), word splitting (word_delimiter, camel_case_split, snake_case), synonyms (synonym, synonym_graph), security masking (credit_card_mask, email_mask, ip_mask, phone_mask, ssn_mask, redact), encoding (base64_encode, hex_encode, url_encode, rot13) and more. See GET /_analysis/components for the live list; the analyze API accepts any of them by name in the filter array.
Use cases # Pick the general analyzer first. standard for prose, keyword for exact whole-value matching, whitespace when punctuation inside terms is meaningful (product codes, tags), pattern for custom delimiters. Use a language analyzer, not a pile of filters. english, german, kuromoji (Japanese), … each bundle the right normalizer, stop list and stemmer for their language; recreate that by hand only when you genuinely need to deviate. Search Chinese by pinyin or across scripts. The pinyin normalizers (pinyin, pinyin_first_letter) and the stconvert components (stconvert_s2t/stconvert_t2s) cover romanized and traditional/simplified matching without changing the source text. Sanitize before you index. The masking and detection filters (credit_card_mask, email_mask, ssn_mask, redact, sql_injection_detect) keep sensitive or hostile content out of the searchable terms in the first place. Related # Analyze text — run any of these components over sample text and watch the token stream stage by stage. match — how the tokens these components produce become term clauses, and/or semantics and BM25 scores. Analysis parameters — binding analyzer, search_analyzer and normalizer to schema fields. Create collection — composing any of these into per-collection custom analyzers. The plugins themselves live under contrib/analysis-* in the source tree.
title: Built-in analysis components

content:
Vector query (kNN) # Finds the k nearest neighbors of a query vector — similarity search over dense_vector / sparse_vector fields. The query vector can be supplied directly, or as natural-language text that the serving layer embeds with the field’s configured model (schema-driven semantic search).
How it works # Execution depends on where the documents live:
Realtime (not yet flushed) — an exact brute-force scan over the mutable store: every vector is scored, a size-k min-heap keeps the best, and a filter (see below) is tested before any distance is computed. Flushed segments — the field’s index_type decides: flat scans the stored f32 vectors (exact, O(N·dims)); the graph types (hnsw_flat, turbo_quant_hnsw, bbq_hnsw) traverse the persisted HNSW graph with distances computed on the flat vectors — scores stay exact and only an ef-bounded neighborhood is evaluated; the quantized scans (turbo_quant, bbq_flat) score compact codes for a k × oversampling candidate pool and rescore it with full precision (approximate). The per-type breakdown is in Index types.
Scores follow the field’s similarity (overridable per query, but it must match the schema): cosine is the cosine similarity in [-1.0, 1.0]; dot_product the raw dot product; l2 scores as the negated squared Euclidean distance — 0 means identical vectors. Higher is always more similar, so one top-k heap serves all three.
k bounds the vector leg, the request’s size bounds the page — a standalone vector query returns min(k, size) hits. Setting min_score changes the shape entirely: every vector above the threshold is returned, no heap, no k.
Filters (bool with the vector clause in must and other clauses in filter) never silently lose results: the brute-force paths test the filter first and skip the distance; the graph path widens its beam to roughly k / selectivity (clamped to the segment size) and post-filters; and when a filter passes under ~5% of the segment and supports ordered iteration, the engine switches to a filter-led exact scan over just the filter’s documents — cheaper than widening the beam a thousandfold.
When the request carries "query" text instead of a vector, the serving layer embeds it through the field’s configured model before execution (see embedding endpoints).
Examples # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "vector": { "field": "embedding", "query_vector": [0.12, 0.45, 0.1, 0.0, -0.3, 0.2, 0.05, -0.1], "k": 10 } } } Text in, embedding server-side (requires an embedding endpoint — see below):
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "vector": { "field": "embedding", "query": "find documents about search engines", "k": 10 } } } Embedding endpoints (server-side inference) # Endpoints are declared in pizza.yml under node.embedding — the full key reference lives in the configuration page.
Pizza embeds text through external, OpenAI-compatible embedding services — configure them once and both the write path (schema-driven) and the search path (text queries) work with plain text:
node: embedding: endpoints: - name: openai url: "https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings" api_key: "sk-…" models: ["text-embedding-3-small"] - name: local url: "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/embeddings" # Ollama models: ["nomic-embed-text"] Each models entry may also declare its dims, its features (embedding, the default, or generation — served through the POST /_chat facade once the endpoint declares chat_url) and its inputs (text, the default, or image) — see
AI Services.
Write time — a dense_vector field mapped with vector_options.source (a text field) and model derives its vector from the source text when the document does not supply one; explicit client vectors always win. Search time — a vector query (or hybrid retrieve vector leg) carrying "query" text and no vector is embedded before execution. The model comes from the field schema, so the search must target exactly one collection. API — POST /_embedding exposes the same capability with the standard OpenAI request/response shapes ({"model", "input"} in, the data[].embedding list out). A model id routes to the endpoint listing it; with exactly one endpoint configured, every model routes there (the backend decides what it serves). Schema declarations (semantic_text, semantic multi-fields, source-mapped dense_vector) are stricter: the model must be listed by exactly one service, or the service must be named — see AI services. Declarative form — semantic_text # The simplest wiring is the semantic_text field type: one declaration, plain-text writes, pure-semantic search (no inverted index on the field):
PUT /my-collection { "schema": { "properties": { "body": { "type": "semantic_text", "service": "zai", "model": "GLM-4.6V", "dims": 3072 } } } } dims may be omitted when the service’s models entry declares it; service disambiguates same-named models across services.
Declarative form — the semantic multi-field # The explicit form underneath: declare a dense_vector sub-field on the text field itself, and the parent becomes the source implicitly (adding "index": false on the parent reproduces the pure-semantic semantic_text layout; by default the parent stays BM25-searchable — hybrid out of the box):
PUT /my-collection { "schema": { "properties": { "body": { "type": "text", "fields": { "embedding": { "type": "dense_vector", "vector_options": { "model": "text-embedding-3-small", "dims": 1536 } } } } } } } Writes stay plain-text ({"body": "some text"}) — the vector derives server-side into body.embedding, and vector/knn queries naming the parent auto-rewrite to the sub-field (the plain dotted path works too).
Preconditions, each enforced with a 400 at schema-apply time:
The parent must be a top-level text or keyword field. The sub-field must be dense_vector (sparse_vector sub-fields are not supported). vector_options.model is required and must be listed by exactly one service (or the named vector_options.service must list it) — list the model under a service in the embedding endpoints configuration first.
vector_options.dims is required unless the service’s models entry declares it (probe a service once with _test to learn the width). vector_options.source must not be set — the source is implicitly the parent field. Semantic query # The semantic query removes the last piece of boilerplate — the field name. (Full parameter reference on the semantic query page.) A collection whose schema declares a semantic field — a semantic_text field, a semantic multi-field, or the standalone dense_vector with source + model — is searchable with plain text alone:
