POST /my-collection/_search {"query": {"semantic": "find documents about search engines"}} # object form — k / field / similarity / min_score all optional {"query": {"semantic": {"query": "search engines", "k": 10}}} # composes like any leaf — hybrid search without the retriever DSL {"query": {"bool": {"should": [ {"semantic": "search engines"}, {"match": {"field": "title", "query": "engines"}} ]}}} The field resolves from the schema: exactly one semantic field is inferred; with several, name one via the semantic query’s field (400 names the candidates otherwise). The text embeds server-side through the field’s configured model — the same inference path as explicit text vector queries. The sugar is translated at the gateway into the native vector query; the search must target exactly one collection (the schema is where the field and model live). Quantized search with per-query overrides:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "vector": { "field": "embedding", "query_vector": [0.12, 0.45, ...], "k": 10, "num_candidates": 200, "vector_options": { "index_type": "turbo_quant", "bit_width": 4, "oversampling": 5.0 } } } } Query parameters # Parameters accepted inside the vector query object.
Parameter Type Required Default Description field string yes — Vector field name (dense_vector or sparse_vector). query_vector number array one of — The query embedding. (The retrieve-style retriever DSL spells this key vector; inside a vector query it is query_vector.) On a sparse_vector field, non-zero positions are read as dimension ids (position-encoded form). query_sparse object / pair array one of — Sparse query as dimension-id → value pairs: {"5": 0.3, "17": 0.9} or [[5, 0.3], [17, 0.9]]. For sparse_vector fields; takes precedence over query_vector. query string one of — Natural-language text; the field’s configured embedding model converts it into the query vector when query_vector is absent. k integer no 10 Nearest neighbors the vector leg produces. The final page is capped by the request’s size — a standalone vector query returns min(k, size) hits; in a retrieve/fuse pipeline k bounds each leg and size bounds the merged result. num_candidates integer no unset Graph beam width for the query (HNSW ef). Unset uses the field’s ef_search. Values below k are clamped up to k. Higher = better recall, more work. similarity string no cosine Similarity metric for ranking: cosine, l2 or dot_product. Must match the field schema’s similarity. min_score number no — Minimum score threshold. When set, returns all vectors above the score instead of top-k — useful for hybrid text+vector intersection. vector_options object no — Per-query overrides of the field schema’s index/search knobs. See below. k vs size, live over the embeddings dataset (24 documents in three well-separated clusters): ask the vector leg for the 8 nearest neighbors but cap the page at 3 — exactly 3 hits come back, ranked by similarity:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Per-query vector_options # Every key is optional; each overrides the field schema’s value for this query only.
Key Type Applies to Description index_type string all Forces a specific read path for this query: flat, hnsw_flat, bbq_flat, bbq_hnsw, turbo_quant, turbo_quant_hnsw. E.g. flat forces an exact scan even when the segment carries quantized codes. bit_width integer TurboQuant Quantization width (2, 3, 4) for the realtime layer’s on-the-fly scan. Persisted segments serve codes at the schema’s width — set it there. oversampling number quantized Candidate-pool multiplier before rescoring (k × oversampling candidates). rescore_vector boolean quantized Rerank the candidate pool with full-precision vectors (recommended true). ef_search integer graph types Query-time graph beam width. The top-level num_candidates takes precedence when both are set. m, ef_construction — — Build-time graph parameters — schema-level only, ignored in queries. Field schema parameters # The vector field declares dimensionality, similarity and index type once in the collection schema. Parameters live in the property itself and in its vector_options object:
PUT /my-collection { "schema": { "properties": { "embedding": { "type": "dense_vector", "source": false, "vector_options": { "dims": 128, "similarity": "cosine", "index_type": "turbo_quant_hnsw", "bit_width": 4, "oversampling": 3.0, "rescore_vector": true, "m": 16, "ef_construction": 128, "ef_search": 64 } } } } } Property-level parameters # Parameter Type Default Description type string — dense_vector (or sparse_vector). source boolean true When false, the raw vector is excluded from _source — it never appears in GET or search-hit rendering, saving storage for large embeddings. Search keeps working through the dedicated vector sections, and merges/reshards recover the vectors from FIELD_VECTOR. Note: this is the storage switch; the embedding input field is vector_options.source below. column, store boolean false Generic storage switches; dense vectors do not use columnar or separate-store paths — leave unset. vector_options parameters # Parameter Type Range / values Default Description dims integer 1..=4096 — Vector dimensionality (required for dense_vector; for sparse_vector it is the dimension-id space hint). TurboQuant additionally requires dims >= 8 and dims % 8 == 0. similarity string cosine, l2, dot_product cosine Similarity metric used at index and query time. index_type string see table below flat Index strategy: brute-force, graph, and/or quantization. bit_width integer 2, 3, 4 4 TurboQuant scalar-quantization width. 2-bit is experimental and requires rescore_vector: true. oversampling number ≥ 1.0 3.0 Candidate-pool multiplier for quantized scans (k × oversampling candidates before rescore). Low-dimension BitQ fields need a higher factor (e.g. 8.0) to hold recall. rescore_vector boolean — true Rerank quantized candidates with full-precision vectors. m integer 2..=256 16 HNSW graph connectivity — max neighbors per node per layer. Higher = better recall, more build time and memory. ef_construction integer 1..=4096 128 HNSW build-time beam width. ef_search integer 1..=4096 64 HNSW query-time beam width (the default ef for queries against this field). source string field name — Embedding input: a text field whose content is embedded into this vector field at index time (schema-driven embeddings). model string model id — Embedding model — a HuggingFace id for local ONNX inference (e.g. all-MiniLM-L6-v2) or the model name for remote endpoints. Effective together with source. Out-of-range values are rejected with HTTP 400 at collection creation.
Index types # Six index types cover the exact / approximate × unquantized / quantized space. Both quantization families persist their codes in the segment (FIELD_TURBOQUANT, FIELD_BBQ), and every graph variant persists the graph (FIELD_HNSW).
index_type Quantization Compression Graph Precision of served scores Parameters that apply flat none 1x no exact dims, similarity hnsw_flat none 1x yes exact dims, similarity, m, ef_construction, ef_search bbq_flat BitQ binary (1 bit/dim) ~32x no approximate + rescore dims, similarity, oversampling, rescore_vector bbq_hnsw BitQ binary (1 bit/dim) ~32x yes exact (graph) / approx (codes fallback) dims, similarity, oversampling, rescore_vector, m, ef_construction, ef_search turbo_quant TurboQuant scalar (2–4 bit) ~8x @ 4-bit no approximate + rescore dims (≥8, %8==0), similarity, bit_width, oversampling, rescore_vector turbo_quant_hnsw TurboQuant scalar (2–4 bit) ~8x @ 4-bit yes exact (graph) / approx (codes fallback) dims (≥8, %8==0), similarity, bit_width, oversampling, rescore_vector, m, ef_construction, ef_search Choosing between them:
Exact results needed, small-to-medium data — flat. Exact results, larger data — hnsw_flat (graph traversal, ~15x faster than the flat scan on a 2 000 × 128d segment, scores identical to brute force). Minimal memory footprint — bbq_flat / bbq_hnsw (~32x compression). BitQ works at any dimensionality; budget oversampling for recall. Balanced quantization, zero training — turbo_quant / turbo_quant_hnsw (~8x at 4-bit). The graph variant measured 12 176 QPS vs 830 (exact flat) with recall@10 0.982 vs the quantized scan’s 0.801 on a 2 000 × 128d segment. How each type executes # flat scans the stored f32 vectors — exact, O(N·dims). turbo_quant / bbq_flat scan the quantized codes for a candidate pool of k × oversampling, then rescore that pool with the flat vectors (rescore_vector: true). Graph types (hnsw_flat, turbo_quant_hnsw, bbq_hnsw) traverse the persisted HNSW graph once the segment is memory-mapped. Distances are computed on the flat vectors, so scores are exact and only an ef-bounded neighborhood is evaluated; the quantized-code scan (for the two quantized variants) serves as fallback when a segment predates the graph or fails to load it. Filtered kNN (bool { must: [vector], filter: [...] }) widens the graph beam proportionally to the filter’s selectivity (ef ≈ max(ef, k · n / |filter|)) and traverses the same graph; quantized-only fields fall back to an exact scan over the filter set. Storage footprint # Two facts drive on-disk size (measured at 1 024d, bytes per vector, whole segment file / vector count):
Configuration B/vector vs raw f32 raw f32 payload (reference) 4 096 1.00x flat 8 294 2.02x flat + source: false 4 134 1.01x turbo_quant 9 342 2.28x turbo_quant_hnsw + source: false 5 336 1.30x By default the vector is stored twice — the FIELD_VECTOR section (the scan/rescore source of truth) and a copy inside the stored document (_source). source: false removes the _source copy: that is the disk-footprint lever. Quantization buys query speed and scan I/O, not disk: the codes are an additional section (TurboQuant 4-bit ≈ 0.5 B/coordinate, BitQ ≈ 0.125 B/coordinate) and the HNSW graph adds ≈ 150 B/vector at m: 16. The flat section must stay — merges, resharding and rescoring rebuild from it (quantization is lossy). The practical speed + storage configuration is a quantized graph index with source: false: 1.30x the raw payload (vs 2.02x default flat) with ~12–15x query speedup. Segments holding vector data always merge in the FireV11 format, which preserves the quantized and graph sections across compaction. Rolling upgrades must reach every data node before relying on this: nodes running older builds still merge vector-bearing segments through the legacy FireV10 path, which drops the quantized sections.
Sparse vectors # sparse_vector fields store per-document (dimension id, value) pairs — the natural shape for learned-sparse embeddings (SPLADE-style) and tag/feature vectors where most dimensions are zero. Only the non-zero entries are stored, so a sparse field costs memory proportional to the number of populated dimensions, not to dims.
PUT /my-collection { "schema": { "properties": { "tags": { "type": "sparse_vector", "vector_options": { "dims": 65536, "similarity": "dot_product" } } } } } Documents accept two value forms (they serialize to the same rows):
PUT /my-collection/_doc/s1 { "title": "one", "tags": {"2": 1.0, "5": 1.0} } # object form PUT /my-collection/_doc/s2 { "title": "two", "tags": [[2, 0.5], [7, 1.0]] } # pair-array form Queries take the same two forms through query_sparse:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "vector": { "field": "tags", "query_sparse": {"2": 1.0, "5": 1.0}, "k": 10, "similarity": "dot_product" } } } How a sparse field executes:
Scoring is a merge-join over the sorted id lists (dot product or cosine) — O(nnz(query) + nnz(doc)) per document, no dense materialization anywhere. Realtime documents are searchable immediately through the mutable store’s sparse index; flush builds a dedicated FIELD_SPARSE section (CSR layout: one row per document, zero-copy from the memory-mapped segment). Filtered kNN (bool { must: [vector], filter: [...] }) scores only the filter’s candidate set. Merges and source: false are safe: compaction rebuilds sparse rows from the FIELD_SPARSE section, so excluding the field from _source (the storage lever, same as dense) never loses the data. The dense index types and their quantization/graph parameters (index_type, bit_width, oversampling, m, …) do not apply to sparse fields; dims and similarity are the relevant knobs. Storage is 8 bytes per non-zero entry plus 8 bytes of per-document row overhead. Combine several vector queries (multi-field, mixed dense/sparse) with the multi_vector query.
Use cases # Semantic similarity search. Match by meaning where keywords fail — synonyms, paraphrases, cross-lingual text. The teaching embeddings dataset is built for this: 24 documents in three well-separated 8-document clusters (search, storage, vector), and querying with the search-cluster centroid at k = 8 returns exactly the eight search documents. Hybrid retrieval. Vector recall beside BM25 precision, fused with RRF — the retrieve/fuse pipeline runs vector legs and text legs side by side over the same dataset.
Recommendations and more-like-this. Embed the item the user is looking at and take its nearest neighbors as the candidate list — no query text ever exists. Thresholded recall for pipelines. min_score returns all vectors above a similarity floor, feeding deduplication, clustering or RAG chunk selection where a fixed k would be arbitrary. Learned-sparse ranking. sparse_vector fields carry SPLADE-style weighted term ids and score by dot product — the same kNN machinery, memory proportional to the populated dimensions. Related # multi_vector — several vector fields (or dense + sparse) searched at once and fused into one ranking. semantic — the same query with the field and model resolved from the schema; the request is plain text. Hybrid search pipeline — vector legs inside the retrieve/fuse/rescore chain. Hybrid search tutorial — a walkthrough over the embeddings dataset.
title: Vector query (kNN)

content:
Terms aggregation # A multi-bucket value source based aggregation where buckets are dynamically built - one per unique value. It answers “group by this field, count (and aggregate) per value” without knowing the values in advance, which a fixed-bucket aggregation like histogram or range cannot do.
How it works # Every matching document is placed in the bucket keyed by its value of field. Multi-valued fields bucket per element: a document whose tags holds ["search", "architecture"] is counted once in the search bucket and once in the architecture bucket. Documents without the field are skipped — unless missing is set, in which case they land together in one bucket keyed by that value.
Buckets are ordered by doc_count descending, with ties broken by key ascending. The tie-break is numeric-aware: when every key parses as a number, keys compare as numbers (so 2 sorts before 10); otherwise they compare as strings. Numeric keys are normalized — an integral double and a long with the same value share one bucket key.
min_doc_count filtering happens before the size truncation, so size counts surviving buckets only. With min_doc_count: 0, terms the query never matched still materialize as count-0 buckets (drawn from the column dictionary) — useful with an explicit include list to guarantee a complete report.
include/exclude restrict candidate keys before counting. Both accept an exact-value array (numeric-aware: "10", 10 and 10.0 are the same key) or a single wildcard string (prefix*, *suffix). include also accepts { "partition": p, "num_partitions": n }: keys are routed to a partition by a Murmur3 hash (numeric keys hashed as longs), so several requests can split a high-cardinality field into disjoint slices — request p = 0..n-1 to cover every key exactly once.
Examples # One bucket per type — GROUP BY on the SQL side (the pill beside the Run button), ordered by the count:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "by_type": { "terms": { "field": "type" } } } } Response:
{ ... "aggregations": { "by_type": { "buckets": [ { "key": "t-shirt", "doc_count": 60 }, { "key": "hat", "doc_count": 30 }, { "key": "mug", "doc_count": 20 }, { "key": "sticker", "doc_count": 10 } ] } } } Use cases # Category leaderboards. sales.terms(type) returns the t-shirt: 60 / hat: 30 / mug: 20 / sticker: 10 ranking shown above; nest a sum sub-aggregation to rank by revenue instead of count. Multi-value tag clouds. articles carry a tags array; a terms aggregation on it spreads each article across every tag it carries, giving per-tag article counts. Log level mix. logs.terms(level) yields info: 100 / error: 25 / warn: 25 — a one-request health summary. Segment rollups. customers.terms(tier) splits the 20 customers into silver: 8 / bronze: 8 / gold: 4 for per-tier metrics. Sliced exhaustive scans. Combine include partitioning with size to walk a high-cardinality field slice by slice when one request cannot hold all buckets. Parameters for terms # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. size (Optional, integer) Maximum number of buckets to return. Defaults to 10. min_doc_count (Optional, integer) Drop buckets with fewer matching documents. Defaults to 1; 0 keeps empty buckets — only meaningful together with an explicit include list. missing (Optional, value) Value substituted for documents without the field (any scalar; those documents land in one bucket keyed by it). include (Optional) Restricts bucket keys: an exact-value array, a wildcard string (prefix* / *suffix), or { "partition": <p>, "num_partitions": <n> }. exclude (Optional) Excludes bucket keys: an exact-value array or a wildcard string (negated include). aggs (Optional, object) Nested sub-aggregations, computed per bucket. Bucket order is fixed to doc_count descending (key-ascending tie-break); the order parameter is not accepted.
Related # multi_terms — same idea over a tuple of fields rare_terms — the mirror image: keep the long tail significant_terms — unusual values in a scope composite — paginated terms for very large key sets
title: Terms aggregation

content:
Term query # Returns documents that contain an exact term in a provided field.
You can use the term query to find documents based on a precise value such as a price, a product ID, or a username. It is also the atom the rest of the term-level family resolves to: terms expands into a should of term clauses, and prefix / wildcard / regexp / fuzzy all resolve to term sets before execution.
Inside a nested query: supported — the value is matched per array element. On text fields prefer match; term targets exact keyword / numeric / date values.
How it works # The value is looked up verbatim in the field’s index — no analyzer and no normalizer runs on it, so what you send must equal exactly what was indexed, including whitespace and capitalization.
Which index serves the lookup depends on the field type:
keyword / text — a point lookup in the inverted index’s term dictionary, then the matching postings list. On text fields the stored terms are the analyzer’s output (the standard analyzer lowercases), so "value": "Error" finds nothing when every token was indexed as error. Prefer match for analyzed text — it runs the analyzer for you. numeric / date — the per-field BKD range index (or the column store’s value-sorted region on merged segments without a BKD index): the dispatcher routes numeric term queries there, because a text-dictionary lookup of a number would always miss. The bound is matched as a single point. boolean — the column store’s Bool column. String values normalize first ("true", "1", "yes", "ok" count as true; "false", "0", "no" as false). Scoring. On keyword / text the hit is scored with BM25 like any postings match, so rare values rank higher. On numeric, date and boolean fields the hit gets a constant score — the boost (1.0 by default) — which makes those forms natural bool filter clauses: they constrain the result set without distorting relevance.
Examples # The following search returns the log lines whose level is exactly error — 25 of the 150 documents in the logs dataset.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. GET /_search { "query": { "term": { "field": "org.id", "value": "infini" } } } Use cases # Enums and statuses. level, status, tier are keyword fields with a closed vocabulary — term on sales.status = "pending" returns 40 of the 120 sales, term on customers.tier = "gold" returns 4 of 20. Exact numeric points. A term on sales.price = 45 matches the 20 sales at that price through the BKD index — the one-value special case of a range query. ID lookups. Slugs, SKUs, hostnames (host = "web-01" → 50 of 150 log lines) — values you want whole, never tokenized or scored by frequency. Filter clauses. Inside bool.filter, a term’s BM25 input is ignored anyway, so exact-value filtering costs nothing in relevance quality. Tag membership. A term on the articles.tags keyword array ("search") matches the 2 articles carrying that tag — array fields index each value as a term. Parameters for term # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search. value (Required, string, number or boolean) Term you wish to find in the provided field. To return a document, the term must exactly match the field value, including whitespace and capitalization. case_insensitive (Optional, boolean) Allows ASCII case insensitive matching of the value with the indexed field values when set to true. Default is false. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Decrease or increase the relevance scores of the query. Related # terms — any-of-a-set over exact values; expands to a bool should of term clauses. range — the interval generalization for numeric and date fields, served by the same BKD index. fuzzy — near-miss matching when the exact term is unknown or misspelled. keys — matching by document identity instead of by field value. match — the analyzed alternative for text fields. terms aggregation — the bucket view of the same keyword vocabulary a term query filters on.
title: Term query

content:
Sort and pagination # Control which documents come back and in what order — sort, from/size, search_after/search_before, and total-hit accounting.
POST /my-collection/_search How it works # sort is an array of sort clauses evaluated in order; the first clause that produces a difference decides the order. Sorting on an indexed field lets the collector skip documents that cannot make the cut (early termination), so field sorts — and _doc above all — are cheaper than score sorts, not just differently ordered.
Three details the engine guarantees:
Ties break by internal doc order. Documents whose sort keys are equal (including two missing values) keep a stable, repeatable order across pages — safe for cursor pagination. Sort keys echo per-field precision. Sorting a date field returns millisecond keys; a date_nanos field returns full nanosecond keys (.123456789 survives), with the key rendered according to each field’s mapping — and the sort works through wildcard index patterns (conformance case 240_date_nanos). Geo proximity is a score, not a sort key. There is no _geo_distance sort clause; order by distance with the distance_feature query, which scores every hit by boost × pivot / (pivot + distance) from an origin — nearest first simply falls out of relevance order.
Sort # JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Parameters # field (Required, string) The field to sort by. Two pseudo-fields are always available: _score (relevance, descending by default) and _doc (index order — the cheapest possible sort). order (Optional, asc | desc) Sort direction. When omitted in a canonical clause the engine sorts descending — for _score and regular fields alike. The Elasticsearch shorthand forms ("sort": "date", bare "date" in the array) are the exception: the gateway normalizes them to asc, so the direction you see depends on the form you send. When in doubt, spell order out. missing (Optional, first | last; the gateway also accepts the Elasticsearch spellings _first / _last) Where documents without a value for the field land, independent of the sort direction. Default: last. Documents whose keys tie (including two missing values) break the tie by internal doc order, so pages are repeatable. script (Optional, string | object) With field: "_script" only: the sort key is computed per hit of the returned page by this script (doc and params in scope) instead of an indexed field. At most one _script clause per request — see scripted queries.
Index-time sorted fields (see field parameters) join _doc among the fastest keys.
Pagination # from (Optional, integer, default: 0) Offset of the first hit to return. size (Optional, integer, default: 10) Number of hits to return. 0 with aggregations skips hit assembly entirely. track_total_hits (Optional, boolean | integer) Whether to compute the exact hit count. false skips counting when you only need the page; a number caps the counting work. The gateway accepts the Elasticsearch form, default cap 10000. collect_size (Optional, integer) Upper bound on candidate documents collected before ranking — a guard rail for very broad queries. Deep from paging re-ranks everything before the offset. Prefer cursors:
search_after (Optional, array) Return the rows that follow the given sort-key tuple. Take the tuple from the last hit of the previous page (sort values of that hit) and pass it back. search_before (Optional, array) The mirror image — the rows that precede the tuple. Together with search_after this enables bidirectional cursored paging. For a stable view across pages, run the search against a point-in-time snapshot (pit — see API conventions).
Examples # Cheapest first page of everything, newest first:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Cursor to the next page with the last hit’s sort tuple — the engine answers the rows strictly AFTER the tuple:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The first page’s newest document is S120 (epoch 1745276400000); the cursor page starts at the second-newest. A multi-key sort array gives the cursor a unique tuple per document (see the wasm note below about float-typed single keys).
Notes # Sorting by a field that is only in the document source (not indexed, not a column) forces full materialization — index the field or accept the cost. The gateway also accepts the shorthand forms ("sort": ["date"], "sort": [{"date":"asc"}]) and normalizes them to the canonical clause above. Use cases # Newest-first feeds. sort: [{field: date, order: desc}] over the 120-sale history (or the 150-log stream) with track_total_hits for the total and cursors for endless scroll. Deterministic exports. _doc order — index order, the cheapest key the engine has — for dump jobs that must replay identically. Composite leaderboards. Multi-clause sorts (price desc, date asc) with explicit missing placement so documents without the field land where the product spec says, not wherever ties dump them. Geo-ordered results. places nearest-first: no _geo_distance sort — sort by _score under a distance_feature query centered on the user (see How it works). Deep pagination at scale. search_after/search_before cursor walks instead of from offsets, pinned to a pit snapshot when the index keeps moving. Related # Field collapsing and rescore — the other two result-shaping stages; collapse pages over groups of the sorted list, rescore re-sorts the top window by blended score. distance_feature query — proximity ordering as scoring, for dates and geo points. Scripted queries — the _script sort key and script_score, the query-time scripting surface. API conventions — pit snapshots and the cursor contract in the wider API.
title: Sort and pagination

content:
Roadmap # A living list of what is planned next. Items land when they are done — the limitations page tracks the counterpart “what does not work today”.
Querying and analytics # SQL — the query subset over the search DSL is live on POST /_sql — filter/aggregate/sort/paginate, $1 parameters, PIT snapshots, grouped cursor pages — with POST /_prql alongside it (see the SQL & PRQL reference and the syntax walkthrough). The frontend now lives in the engine (feature sql), and the WebAssembly build runs statements through the same parse/lower (search_with_sql) — the base for SQL demos in the live playground. What remains: JOIN across collections, subqueries, window functions, the EXPLAIN lowering trace, the two-layer cache closeout, and the playground rollout (envelope parity plus demo pages).
Storage # Object storage backends — the segment file layout is already object-storage-friendly (content-addressed write-once files, generationed manifests with replication-safe publish ordering, so an external replicator can mirror a shard to S3/OSS). What remains is the first-class option: storage-tier configuration, bucket lifecycle and recovery straight from remote storage. Parquet interop — the engine already reads Parquet columns through its column API (opt-in engine feature). What remains is the user-facing mount: exposing standard Parquet data as a collection, as an exchange format with big-data systems. Operations # Backup and restore API — point-in-time snapshots with restore semantics, replacing today’s manual data-directory procedure (see Backup and restore). Cluster-wide state and health — aggregating /_cluster/state and health across regions instead of the serving region only. AI and semantic search # Chunking for semantic_text — long-document semantic search: split field text into overlapping chunks, embed each, keep several vectors per document, score by the best-matching chunk. Blocked on engine support for multiple vectors per (document, field) — today’s vector store keeps exactly one (FlatVectorStore::add overwrites), so this spans the mutable store, the epoch builder, the HNSW index and score aggregation. Until then the field embeds whole texts in one call (fine for titles, names, log lines; bounded by the model’s input limit), and long documents have a working pattern: chunk into child documents at write time, search with the semantic query and collapse by parent id (see field collapsing).
Multi-tenancy # Tenant grouping — namespaces grouped under one tenant identity, generalizing today’s 1:1 namespace mapping.
title: Roadmap

content:
Relations that route — joins, FK placement, salting # A fact collection can now behave like one. Declare the relationship in the schema and the engine takes over:
"org_id": { "type": "keyword", "immutable": true, "references": {"collection": "orgs"}, "routing": true, "ref": true } Join queries are live — a semi-join over the wire: the inner query runs on the referenced collection, its matching keys become a membership filter on the outer side, and joins through a declared references field resolve without a second fan-out. Writes place by the foreign key’s value — hash(org_id) picks the home partition, not the document key, so an org’s facts colocate. Key-addressed operations take ?routing=<value> ( fetch, update,
delete).
Salting splits the hot org — when one routing value dominates, the _salting API spreads its writes across a partition SET (deterministic per key, round-robin for auto-IDs), with a terms feed that flags candidates against your threshold. Assignments are never auto-applied and searches stay oblivious — salting changes placement, never visibility.
One declaration, three consequences:
graph LR D["one field declarationreferences: orgs · routing: true"] --> J("joins — a semi-join,keys ride the declared field") D --> P("placement — hash(org_id)picks the home partition") D --> S("salting — a hot value spreadsover a partition SET") The joins tutorial walks the whole story against a running node — placement observable in the response _id, fail-closed 400s, the salting feed, the salt-split spread, joins before and after.
title: Relations that route — joins, FK placement, salting

content:
PRQL queries # POST /_prql accepts PRQL pipeline text in the same request shape as POST /_sql — query, plus cursor, params, snapshot_id and timeout riding alongside exactly as they do for SQL. The statement is compiled by a pinned prqlc and executed as its equivalent SQL through the identical pipeline, so cursors, snapshots, timeouts and the response envelope behave the same (see SQL & PRQL).
A cursor walk resubmits the SAME PRQL text plus the cursor object; the compiled statement is cached by text, so the walk compiles once.
Pipelines and the SQL they lower into # Every pipeline compiles into ONE SELECT statement inside the SQL subset — the transforms map onto clauses:
PRQL transform lowers into from sq_nulls FROM sq_nulls filter price > 15 WHERE price > 15 sort {price} / sort {-price} ORDER BY price / ORDER BY price DESC take 2 LIMIT 2 select {_key, price} the SELECT list group {tag} ( aggregate { … } ) GROUP BY tag with the aggregate list The canonical pipeline, with the SQL it compiles to:
POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | filter price > 15 | sort {-price} | take 2 | select {_key, price}" } SELECT _key, price FROM sq_nulls WHERE price > 15 ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 2 No select at all is SELECT * — the lane’s dynamic column expansion:
POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | filter tag == 't1' | take 2" } select renames with = and may sit before sort (then the sort uses the new names):
POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | select {k = _key, p = price} | sort {-p} | take 2" } The idiomatic multi-line spelling — a leading | starts each stage — normalizes into the single-line pipeline before compiling, with error positions mapped back onto your text:
from sq_nulls | filter price > 15 | sort {-price} | take 2 | select {_key, price} Compound conditions: the pinned compiler takes && and || (see the syntax notes below), and chained filter stages AND together. != null tests existence with SQL’s three-valued semantics — a document without the field drops, on either polarity:
POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | filter price > 15 && tag != 't0' | take 3" } POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | filter price > 15 | filter tag != 't0' | take 3" } POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | filter price != null | take 2" } Grouped aggregation and cursors # The aggregate BLOCK form carries the aggregates: count this lowers to COUNT(*), and average/min/max lower to AVG/MIN/MAX (sum does not make it through — see the boundaries below):
POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | group {tag} ( aggregate { n = count this, avg_price = average price, lo = min price, hi = max price } ) | sort {tag}" } Grouped queries ride the composite keyset cursor exactly like SQL — sort {tag} ascending over the group key with a take is the addressable order:
POST /_prql { "query": "from sq_nulls | group {tag} ( aggregate { n = count this } ) | sort {tag} | take 2" } The response carries the cursor object; resubmit the SAME text plus it for page two, and the walk retires on cursor: null (see SQL & PRQL for the envelope).
The pinned compiler’s shapes # prqlc is version-pinned (0.13.14) and its emitted SQL must stay inside the SQL subset above. Syntax notes for this pin:
Pipelines are single-line to the pinned compiler, but the idiomatic leading-pipe continuation (from x then lines starting with |) is accepted: the lane normalizes it into the single-line pipeline before compiling, and compile-error positions map back onto the submitted text. A continuation joins only onto a code line — after a blank line or a comment it stays put and the compiler’s own positioned error answers. The parenthesized form (from x\n( filter … | take 3 )) keeps working. aggregate takes the block form — aggregate { n = count this }. Compound conditions spell && and ||. The word spellings (and / or) and in […] lists do not parse with this pin — the compiler answers a positioned prql_error; chain filter stages or write the comparisons with && instead. s-strings are rejected # PRQL s-strings (s"SELECT …") escape into arbitrary SQL that the subset cannot guarantee, so they are rejected outright with a source-positioned error — before compilation:
{ "error": { "type": "prql_error", "reason": "s-strings are not allowed — they escape into arbitrary SQL (OQ-3); lower the logic into PRQL or submit the SQL directly to /_sql", "position": { "line": 1, "column": 24 } } } The same text inside a comment or a plain string literal never trips the scan.
Fail-closed boundaries # Boundaries answer a positioned error — never a silently different answer:
A pipeline that lowers into a CTE (WITH table_0 AS …) is outside the SQL subset. Two shapes trigger it: a derive feeding a later stage (from x | derive bumped = price + 1 | filter bumped > 40), and a trailing select that drops a sort column (… | sort {-price} | take 2 | select {_key}) — prqlc wraps both to preserve semantics. Keep every sort column in the final select, or select before sort, or skip the select. sum — PRQL defines sum over an empty input as 0, so prqlc emits COALESCE(SUM(price), 0), which is not a bare aggregate; the SQL frontend rejects it positioned. average, min and max emit bare aggregates and pass; for a sum, submit the SQL directly to /_sql. Both answer the shared error contract: compile diagnostics map to type: "prql_error" with the position on the PRQL source (hints join the reason); a shape that compiles but leaves the subset answers type: "sql_error" from the SQL frontend, positioned onto your text. PRQL has no $1 surface of its own, so a params array fails closed through the SQL lane exactly like an unused SQL param.
title: PRQL queries

content:
Nested query # Matches parent documents whose nested sub-documents — objects mapped with "nested": true — satisfy a query within one element at a time. It exists because a flattened object index cannot keep two field values inside the same array element together — the pitfall the next section makes concrete.
The cross-element problem # A flattened index correlates across array elements, not within them: variants.color = blue AND variants.size = L matches a document as soon as some element is blue and some element is L — not necessarily the same one. The teaching dataset’s products makes the difference visible (each element pairs blue with L, never with M):
graph LR subgraph flat["flattened — one shared field space"] F1("variants[0] is blue") F2("variants[1] is M") F1 --> FM["matches — 10 documentsthe two values may comefrom different elements"] F2 --> FM end subgraph nest["nested — one element at a time"] N1("variants[0]blue, L — no M") N2("variants[1]red, M — no blue") N1 --> NM["no match — 0 documents"] N2 --> NM end JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The flattened query above reports 10 documents — every product with some blue variant and some M variant, even when they are different elements. The nested query below evaluates each variant as a whole element and reports 0: in this dataset blue variants only ever come in size L.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Same-element matching # When the pair lives in one element, only the nested query is guaranteed correct (blue always pairs with L in this dataset):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. 20 of 30 products have a blue/L variant. Any leaf composes inside the inner query:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Inner queries and minimum_should_match # The inner query supports:
term, match, multi_match,
phrase (also accepted: match_phrase),
range, exists
bool — minimum_should_match included, scoped to one element nested itself, for sub-objects Not supported inside nested yet: terms, prefix, wildcard, fuzzy, regexp, suffix, the span family and query_string. These are rejected with an HTTP 400 naming the offending clause and the nested path — never a silent zero-hit answer. The same shapes keep working at the top level.
bool.minimum_should_match applies within one element: a parent matches when at least one element satisfies that many should clauses by itself. Clauses matched by different elements never add up — minimum_should_match: 2 over two should clauses is the same-element AND:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The same 20 blue/L products as the must example above — with minimum_should_match dropped to 1 (the default when the bool has no must/filter) it becomes the same-element OR.
Phrases compose with the same element scoping — the adjacent word pair must live in ONE element, and slop (default 0) buys holes between the words, in query order:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "nested": { "path": "reviews", "query": { "phrase": { "field": "reviews.body", "query": "quick fox", "slop": 1 } } } } } quick fox with slop: 1 matches an element holding “quick brown fox” (one word between); at slop: 0 nothing matches unless the words are adjacent. Reversed word order ("fox quick") never matches at any slop — phrase terms keep query order.
Schema requirement # Declare the object as nested so elements are indexed with ordinal-tagged postings (server-side collections). Both forms are accepted — they are the same schema:
PUT /my-collection { "schema": { "properties": { "variants": { "type": "nested", "properties": { "color": { "type": "keyword" }, "size": { "type": "keyword" } } } } } } The explicit form spells the parameter out ("type": "object" + "nested": true) for readers who prefer it.
Documents index variants as an array of objects; each element is addressable through its dotted sub-fields inside the nested query.
How it works # nested rides the same block pipeline as every other query, with one extra channel — the ordinal that identifies which array element produced a posting:
The inner query resolves against ordinal-tagged postings, where each entry is a (doc_id, ordinal, score) triple instead of the usual (doc_id, score). Boolean combination happens on the composite key: intersection and union match on (doc_id, ordinal) pairs, so two clauses agree only when ONE element satisfies both — never element 0’s color plus element 1’s size. A collapse producer folds the per-element matches back to unique parent ids, combining the per-element scores by score_mode. Flat queries never touch the ordinal channel — the same block operators fall back to plain doc-id intersection — so non-nested traffic pays nothing for the feature. Documents still in the realtime layer (not yet frozen into segments) take the per-element stored-array path described under Performance characteristics below.
Performance characteristics # Correlation is resolved in one of two ways, depending on where the matching documents live:
Built segments — every element’s postings carry a (doc_id, ordinal) pair, and the engine intersects / unions on that composite key. Nested queries resolve at close to ordinary bool cost. Realtime (not yet frozen) documents — the inner query is evaluated against each stored array element, one document at a time. Exact and available immediately after the write, but the cost is linear in documents × elements: a nested query over 20 000 documents × 5 elements measured roughly 10–15× the latency of the equivalent flattened bool (sub-second either way). Keep realtime buffers bounded when nested queries dominate a large collection. Scoring note: realtime-layer elements match with a constant score, so score_mode only differentiates on built segments.
Use cases # Variant correlation. The products pair above — color and size must describe one SKU. Any catalog with option arrays has this shape; the flattened query overstates the match count (10 vs 0 in the teaching data). Per-review constraints. “Reviews containing ‘quick fox’ AND rated = 4” must hold within one review, not across the array — a phrase and a range scoped to the same element.
Line-item queries. Orders and invoices whose line items pair a SKU with a quantity or a price band — the same-element AND, per line. Explaining the match. inner_hits returns the exact elements that matched (identity, source, score), so a UI can highlight the blue/L variant instead of the whole product. Sub-object nesting. nested inside nested walks multi-level arrays (variant → components) with the same element-at-a-time rule at each level. Parameters for nested # path (Required, string) Path of the nested object (e.g. "variants"). query (Required, object) The query applied to each inner element; a parent matches when at least one element satisfies it. score_mode (Optional, string) How per-element scores collapse into the parent’s score: sum (default), avg, min, max, or none (constant 1.0). inner_hits (Optional, object) When present, every top-level hit carries an inner_hits block keyed by the path: the matched ELEMENTS of that document’s nested array, each with _nested: {field, offset} identity, the element _source, and its score (default window: 3, from/size adjustable). Sub-nested requests materialize recursively inside each inner hit. An optional highlight block highlights inner hits against the inner query; multi-field sub-fields (field.vectors) fall back to the parent field’s text. Related # join — the cross-collection counterpart: membership by key against another collection, instead of correlation inside one document. traverse and graph — relations between documents over a relation edge field. Nested aggregation — bucket analytics over the same nested structure. Children aggregation — the parent/child aggregation over joined hierarchies. Relational parameters — the schema family (references, ref, routing) the cross-collection pages build on.
title: Nested query

content:
Match query # Returns documents that match a provided text, number, date or boolean value. The provided text is analyzed before matching — this is the primary full-text query.
Inside a nested query: supported — the text is matched per array element.
How it works # The engine resolves the analyzer first — the analyzer parameter when given, else the field’s search analyzer, else the built-in standard analyzer — and runs it over the query text. Each resulting token becomes one term clause:
operator: "or" (default) — the term posting lists are unioned. A document matches when it contains any token, and its score is the sum of the BM25 scores of the tokens it contains. operator: "and" — the posting lists are intersected. A document must contain every token; a token missing from the dictionary makes the whole query match nothing, while under or the missing token is simply dropped. A single-token query runs on a dedicated single-term producer; multi-token AND cursors are sorted rarest-first so the intersection drives from the shortest posting list. Scores are BM25 with k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75:
idf = ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)) score = idf * tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl / avgdl)) N counts the documents that have the field, df is the term’s document frequency, tf its frequency in the matched document, dl the document’s raw token count (stored as a quantized field norm), and avgdl the field’s total tokens over N — guarded to 1.0 for an empty field. Cross-segment queries correct per-segment IDF to the global statistics, so a term scores the same wherever its document lives.
When the field is not analyzed text, a rewrite happens first: a match on a keyword, numeric, date or boolean field becomes an exact term lookup — the field’s normalizer applied when configured — instead of tokenizing. boost multiplies into the BM25 chain; fuzziness is rejected outright (see parameters below).
Examples # POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "match": { "field": "message", "query": "this is a test" } } } The match query applies the field’s search analyzer (or analyzer when given) to the text, then matches the resulting tokens with OR semantics by default. Require all tokens with operator. Below, the single token search finds the GET /search lines — 25 of the 150 documents:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "match": { "field": "message", "query": "this is a test", "operator": "and" } } } Use cases # The search box. Free-typed user input is the canonical match: analyzed, OR-ed, BM25-ranked. In the logs dataset all 25 messages carrying cluster node left contain the full phrase, so or and and return the same 25 documents — the operator dial only matters once words scatter across documents. A precision dial. operator: "and" switches the same query text from “any word” to “every word” — the strict mode of the same box. Exact values without a term query. On keyword, numeric, date or boolean fields the rewrite to a term lookup means one query shape serves both analyzed text and structured fields. Typo tolerance — deliberately elsewhere. fuzziness is rejected with a 400 rather than silently ignored; use the fuzzy query or query_string’s ~.
Parameters for match # field (Required, string) Field you wish to search.
query (Required, string) Text, number, boolean value or date you wish to find in the provided field.
analyzer (Optional, string) Analyzer used to convert the text in the query value into tokens. Defaults to the field’s search analyzer.
operator (Optional, string) Boolean logic used to interpret the text: or (default) or and.
minimum_should_match (Optional, string) Minimum number of clauses that must match for a document to be returned.
fuzziness (unsupported) Fuzzy matching inside match is not implemented. Setting fuzziness is rejected with HTTP 400 naming the parameter, rather than silently ignored — a body carrying it would otherwise run as an exact analyzed match, which is not what the writer intended. Use the fuzzy query or the query_string ~ operator instead:
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "match": { "field": "title", "query": "hello", "fuzziness": "AUTO" } } } # 400 — match.fuzziness is not supported yet — use the `fuzzy` query # (or the query_string `~` operator) instead prefix_length (Optional, integer, default: 0) Number of beginning characters left unchanged for fuzzy matching.
max_expansions (Optional, integer, default: 50) Maximum number of terms to which the query expands.
fuzzy_transpositions (Optional, boolean, default: true) Edits for fuzzy matching include transpositions of two adjacent characters (ab → ba).
auto_generate_synonyms_phrase_query (Optional, boolean, default: true) If true, match phrase queries are automatically created for multi-term synonyms.
lenient (Optional, boolean, default: false) If true, format-based errors (such as a text value for a numeric field) are ignored.
boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0) Decrease or increase the relevance scores of the query.
fuzzy_rewrite (Optional, string) Method used to rewrite the fuzzy expansion (constant_score, scoring_boolean, …).
zero_terms_query (Optional, string) What to match when the analyzer removes every token (e.g. a stop filter): none (default, matches nothing) or all.
cross_fields_strategy (Optional, string) Score combination used when one field name resolves to several analyzed sub-fields: most_fields (sum — the default) or best_fields (max).
Related # multi_match — the same analyzed matching fanned out over several fields, with per-field boosts. phrase — when the order of the tokens matters as much as their presence. bool — combines match clauses with filters and exclusions; every compound query ends up a bool. Analyzers — what produces the tokens that match matches on. API conventions — request envelope and strict-gate parameter handling.
title: Match query

content:
Lesson 2 — Text search # How text actually matches: analysis, exact terms, phrases, and the error-tolerant family. Everything below runs live on the logs collection (150 documents with message, level, host, url.path).
The use case # The search box in front of users — application logs, product descriptions, support tickets. Users type in one casing, with typos, and your data is cased differently; the craft is choosing the right amount of looseness per question:
“Exactly this level / status / tag, nothing else” — term on a keyword field: exact, fast, predictable. “Documents that talk about search” — match: the analyzer absorbs casing and word forms. “The words HTTP/1.1 200 together, in order” — phrase. “The user typed serch” — fuzzy tolerates the typo. “Every host named web-0 … web-9” — wildcard / regexp. “Why did my query match nothing?” — analysis: the analyzer decides what matches, and this lesson shows it in numbers. Exact terms vs analyzed text # A term query matches the stored value exactly — no tokenization, no casing help. A match query runs the field’s analyzer first, so casing and punctuation stop mattering:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Compare with a term on the keyword field level — exact, and therefore fast and predictable:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. 25 of the 150 log lines are errors. If you had written "ERROR" the count would be 0 — that is the analyzer difference in one number.
Both rows of that table have a SQL spelling — MATCH is the analyzed full-text lane, = is the exact lane (the SQL reference maps every construct):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. SCORE() in the ORDER BY ranks by relevance — same as sorting on _score in the DSL.
Phrases # phrase (alias match_phrase) requires the tokens in order, with slop budget for gaps. The dataset’s known answer — HTTP/1.1 200 appears in 75 documents — shows why analysis matters: the tokenizer folds HTTP/1.1 into one token, and the phrase matches it exactly:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. MATCH_PHRASE is the SQL spelling — same tokenizer, same ordering rule:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The error-tolerant family # Typos ( fuzzy), prefixes ( prefix), patterns ( wildcard and regexp), and endings ( suffix). The fuzzy query below misspells search as serch — one dropped letter — and still finds the same 25 GET /search requests the exact match at the top of this page found:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The typo survives the SQL spelling too — FUZZY with an explicit fuzziness (AUTO lets the engine pick by term length):
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. One string, full mini-language # query_string packs booleans, fields, ranges and wildcards into one expression:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Combining with bool # bool is the workhorse — must for scoring clauses, filter for cheap yes/no:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. SQL composes the same way — AND chains a scoring clause with an exact one:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. What you learned # term = exact value, match = analyzed text. Phrases order tokens; slop buys distance. Fuzzy/prefix/wildcard/regexp/suffix cover the typo and pattern cases. bool composes everything, with filter for scoring-free clauses. The SQL lane covers the same ground: MATCH/MATCH_PHRASE for analyzed text and phrases, FUZZY for typos, AND/NOT for composition — see the SQL syntax page. Next: Lesson 3 — structure and numbers, or read the analysis API to inspect what any analyzer does to a string.
title: Lesson 2 — Text search

content:
Geo-bounding-box query # Matches documents whose geo_point field falls inside a rectangle defined by its top-left and bottom-right corners. Coordinates are WGS-84 degrees; filtering only (does not contribute distance scoring).
It is the cheapest geographic filter. When the region you need is a rectangle of latitude and longitude — a map viewport, a city’s extents, a country’s outline approximated by its bounds — the engine answers with a single index range and no per-document geometry math.
How it works # A geo_point field is indexed as a two-dimensional BKD tree keyed by (lat, lon). At ingest a point may arrive in any of three forms — the object {"lat": .., "lon": ..}, the array [lon, lat] (longitude first), or the string "lat,lon" — all normalized to the same pair before they reach the tree.
The query is that tree’s range. The walk visits only leaves between (bottom_right_lat, top_left_lon) and (top_left_lat, bottom_right_lon), and every document in a visited leaf matches — the rectangle is the index predicate itself, so there is no second verification phase. Results are exact, with points on all four edges included.
The box must have its west edge at or left of its east edge (top_left_lon <= bottom_right_lon); a box that would cross the antimeridian is not split into two — issue two queries joined by a bool should instead.
The nested form is accepted too and rewritten at the gateway: {"geo_bounding_box": {"location": {"top_left": <pt>, "bottom_right": <pt>}}} with each corner in any of the three point forms. Options such as validation_method are accepted for compatibility and ignored.
Examples # The live query frames a box over eastern China — latitude 30–42, longitude 116–123. Five of the fifteen places match: the two Beijing places, the two Shanghai places and the Hangzhou store.
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "geo_bounding_box": { "field": "location", "top_left_lat": 40.73, "top_left_lon": -74.1, "bottom_right_lat": 40.01, "bottom_right_lon": -71.12 } } } Use cases # Map viewport search. “Everything inside the rectangle the user is looking at” is the canonical bounding-box question — one range per pan or zoom, served straight from the BKD tree. Rectangular geofencing. Alerting or access rules tied to a box (a warehouse district, a no-fly rectangle) filter with this query before any scoring happens. Cheap prefilter for expensive stages. Narrow a large index by area first, then aggregate or score the survivors — the box costs one tree range, so it composes well inside a bool filter. Coverage checks. Which of our stores fall inside the region’s bounding box — a quick audit before finer tools such as geo_polygon trim the corners.
Parameters for geo_bounding_box # field (Required, string) The geo_point field to filter on. top_left_lat (Required, number) Top-left corner latitude (north edge). top_left_lon (Required, number) Top-left corner longitude (west edge). bottom_right_lat (Required, number) Bottom-right corner latitude (south edge). bottom_right_lon (Required, number) Bottom-right corner longitude (east edge). The four corners are plain numbers; both the flat form above and the nested form (corners as point objects) deserialize into the same query.
Related # geo_distance — round regions: everything within a great-circle radius of one centre point. geo_polygon — arbitrary rings, when the region’s corners matter. geo_shape — full geometries indexed per document and tested against a query shape. geo-distance aggregation — after filtering, bucket the survivors by distance rings. geo-centroid aggregation — the mean centre of the matched points.
title: Geo-bounding-box query

content:
Distance feature query # Recalls every document and scores each by its proximity to an origin — the closer, the higher:
score = boost × pivot / (pivot + distance(document, origin)) A document exactly at the origin scores boost; one pivot units away scores boost / 2. The decay is gradual — unlike a range filter, a document three pivots out still scores boost / 4, so nothing is excluded, only demoted. It answers “rank by recency or by distance” without a second index or a script.
POST /my-collection/_search { "query": { "distance_feature": { "field": "production_date", "pivot": "7d", "origin": "now" } } } How it works # The pivot’s unit decides what distance means for the query: a duration makes it a time difference (epoch millis, or raw nanos with a nanos pivot for date_nanos fields), a distance makes it metres (geo_point fields), and a plain number compares the field’s numeric values directly. Each document’s stored field value is read, its distance to the origin computed — absolute difference for numbers and dates, haversine for geo points — and run through the formula above; distance is floored at zero, so values on either side of the origin score identically.
origin resolves lazily: "now" pins at evaluation time (every segment of one request sees the same instant), an ISO-8601 date parses to epoch millis, a number passes through, and geo origins take the [lon, lat] array or the "lat,lon" string. Pivot durations accept ms, s, m, h, d, w and nanos/ns; distances accept km, m-less bare numbers (metres), mi, yd, ft, in, cm, mm and nmi. When a millis-scale pivot meets nanosecond-scale doc values (values ≥ 10^17), the values are divided down to millis so the two sides of the subtraction agree — the same normalization the date_nanos paths apply elsewhere.
The geo form, ranking every document by distance from one point:
POST /places/_search { "query": { "distance_feature": { "field": "location", "pivot": "1000km", "origin": [116.4074, 39.9042] } } } Parameters for distance_feature # field (Required, string) A numeric, date, date_nanos, or geo_point field. origin (Required) The anchor: "now", an ISO-8601 date, an epoch number for numeric/date fields; [lon, lat] or "lat,lon" for geo fields. pivot (Required) The distance at which the score halves: a duration ("1h", "7d", "100000000nanos"), a distance ("1km", "500m", "2mi"), or a plain number for numeric fields. boost (Optional, float, default: 1.0). Use cases # Recency re-ranking. As a bool.should clause next to the text query, origin: "now" with pivot: "7d" adds up to one unit of score to fresh log lines and products — recent hits win ties without excluding old ones. “Nearest first” without geo infrastructure. On a geo_point field, standalone distance_feature orders every place by distance from the shopper’s coordinates; pivot sets how quickly relevance falls off (within pivot, scores stay above half). Freshness-ordered feeds. Standalone on a date field it is a pure recency sort whose scores are comparable across requests — handy for TTL dashboards and “last seen” views. Nanos-precision timelines. date_nanos fields with a "100000000nanos" pivot (100 ms) resolve orderings that collapse at millisecond resolution. Notes # The query recalls every document that carries the field — each hit scores above zero, whether the value is stored as a number, an ISO date string, or any accepted geo form ([lon, lat] array or "lat,lon" string). Documents missing the field, or with values that do not parse for it, are simply not recalled. It pairs naturally as a bool.should clause (relevance re-ranking) or standalone as a recency/proximity ordering. Inside nested queries it is not supported yet (rejected with a named error).
Related # hybrid — score_functions, the declarative alternative when the decay should combine with other scoring functions. rescore — re-scoring the top window of an already-ranked result, the other place proximity boosts are applied. geo_distance — the filter form: a hard radius that excludes, where distance_feature demotes. sort — _geo_distance sorting when you need distance ordering without score decay.
title: Distance feature

content:
Avg bucket aggregation # A sibling pipeline aggregation computing the average of a metric across another aggregation’s buckets. Bucket aggregations answer “what is the revenue per day / per category / per range”; avg_bucket rolls those per-bucket numbers into one mean — “what does a typical day or category bring in” — without a second query or client-side arithmetic.
"avg_day": { "avg_bucket": { "buckets_path": "per_day>revenue" } } How it works # avg_bucket is declared next to the bucket aggregation it consumes (a sibling in the same aggs object) and runs after every regular aggregation has finished — after the merge, too, in a distributed search. It reads the parent’s finished buckets, collects one number per bucket, and divides their sum by their count. The result is a single-value metric ({"value": 56.25}) placed alongside the parent.
The buckets_path names what to collect:
"per_day>revenue" — the > separates the bucket aggregation from the sub-metric inside each of its buckets. A . works the same way ("range.v"). The sub-metric must be single-valued (sum, avg, min, max, value_count, cardinality, …). A multi-value metric such as percentiles has no single number to take; a stats sub-agg contributes its sum. A bare parent name ("per_day", no separator) aggregates the buckets’ doc_counts instead of a sub-metric. Gaps follow gap_policy:
skip (default) — a bucket whose metric is missing or null is left out; it does not count toward the divisor. An empty bucket (doc_count 0, e.g. a declared range no document falls into) is skipped even though its sum serializes as 0. insert_zeros — such buckets contribute 0 and still count. Three range buckets with sums 1, 5, 0 (the last empty) average to 3 under skip — not 2. If every bucket is missing, the result is {"value": null}.
Examples # Average daily revenue across the date-histogram buckets:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. The teaching dataset holds one sale per calendar day, so every bucket holds exactly one document and the daily revenues average 56.25 — 6750 / 120, the same figure the plain avg returns over amount. With multiple sales per day the two diverge: avg_bucket weighs each bucket equally, avg each document.
Use cases # Typical period revenue — date_histogram per month plus avg_bucket over the monthly sum(amount): the 16 months in the dataset average 421.875, a steadier baseline than any single month. Compare groups, not documents — average the per-category totals of a terms aggregation to say “an average product line brings 1687.5”, immune to how many documents each category happens to have. Baseline for alerting — feed avg_bucket into dashboards as the expected value a current bucket is judged against. Empty-bucket hygiene — over buckets that can be empty (declared ranges, filters), skip keeps the mean over populated buckets only; switch to insert_zeros when a missing bucket genuinely means zero. Parameters for avg_bucket # buckets_path (Required, string) Path to the consumed metric: "<bucket_agg>><metric>". format (Optional, string) Output number format. Accepted for compatibility; not applied to the value in the current engine. gap_policy (Optional, string) What to do with missing buckets: skip (default) or insert_zeros. Related # Sibling family: sum_bucket, min_bucket, max_bucket,
stats_bucket,
extended_stats_bucket,
percentiles_bucket
Document-level counterpart: avg
title: Avg bucket aggregation

content:
Avg aggregation # A single-value metrics aggregation that computes the average of numeric values that are extracted from the aggregated documents. It summarizes “what does a typical matching document look like on this field” into one number — the question SQL spells AVG(price) — without fetching a single document.
How it works # The engine walks the matching documents once, keeping a running sum and count; the result is sum / count. Nothing is estimated: the average is exact. Values are coerced to doubles as they are read — integers, floats and booleans (true = 1, false = 0) contribute, non-numeric values such as keyword strings do not.
Documents that lack the field are skipped by default, lowering the count. With missing set, every such document contributes the default to both the sum and the count, exactly as if the field had carried that value. A non-numeric missing string cannot be coerced and is dropped.
On the column-store fast path (the production executor) each segment’s column is decoded once and reduced in a single batch (sum_f64) instead of dispatching per document; segments accumulate into one running sum/count. That pair also makes distributed requests exact: in partial mode avg is rewritten to stats on the shards, so count and sum combine losslessly across shards and the coordinator projects the merged pair back to {"value": …} when finalizing.
When no document contributed a value, the result is null.
Examples # The average price over every sale — flip to SQL (beside the Run button) to ask the same question as one AVG(price) statement:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. POST /sales/_search { "aggs": { "avg_price": { "avg": { "field": "price" } } } } The aggregation type is avg and the field setting defines the numeric field of the documents the average will be computed on. Over the teaching dataset’s 120 sales this returns:
{ ... "aggregations": { "avg_price": { "value": 27.5 } } } The name of the aggregation (avg_price above) also serves as the key by which the aggregation result can be retrieved from the returned response.
Use cases # Sanity-check a filter. sales.avg(price) is 27.5; the same aggregation inside a term filter on type = "hat" returns 30.0. One number tells you the filter selects what you think it selects. Compare groups. Nest avg under terms: avg price per type comes out t-shirt: 15 / hat: 30 / mug: 45 / sticker: 60 — the teaching dataset’s deliberate price ladder. Dashboard KPIs. Average order size (sales.avg(amount) = 56.25) or catalogue price point (products.avg(price) ≈ 15.43 over 30 products) refresh in one request. Average of a magnitude-bearing field. A 3-unit sale counts as much as a 1-unit sale here; when each document carries a qty, switch to weighted_avg — price weighted by quantity sold is 28.125, a half point above the plain 27.5.
Parameters for avg # field (Required, string) Field you wish to aggregate. script (Optional, object) Script evaluated per document as the value source — mutually exclusive with field. missing (Optional, number) Value used for documents missing the field; they contribute it to both the sum and the count. Related # stats — avg plus count/min/max/sum in one request weighted_avg — weight each document before averaging sum — the total behind the average terms — avg per group with a sub-aggregation
title: Avg aggregation

content:
Analyze text # The analysis workbench: run the server’s tokenizers, normalizers, token filters and analyzers over sample text and see the exact token stream — the same components the indexing path uses, so what you debug here is exactly what collections run. The analysis chain decides what is searchable: query and document must reduce to the same tokens.
How it works # Every analyzer is assembled from three stages, run in this order:
Normalizers rewrite the raw text as a whole, before tokenization (lowercase, html_strip, stconvert_t2s, …). Tokenizer splits the rewritten text into tokens. Token filters transform the stream one token at a time, in order (stopwords, asciifolding, …). A filter may delete a token or emit extras (synonyms, n-grams); extras continue with the next filter, so self-expanding filters cannot loop. There is no separate char-filter stage — pre-tokenization transforms are normalizers. They also cover the keyword field path: a keyword field is never tokenized, it just runs one normalizer (e.g. lowercase) over the whole value, so the field stays one exact term that term queries hit case-insensitively.
The engine core provides the standard/whitespace tokenizers, the lowercase normalizer, the lowercase/uppercase/stopwords filters, and the standard and whitespace analyzers. The rest of the catalog comes from the ~40 plugin crates under contrib/analysis-*, registered at startup into the same registry this API reads — so workbench results equal indexing results.
Collections define named analyzers at creation time under settings.analysis.analyzer.custom; fields reference them by name like a built-in (see custom analyzers). The bundled articles dataset ships one, folding accents on bodies:
"content_an": { "tokenizer": "standard", "token_filters": ["asciifolding"] } …used by "body": { "type": "text", "analyzer": "content_an" } — so cafe matches café in bodies, while titles index with standard.
List components # GET /_analysis/components Every registered component — the set a schema may reference. The server ships 83 analyzers, 50 tokenizers, 15 normalizers and 327 token filters; the full catalog.
Examples # Run a named analyzer and inspect the token stream:
POST /_analysis/analyze { "analyzer": "standard", "text": "The Quick Brown Fox" } Response — four tokens; offsets are UTF-16 code units (the JSON convention):
{ "tokens": [ { "token": "the", "start_offset": 0, "end_offset": 3, "position": 0 }, { "token": "quick", "start_offset": 4, "end_offset": 9, "position": 1 }, { "token": "brown", "start_offset": 10, "end_offset": 15, "position": 2 }, { "token": "fox", "start_offset": 16, "end_offset": 19, "position": 3 } ] } Or an ad-hoc pipeline — normalizers first, then tokenizer, then filters:
POST /_analysis/analyze { "text": "Café Olé", "normalizer": ["lowercase"], "tokenizer": "standard", "filter": ["asciifolding"] } The pipeline yields cafe, ole. Named analyzers compose the same components with language tuning — english strips possessives, drops stop words and applies Krovetz stemming ("The Quick Foxes running" → quick, fox, run).
Add "explain": true to also get the snapshot after every stage (a named analyzer runs as-is — no detail comes back):
"detail": [ { "name": "normalizer: lowercase", "text": "café olé" }, { "name": "tokenizer: standard", "tokens": [ ... ] }, { "name": "filter: 1/1 asciifolding", "tokens": [ ... ] } ] An unknown name in the chain fails with a 400 naming it — no silent skip.
Use cases # “Why doesn’t it match?” Run the field’s analyzer over the indexed text and over the query text; where the streams disagree is the relevance bug no amount of query tweaking fixes. Mixed CJK and Latin text. standard emits one token per CJK ideograph and whole Latin words (Pizza搜索引擎 → pizza, 搜, 索, 引, 擎); for word-level CJK use a dictionary-backed plugin analyzer (ik_smart, jieba, kuromoji). Folding and noise. lowercase + asciifolding make CAFE, café and cafe one term; stop filters keep high-frequency words out of the index — smaller posting lists, cleaner scoring. Pinyin and traditional/simplified. The pinyin and stconvert plugins index Chinese text so queries in either script or romanized form still match — see the catalog. Parameters for _analysis/analyze # text (Required, string) The text to analyze. analyzer (Optional, string) A named analyzer; overrides the pipeline fields. tokenizer (Optional, string) Tokenizer for an ad-hoc pipeline; default standard. normalizer (Optional, array) Normalizers applied to the raw text, in order. filter (Optional, array) Token filters applied in order. explain (Optional, boolean) Per-stage snapshots; ad-hoc only. Default false. Related # Built-in analysis components — the full catalog this API draws from. match — the query that consumes these tokens: analyzer output becomes term clauses and scores. Analysis parameters — analyzer, search_analyzer and normalizer on schema fields. Create collection — custom analyzers.
title: Analyze text

content:
Use cases # Pizza is built for latency-sensitive search over fresh, mutable data at scale. The scenarios below map to concrete features — follow the links for the mechanics.
Operational logs and events, searchable the moment they land # Observability and security pipelines need indexed events and fresh results — “what happened in the last minute” cannot wait for a refresh window. Pizza’s realtime write path makes every acknowledged write searchable immediately, rollings absorb unbounded growth without reindexing, and high-volume ingest is served by batched WAL writes plus background segment builds that never gate reads.
E-commerce and marketplace data # Catalogs are a wide-but-shallow update problem: prices, stock levels and flags churn constantly while titles and descriptions stay put.
In-place columns turn stock and price updates into O(1) column writes — no document rebuild per change. Online resharding scales shard counts through traffic spikes without a reindex window. Filter-heavy faceting maps to term-level queries and terms / range aggregations.
Hybrid and semantic search # The same query can mix full-text, filters and vector similarity: match for text,
vector for embeddings (text-in, embedded server-side), fused across fields with
multi_vector — RAG retrieval and semantic cache lookup without a separate vector database.
Entity and relationship search # Documents that reference each other — products and merchants, users and groups, knowledge graphs — are served by join (semi-join against another index) and traverse (bounded graph traversal over relation fields), with
nested for per-element matching inside nested arrays.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends # Namespaces isolate tenants, API keys with roles ( Security) scope each tenant’s access, and per-tenant data can be mirrored elsewhere with the change feed (CDC) — off-site copies, secondary indexes, audit pipelines.
Hot counters and live analytics # View counts, rankings, feature flags: frequent small updates plus analytics over their distributions. Partial updates with the ops operator list apply atomically; percentiles, histograms and composite aggregations summarize them without fighting the write rate.
When Pizza is not the fit # You need SQL-first analytics over immutable data lakes — Pizza is a mutable-data search engine, and SQL is a subset without JOIN across collections, subqueries, CTEs, or window functions (see Limitations). You need multi-namespace tenant grouping — tenancy is namespace-scoped 1:1 today.
title: Use cases

content:
Lesson 1 — First search # Start the node, index documents, run your first queries, and watch them update in real time.
The use case # Your application produces a stream of documents — logs, events, messages — and they are only useful if they are searchable the moment they land: no nightly batch, no refresh call, no second system to keep in sync. The questions this lesson answers:
“Did my document land — and can I find it right now?” — index and search in the same breath; that is Pizza’s core promise. “Can I try queries without running anything?” — the identical engine, compiled to WebAssembly, runs in the browser. “Prefer SQL?” — the same questions have SQL spellings; every lesson shows both front doors side by side. You need a running node — installation covers it in one command. With the node up, index your first document:
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"message": "hello pizza", "level": "info"}' \ http://localhost:28000/playground-logs/_doc There is no refresh call, no flush step — search for it in the same breath:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ http://localhost:28000/playground-logs/_search?q=pizza The document is already there. That is Pizza’s core promise: true real-time.
Now try the same query shape in the browser — this is the identical engine, compiled to WebAssembly, over the lesson dataset:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Prefer SQL? The same engine answers SQL statements — one MATCH, three rows, no server involved:
JavaScript is disabled — use the curl form of this example instead. Next: Lesson 2 — text search, or read the search reference for every query type.
title: Lesson 1 — First search

content:
